The site was submerged by the Nagarjunasagar reservoir; its monuments were moved to an island museum (1960s).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Decline of the Satavahanas.
outcomes: Followed by the Pallavas, Salankayanas and Vishnukundins in Andhra.
events.yearHook: About 225 CE, when the Satavahanas end. The Ikshvakus last about 100 years (about 225–325 CE).
events.before: The last great Satavahana king, **Yajna Sri Satakarni**, died around 200 CE. Their feudatories (vassal chiefs) in the Krishna valley took over. One of them, **Vasishthiputra Chamtamula**, started the Ikshvaku line at **Vijayapuri** (Nagarjunakonda).
events.after: Around 300–325 CE the Ikshvakus were overthrown by the **Pallavas** (and the Abhiras). Then small dynasties held Andhra: the **Salankayanas** at Vengi (the next event), the Brihatphalayanas and the Anandagotrikas. After them came the **Vishnukundins** (from about 420 CE).
events.today: When the **Nagarjunasagar dam** (finished 1967) flooded the valley, Nagarjunakonda's monuments were moved to an island museum in the lake. The dam and the town are named after **Acharya Nagarjuna**.
events.mnemonic: Ikshvaku kings in order: "Very Very Easy Ride" = Vasishthiputra Chamtamula, Virapurushadatta, Ehuvala Chamtamula, Rudrapurushadatta.

examAngle.point: The kings performed Vedic sacrifices, while the queens and princesses funded Buddhism: Chamtisiri (Chamtamula's sister) and Shantisri.
examAngle.context: One family, two faiths. The men did Vedic sacrifices such as the ashvamedha for royal glory; the women built monasteries. A lay woman devotee (**upasika**) named **Bodhisiri** also built many shrines.

examAngle.point: Virapurushadatta's reign was the golden age of Buddhism in Andhra. The last king was Rudrapurushadatta.
examAngle.context: Use the "Very Very Easy Ride" memory trick: Chamtamula, Virapurushadatta, Ehuvala Chamtamula, Rudrapurushadatta. The golden age is the second king, the end is the fourth.

examAngle.point: The Puranas call them "Sri Parvatiyas". They married into the Shaka (Western Kshatrapa) family of Ujjain. Their inscriptions do NOT claim descent from the Ikshvakus of Ayodhya.
examAngle.context: "Sri Parvata" is the Nagarjunakonda–Srisailam hill country. The name "Ikshvaku" sounds like the family of Rama of Ayodhya, but their own records never say so. APPSC tests exactly this.

examAngle.point: The Manchikallu inscription of Pallava Simhavarman (in Prakrit) shows that the Pallavas replaced the Ikshvakus at Vijayapuri.
examAngle.context: This is how we know the Ikshvaku line ended: the next inscription in their old land belongs to a Pallava king. The early Pallavas began in the Krishna region before they moved south to Kanchi.

examAngle.point: Acharya Nagarjuna founded the Madhyamika school, taught the Prajnaparamita ideas, and wrote the Suhrillekha ("letter to a friend") to a Satavahana king.
examAngle.context: Tradition links him with Nagarjunakonda. He lived in the late Satavahana age, and his ideas grew strong in the Ikshvaku monasteries. Madhyamika and Mahayana Buddhism later spread to Tibet, China and Japan.

events.title: Close of the Sangam Age; Kalabhra interregnum
events.summary: The Sangam age ends around 300 CE; the Kalabhras then rule the Tamil country until the Pallavas and Pandyas revive in the sixth century.
events.detail: The Tamil epics Silappadikaram (Ilango Adigal, about Kannagi and Kovalan) and Manimekalai belong to the post-Sangam period. The Kalabhra period is sometimes called a "dark age" because of few sources.
causes: Kalabhra invasion.
outcomes: Pallavas of Kanchi and Pandyas of Madurai rose later.
events.yearHook: About 300 CE: the Gupta empire begins soon after in the north (320 CE).
events.before: The Sangam kingdoms had been rich from trade, but Roman trade faded in the 3rd century CE.
events.after: The **Kalabhras** ruled for about 300 years (a "dark age" with few records). From the 6th century the **Pallavas** of Kanchi and the **Pandyas** of Madurai rose again.
events.today: Jain and Buddhist works such as the Tamil epics came from this post-Sangam time.

events.title: Chandragupta I founds the Gupta Empire
events.summary: Chandragupta I begins Gupta rule (c. 320 CE) (NCERT), marries the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi and takes the title Maharajadhiraja; the Gupta era starts in 319–320 CE.
events.detail: The Guptas began as a small family in the Ganga valley. Gold coins show Chandragupta I with Kumaradevi, showing the value of the Lichchhavi alliance. NCERT notes that Gupta history is built from literature, coins and inscriptions, including prashastis.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Marriage alliance with the Lichchhavis.
outcomes: Samudragupta's conquests (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 320 CE: the Gupta era begins. About 90 years after the Kushana decline (230 CE).
events.before: After the Kushanas faded (about 230 CE), the north was split among small kingdoms and republics (Nagas, Yaudheyas, Malavas). **Sri Gupta** and **Ghatotkacha** were minor chiefs in Magadha.
events.after: **Chandragupta I** married **Kumaradevi**, a Lichchhavi princess; coins show the royal couple. His son **Samudragupta** (335 CE) built the empire (next event).
events.today: The Gupta era (from 320 CE) was used in north Indian inscriptions for centuries.
events.mnemonic: Gupta kings "S-G-C-S-C-K-S": Sri Gupta, Ghatotkacha, Chandragupta I, Samudragupta, Chandragupta II, Kumaragupta I, Skandagupta. "Some Good Clever Scholars Can Keep Secrets".

events.title: Samudragupta; Allahabad Prashasti
events.summary: Samudragupta (c. 335–375 CE) conquers widely; his court poet Harisena records it in the Prayaga prashasti on the Allahabad pillar (NCERT).
events.detail:
NCERT quotes the prashasti: he uprooted the kings of Aryavarta, captured and then freed twelve rulers of Dakshinapatha (including Vishnugopa of Kanchi and kings in coastal Andhra such as Hastivarman of Vengi), made forest kings his servants, and took tribute from frontier states and the Shakas and Kushanas.

His coins show him playing the veena. The same pillar has an Ashokan edict and a Jahangir inscription. V.A. Smith called him the "Napoleon of India".
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Gupta ambition to unify the north.
gains: Aryavarta annexed; the south made tributary.
outcomes: Gupta empire at its height.
facts: Prayaga prashasti by Harisena (NCERT).
Kings of Dakshinapatha were captured and released (grahana-moksha-anugraha).
Gupta founders: Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha before Chandragupta I.
events.yearHook: About 335 CE: 15 years after the Gupta era begins (320).

participants.role: The same pillar carries his edict.
His inscription is on the same pillar.

events.before: **Chandragupta I** (320 CE) left a kingdom in Magadha and the middle Ganga plain.
events.after: Samudragupta's son **Chandragupta II** (375 CE) married into the **Vakataka** family and ended the Shaka rule in the west (next event).
events.today: The **Allahabad (Prayagraj) pillar** carries Ashoka's edicts, Samudragupta's prashasti by **Harishena**, and later a Jahangir inscription — three kings on one pillar.
events.mnemonic: Prayaga prashasti lists: "uprooted in the north (Aryavarta), freed in the south (Dakshinapatha), tribute from the borders".

examAngle.point: Samudragupta defeated and restored southern kings, including Hastivarman of Vengi and Vishnugopa of Kanchi; V. A. Smith called him the "Napoleon of India".
examAngle.context: The south was not annexed: kings were captured and set free (grahana-moksha-anugraha). Two of them ruled in Andhra (Vengi) and near it (Kanchi). His coins show him playing the veena.

events.title: Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya)
events.summary: Chandragupta II Vikramaditya (c. 375–415 CE) (NCERT) ends Shaka rule in western India; Kalidasa, Fa-Hien's visit and the Mehrauli iron pillar belong to his age.
events.detail:
He defeated the last Western Kshatrapa and took Gujarat with its ports, issuing silver coins. His daughter Prabhavati married the Vakataka king, securing the Deccan (NCERT notes the Vakatakas c. 375–415 CE).

The Mehrauli iron pillar, which has not rusted, records a king Chandra. By tradition nine gems (navaratnas) — Kalidasa, Amarasimha, Varahamihira, Dhanvantari and others — adorned his court.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Shaka control of the western coast.
gains: Gujarat, Saurashtra and Malwa.
outcomes: Gupta "golden age" of art and literature.
events.yearHook: 375–415 CE (NCERT). Fa-Hien visits in his reign (about 405).

participants.role: One of the nine gems, by tradition.

facts: Gupta administration: bhukti (province), vishaya (district), vithi, grama; shrenis (guilds); gold coins called dinaras.
Sultanganj Buddha (copper) is a Gupta masterpiece; Devichandragupta (Vishakhadatta) tells of Ramagupta.
events.before: **Samudragupta** (335 CE) had built the empire; the Shaka **Western Kshatrapas** still ruled Gujarat and Malwa.
events.after: He married his daughter **Prabhavati Gupta** to the **Vakataka** king, defeated the Shakas (about 400 CE) and won the western ports. His son **Kumaragupta I** (415 CE) founded **Nalanda**.
events.today: The **Mehrauli iron pillar** (Delhi), probably of his time, has not rusted for about 1,600 years.
events.mnemonic: Chandragupta II = "Vikramaditya, Vakataka in-law, Vanquisher of Shakas".

examAngle.point: Gupta guilds (shrenis) were self-governing: they had their own seals and coins, kept armed bands and worked as bankers.
examAngle.context: Seals of guilds found at Vaishali and Bhita prove it. Guilds are a thread running from the Satavahanas (deposits at 12%) to the Guptas.

events.title: Fa-Hien travels through Gupta India
events.summary: The Chinese monk Fa-Hien travels in India (c. 399–414 CE) in Chandragupta II's reign, collecting Buddhist texts, and describes a peaceful, prosperous land.
events.detail: He came overland through Central Asia and returned by sea via Sri Lanka. He noted free hospitals in Pataliputra, light taxes, and that Chandalas (untouchables) lived outside towns and had to strike a piece of wood to announce themselves.
causes: Search for Buddhist texts.
outcomes: His record is a key source for the Guptas.
events.yearHook: About 405 CE (he travelled 399–414). Xuanzang came about 225 years later (630).
events.before: Buddhism had spread to China along the Silk Road (Fourth Council, about 100 CE). Chinese monks wanted true copies of the Vinaya texts.
events.after: His book **Fo-kuo-ki** ("Record of Buddhist Kingdoms") praised the peace and mild punishments of Gupta India, but also described the **Chandalas**, who lived outside towns and struck a wooden clapper to warn others — early proof of untouchability.
events.today: He also visited Sri Lanka and sailed home through Java; his book is used by historians worldwide.
events.mnemonic: Chinese pilgrims in order "F-X-I": Fa-Hien (405, Guptas), Xuanzang (630, Harsha), I-tsing (about 671, Nalanda).

events.title: Vishnukundins rule coastal Andhra
events.summary: The Vishnukundins rule coastal Andhra and Telangana (c. 420–620 CE); Madhava Varma I makes them powerful, and they build the Undavalli and Mogalrajapuram cave temples.
events.detail: They worshipped Sri Parvata Swami (Srisailam) and performed Vedic sacrifices. Capitals included Indrapalanagara (Nalgonda) and later Amarapura/Denduluru. The Undavalli caves near Vijayawada have a reclining Vishnu. They were overthrown by the Badami Chalukya Pulakeshin II, whose brother founded the Eastern Chalukya line in Vengi (624 CE).
causes: Decline of the Ikshvakus and Salankayanas.
outcomes: Replaced by the Eastern Chalukyas (624 CE).
events.yearHook: About 420 CE to 624 CE. They end the year Pulakeshin II takes Vengi (624).
events.before: After the Salankayanas and Samudragupta's raid, the **Vishnukundins** rose in the hills of Telangana (capital **Indrapalanagara**, Nalgonda) and spread down to coastal Andhra.
events.after: **Pulakeshin II** of Badami defeated them. In 624 CE he gave Vengi to his brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana**. That began the **Eastern Chalukyas**, who made Telugu a language of the court. That is the start of lesson 2.
events.today: The **Undavalli caves** (near Vijayawada, on the Krishna) with a 5-metre reclining Vishnu, and the **Mogalrajapuram caves** in Vijayawada, are open to visitors.
events.mnemonic: Vishnukundins = "V to V": they begin in the hills of Telangana and end at Vengi.

examAngle.point: Madhava Varma had the title "Janasraya" and moved the capital from Amarapuri to Denduluru.
examAngle.context: Denduluru is near Eluru, close to old Vengi. The move brought the kingdom down from the hills to the rich delta.

examAngle.point: They issued iron coins with a thin coating of copper, often with a lion on them.
examAngle.context: Such coated coins are rare in India. The lion was their royal emblem.

examAngle.point: Historian N. Venkataramanaiah identified their family god, "Sri Parvata Swami", with the Buddha.
examAngle.context: Most historians see Sri Parvata Swami as **Shiva of Srisailam**. But APPSC 2018 keyed Venkataramanaiah's view. Learn both: Shiva is the usual view; the Buddha is his view.

events.title: Nalanda Mahavihara flourishes
events.summary: Kumaragupta I founds the Buddhist monastery-university at Nalanda (c. 427 CE); it later draws students from China, Korea and Tibet.
events.detail: Xuanzang studied there under Shilabhadra and said it had 10,000 students and teachers. It was supported by the revenue of many villages. Harsha and the Pala kings patronised it. Bakhtiyar Khalji destroyed it about 1193. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
causes: Gupta patronage of learning.
outcomes: Asia's greatest centre of Buddhist learning.
events.yearHook: About 427 CE under the Gupta king Kumaragupta I; destroyed about 1193 — some 750 years of learning.
events.before: Monasteries had been places of study since the Mauryan age. Under the **Guptas** large monastery-universities grew with land grants from kings.
events.after: Harsha (7th century) and the **Pala** kings of Bengal (8th–12th century) supported it; the Palas also founded **Vikramashila**. **Bakhtiyar Khalji** destroyed both about 1193, which hastened Buddhism's decline.
events.today: The ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2016). A new Nalanda University opened nearby at Rajgir (2014).

events.title: Skandagupta repels Hunas; Gupta decline
events.summary: Skandagupta (c. 455–467 CE) repels the first Huna invasion, but after him the Gupta empire declines through Huna attacks, weak rulers and rising feudatories.
events.detail: His Bhitari pillar records the Huna war; his Junagadh inscription records repairs to the Sudarshana lake. Toramana and Mihirakula later took the north-west. Feudatories such as the Maukharis of Kanauj and the Maitrakas of Valabhi broke away. Gupta rule ended about 550 CE.
causes: Huna invasions.
Rise of feudatories.
outcomes: Regional kingdoms; later Harsha united the north.
events.yearHook: About 455 CE: Skandagupta pushes back the Hunas. The Guptas fade by about 550 CE.

participants.role: Huna king who took the north-west.

events.before: **Kumaragupta I** (415–455 CE) ruled a peaceful empire, but the **Hunas** (White Huns) from Central Asia were pressing on the north-west.
events.after: Huna leaders **Toramana** and **Mihirakula** took the north-west and Malwa; **Yashodharman** of Malwa beat Mihirakula (about 528 CE). Feudatories such as the **Maukharis**, **Maitrakas** and later Guptas broke away.
events.today: Skandagupta's **Junagadh inscription** records his repair of the Sudarshana lake, the same lake Rudradaman had repaired 300 years before.

events.title: Pulakeshin I founds the Chalukyas of Badami
events.summary: Pulakeshin I founds the Chalukya dynasty of Badami (Vatapi) in Karnataka (c. 543 CE) (NCERT notes the rise of the Chalukyas c. 500–600 CE).
events.detail: He performed the ashvamedha and fortified Vatapi. His successors Kirtivarman I and Mangalesha expanded the kingdom; the cave temples of Badami were cut under them. Pulakeshin II became the greatest king.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Decline of the Vakatakas and Kadambas.
outcomes: Chalukya–Pallava rivalry.
events.yearHook: About 543 CE: Pulakeshin I performs the ashvamedha and fortifies Vatapi (Badami).
events.before: In the Deccan, after the Vakatakas and Kadambas, local chiefs rose. **Pulakeshin I** made **Vatapi** (Badami, Karnataka) a fort-capital.
events.after: His grandson **Pulakeshin II** (from about 610) beat Harsha on the Narmada (about 634) and placed his brother **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** at **Vengi** (624), the start of the Eastern Chalukyas of Andhra.
events.today: Badami cave temples, Aihole and **Pattadakal** (UNESCO) show Chalukya art.
events.mnemonic: Three Chalukya houses: "Badami (543), Vengi (624, Eastern), Kalyani (973, Western/later)".

events.title: Aihole–Badami temple architecture
events.summary: The Chalukyas build early stone temples at Aihole, Badami and Pattadakal; Aihole is called the "cradle of Indian temple architecture".
events.detail: The Lad Khan and Durga temples at Aihole are experiments in temple form. Pattadakal (UNESCO) has temples in both northern (nagara) and southern (dravida) styles; the Virupaksha temple was built by queen Lokamahadevi. In Kanchi the Pallava Mahendravarman I began rock-cut temples.
causes: Chalukya and Pallava patronage.
outcomes: Nagara and dravida styles developed side by side.
events.yearHook: About 600 CE; the Aihole inscription is 634 CE.
facts: Meguti Jain temple, Aihole, carries the Aihole inscription (634 CE).
Temple styles: Nagara (north), Dravidian (south, with vimana), Vesara (mixed, Deccan).
events.before: The Guptas had built the first stone temples in the north (about 400–500 CE).
events.after: At **Pattadakal** (8th century) the Chalukyas built Nagara and Dravida temples side by side; the Virupaksha temple there copies the Pallava Kailasanatha of Kanchi.
events.today: Aihole is called "the cradle of Indian temple architecture"; its Durga temple has an apsidal (rounded) back.

events.title: Harshavardhana ascends; capital at Kanauj
events.summary: Harshavardhana becomes king of Thanesar and Kanauj (606 CE) (NCERT) after his brother Rajyavardhana is killed; his reign is described by Banabhatta and Xuanzang.
events.detail:
His sister Rajyashri had married the Maukhari king of Kanauj, who was killed by the king of Malwa; Rajyavardhana was then killed by Shashanka of Gauda. Harsha rescued Rajyashri and made Kanauj his capital.

The Harshacharita of Banabhatta is a biography in Sanskrit (NCERT). Harsha wrote the plays Ratnavali, Nagananda and Priyadarshika. The Harsha era begins in 606 CE.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Murder of his brother by Shashanka.
outcomes: Harsha ruled much of the north for 41 years.
events.yearHook: 606 CE: the Harsha era begins. He rules 41 years (606–647).
facts: Harsha was a Vardhana (Pushyabhuti); ally of Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa (Assam).
Administration: bhukti (province), vishaya (district), grama (village); tax bali and bhaga.
Harsha sent an embassy to China (c. 641); traditionally his first campaigns c. 618–619 CE.
events.before: After the Hunas, the **Pushyabhutis** of Thanesar rose. Harsha's elder brother **Rajyavardhana** was killed by **Shashanka** of Gauda (Bengal), and his sister **Rajyashri** was widowed when the Maukhari king of Kanauj was killed.
events.after: Harsha moved the capital to **Kanauj**, tried to conquer the south, and was checked by **Pulakeshin II** on the Narmada (about 634). The Chinese pilgrim **Xuanzang** came to his court (about 630).
events.today: Kanauj became the prize of north India for 300 years (the tripartite struggle of the Palas, Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas).
events.mnemonic: Harsha's plays "N-R-P": Nagananda, Ratnavali, Priyadarshika. Bana's books "H-K": Harshacharita, Kadambari.

events.title: Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi in Andhra
events.summary: Pulakeshin II conquers Vengi in coastal Andhra and makes his brother Kubja Vishnuvardhana its ruler (624 CE), founding the Eastern Chalukya dynasty that rules for about 450 years.
events.detail: The capital moved from Pishtapura (Pithapuram) to Vengi and later Rajamahendravaram (Rajahmundry). The Eastern Chalukyas fought the Rashtrakutas and later allied with the Cholas by marriage. Telugu literature began under Rajaraja Narendra with Nannaya's Mahabharata (11th century).
causes: Pulakeshin II's conquest of the Vishnukundin lands.
outcomes: Eastern Chalukya rule; merger with the Cholas (Chalukya-Cholas, 1070).
events.yearHook: 624 CE: two years after the Hijra (622), the start of the Islamic calendar. The Eastern Chalukyas rule Vengi for about 450 years (to 1076).

participants.role: Poet at the Eastern Chalukya court.

facts: Vijayaditya II is said to have built 108 Saiva temples; Vijayaditya III developed Kandukuru on the lines of Bezawada (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
The early Chalukyas worshipped the mother-goddess Hariti; the Kapalikas emerged from the Misra Saivam school (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
events.before: The **Vishnukundins** (about 420–624) ruled coastal Andhra. **Pulakeshin II** of Badami (about 610–642) conquered Vengi.
events.after: The Eastern Chalukyas ruled Vengi for about 450 years, fighting the **Rashtrakutas** and making marriage ties with the **Cholas**. Under **Rajaraja Narendra**, **Nannaya** began the Telugu Mahabharatam (about 1050). In 1070 **Kulottunga I** united Vengi with the Chola empire.
events.today: **Draksharama** (Bhimeswara, one of the Pancharama Kshetras), **Biccavole** and **Penugonda** temples belong to this age. Vengi is Pedavegi near Eluru.
events.mnemonic: Eastern Chalukya kings to remember "K-V-V-R-R": Kubja Vishnuvardhana (founder), Vijayaditya II (108 temples), Vijayaditya III (Gunaga), Rajaraja Narendra (Nannaya), Rajendra (Kulottunga I).

examAngle.point: The Eastern Chalukyas get the credit for making Telugu a language of administration and literature: Telugu inscriptions multiply (Addanki, Dharmavaram) and Nannaya wrote under Rajaraja Narendra.
examAngle.context: Kalamalla (about 575) was the first full Telugu inscription, but it was a Renati Chola record. Under the Eastern Chalukyas Telugu became normal in royal records and then in poetry. The **Addanki** inscription of **Pandaranga** (Gunaga Vijayaditya's general) has the first Telugu verse (**taruvoja** metre).

examAngle.point: Royal marriages with the Cholas: Vimaladitya married Kundavai (daughter of Rajaraja Chola I); Rajaraja Narendra married Ammangadevi (daughter of Rajendra Chola I); Rajendra Chalukya (Kulottunga I) married Madhurantaki (daughter of Rajendra Chola II).
examAngle.context: Three generations of marriages bound Vengi to the Cholas. That is why the son of such a marriage, **Kulottunga I**, could take the Chola throne itself in 1070.

examAngle.point: Temples: Vijayaditya II is credited with 108 temples; Chalukya Bhima built the Bhimeswara Swamy temple at Draksharama; the Rajarajeswara temple at Biccavole was NOT built by Rajaraja Narendra. Draksharama shows a Chalukya-Chola style with Pallava and early Chalukya touches.
examAngle.context: The Eastern Chalukyas were Shaiva builders. The **Pancharama** temples (Amaravati, Draksharama, Bhimavaram, Palakollu, Samalkota) are linked with them.

examAngle.point: Religion and culture: Pulakeshin II's Marturu inscription calls Mangalagiri "Mangalapura"; Chellavva got the title "Gandharva-Vidya-Visarada"; Ugradityacharya wrote the medical book Kalyanakaraka; Ayyana Mahadevi, queen of Kubja Vishnuvardhana, built the Jain temple Nedumba Vasati near Vijayawada; Penugonda is the seat of goddess Vasavi (Kanyaka Parameswari).
examAngle.context: APPSC asks many small "who built or wrote what" points about this age. Group them: Jainism (Nedumba Vasati), Shaivism (108 temples, Kapalikas from Misra Shaivism), goddess cults (Hariti, Vasavi), learning (Kalyanakaraka) and music (Chellavva).

events.title: Hiuen Tsang at Harsha's court
events.summary: Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) travels in India (c. 629–645 CE) in search of Buddhist texts (NCERT), studies at Nalanda and writes the Si-yu-ki (Records of the Western World).
events.detail: He visited Harsha's court, attended the assemblies at Kanauj and Prayaga (643 CE), visited Pulakeshin II's kingdom, Kanchi and Andhra, including Dhanyakataka (Amaravati), where he found Buddhism declining. He returned with 657 texts.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Search for Buddhist texts (NCERT).
outcomes: Si-yu-ki is a major source for 7th-century India.
events.yearHook: About 630–644 CE: he spends about 14 years in India.
facts: Xuanzang travelled 629/630–643/645 CE.
I-Tsing (Yijing) visited 671–695 CE and studied at Nalanda.
Later Chinese visitors: Ma Huan with Zheng He's fleets (15th century).
events.before: Xuanzang left China in 629 to collect Buddhist texts. **Fa-Hien** had come about 225 years earlier (405).
events.after: He studied at **Nalanda** under **Shilabhadra**, attended Harsha's **Kanauj** and **Prayag** assemblies, and took 657 texts back to China. His book is the **Si-yu-ki** ("Records of the Western World").
events.today: The Nalanda museum has a Xuanzang memorial hall. His journey inspired the Chinese novel "Journey to the West".

events.title: Pulakeshin II checks Harsha on the Narmada
events.summary: Pulakeshin II stops Harsha on the banks of the Narmada; the Aihole inscription (634 CE), written by Ravikirti, records the victory (NCERT).
events.detail: Harsha, "lord of the north" (Uttarapathapati), tried to expand south. Pulakeshin II, "lord of the south" (Dakshinapathapati), defeated him; Ravikirti says Harsha's joy melted away when he saw his elephants fall. The Narmada became the boundary between the two.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: Harsha's southern expansion.
losses: Harsha's army and elephants.
outcomes: Narmada fixed as the frontier.
facts: Aihole inscription by Ravikirti, dated 634 CE (NCERT).
events.yearHook: About 634 CE (Aihole inscription, "6-3-4"); the battle itself is placed about 618–634.
events.before: **Harsha** (606 CE) ruled the north and wanted the Deccan. **Pulakeshin II** of Badami ruled the Deccan and had taken Vengi (624).
events.after: The **Narmada** became the border between north and south. Pulakeshin II was later killed when the Pallava **Narasimhavarman I** sacked Vatapi (642).
events.today: The **Aihole inscription** was written by the Jain poet **Ravikirti**; it records the win. Pulakeshin II also sent an embassy to the Persian king Khusrau II.

events.title: Pallava Narasimhavarman I sacks Vatapi
events.summary: The Pallava king Narasimhavarman I defeats and kills Pulakeshin II and captures Vatapi (642 CE), taking the title "Vatapikonda".
events.detail: Mahendravarman I had lost land to Pulakeshin II. His son Narasimhavarman I, called Mamalla, took revenge with the help of the Sri Lankan prince Manavarma. He built the monolithic rathas (Pancha Rathas) at Mamallapuram (Mahabalipuram). The Chalukyas recovered under Vikramaditya I.
causes: Chalukya–Pallava rivalry; Pulakeshin II's earlier victories.
losses: Pulakeshin II killed; Vatapi sacked.
outcomes: Pallava supremacy for 13 years.
events.yearHook: 642 CE: eight years after the Aihole inscription (634).

participants.role: His father, who had lost to Pulakeshin.

events.before: Pulakeshin II had beaten **Mahendravarman I** of Kanchi (about 610–630).
events.after: Narasimhavarman I took the title **Vatapikonda** ("conqueror of Vatapi"). The Chalukyas recovered under **Vikramaditya I**, and the Pallava–Chalukya wars went on for a century until the **Rashtrakutas** replaced the Chalukyas (753).
events.today: Mamallapuram, named after Narasimhavarman I (Mamalla), is a UNESCO site.

events.title: Death of Harsha; his empire disintegrates
events.summary: Harsha dies in 647 CE without an heir; his empire breaks up, and Kanauj becomes the prize for which later dynasties fight.
events.detail: In 643 CE Harsha held a great assembly at Kanauj in honour of Xuanzang and a quinquennial gift-giving at Prayaga, where he gave away his wealth. After his death a minister seized the throne; the tripartite struggle for Kanauj followed in the 8th century.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History I, Ch. 2 "Kings, Farmers and Towns"
causes: No heir.
outcomes: Political fragmentation of the north; later the tripartite struggle.

alsoOn.text: Harsha holds assemblies at Kanauj and Prayaga in honour of Xuanzang.

events.yearHook: 647 CE: 41 years after he came to the throne (606).
events.before: Harsha had ruled a large but loose empire held together by feudatories.
events.after: His empire broke up at once. From the 8th century the **Palas**, **Pratiharas** and **Rashtrakutas** fought for **Kanauj** (the tripartite struggle) — the start of the medieval chapter.
events.today: The year 647 is used as the line between "ancient" and "early medieval" India in many books.

events.title: Rashtrakutas dominate the Deccan
events.summary: Dantidurga overthrows the Chalukyas of Badami and founds the Rashtrakuta dynasty (c. 753 CE) (NCERT); Krishna I builds the Kailasa temple at Ellora.
events.detail:
NCERT notes that Dantidurga, a Chalukya subordinate, performed the hiranyagarbha ("golden womb") ritual so that he would be "reborn" a Kshatriya. Rashtrakuta capital later moved to Manyakheta.

Krishna I carved the Kailasanatha temple at Ellora out of a single rock. Amoghavarsha I wrote the Kavirajamarga, the earliest Kannada work on poetics. The Rashtrakutas fought the Palas and Pratiharas for Kanauj and the Eastern Chalukyas for Vengi.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Weak later Chalukyas.
outcomes: A Deccan power for 200 years; replaced by the Chalukyas of Kalyani (973).
events.yearHook: 753: Dantidurga overthrows the Badami Chalukyas. Rashtrakutas 753–973, about 220 years.
events.before: The **Badami Chalukyas** (from 543) were worn out by the long wars with the Pallavas.
events.after: The Rashtrakutas joined the **tripartite struggle** for Kanauj. In 973 **Tailapa II** overthrew them and founded the **Chalukyas of Kalyani**.
events.today: Malkhed (Manyakheta, Karnataka) was their capital.
events.mnemonic: Rashtrakuta kings "D-K-A-K": Dantidurga (founder), Krishna I (Ellora Kailasa), Amoghavarsha I (Kavirajamarga), Krishna III (beat the Cholas at Takkolam, 949).

examAngle.point: Krishna I (not Krishna III) built the Kailasa temple at Ellora. Amoghavarsha I wrote the Kavirajamarga, the first Kannada book on poetics. The Arab Al-Masudi called the Rashtrakuta king "Vallabharaja" (Balhara).
examAngle.context: Two Krishnas, two jobs: **Krishna I** built (Ellora, about 760); **Krishna III** fought (Takkolam, 949). Amoghavarsha I was also a Jain patron.

examAngle.point: Ellora caves in order of building: Dashavatara (cave 15), Ravan ki Khai, Dumar Lena, then the Kailasa. Ellora has Buddhist (1–12), Hindu (13–29) and Jain (30–34) caves.
examAngle.context: The Kailasa (cave 16) was carved last among these because it needed the greatest skill.

events.title: Tripartite struggle for Kanauj
events.summary: The Gurjara-Pratiharas, Rashtrakutas and Palas fight for control of Kanauj in the Ganga valley for about 200 years — the "tripartite struggle" (NCERT).
events.detail:
Kanauj had been Harsha's capital and was the symbol of power in the north. NCERT explains that the three dynasties fought for it over centuries. The Pala Dharmapala placed his nominee there; the Pratihara Nagabhata II captured it (c. 816); the Rashtrakutas raided the north several times.

The Pratiharas, under Mihira Bhoja, finally held Kanauj and also stopped the Arabs of Sind. The long war exhausted all three.
causes: Prestige and wealth of Kanauj (NCERT).
outcomes: All three weakened; regional Rajput kingdoms rose.
events.yearHook: About 800 to 950: about 150 years of war for Kanauj.
facts: Pratihara kings: Vatsaraja, Nagabhata II, Mihira Bhoja; they claimed the Agnikula myth (born from fire).
Other Rajput kingdoms: Paramaras (Bhoja built Bhojeshwar temple), Chaulukyas/Solankis (Bhimadeva I faced Mahmud), Gahadavalas of Kannauj (Jaichandra), Tomaras of Delhi (Dhillika, Lal Kot).
Dharmapala called himself Sakalottarapathanatha (lord of the north); he founded Vikramshila.
events.before: After Harsha (647) **Kanauj** on the Ganga was the symbol of power over north India.
events.after: All three powers were weakened. In the north the **Rajput** kingdoms rose; in the south the **Cholas** grew strong.
events.today: Kanauj (UP) is now known for perfume (attar).

events.title: Imperial Cholas rise; Rajaraja I
events.summary: Rajaraja I becomes Chola king (985), builds a navy, conquers Sri Lanka and the Maldives, and builds the Brihadeshvara temple at Thanjavur (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Cholas rose from Uraiyur when Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur (mid-9th century) (NCERT). Rajaraja I was the most powerful early Chola ruler and reorganised the administration (NCERT).

Chola villages were run by sabhas (brahmana assemblies) and urs (non-brahmana villages); the Uttaramerur inscriptions describe how sabha members were chosen by lot (NCERT). Chola bronzes, such as the Nataraja, are world famous (NCERT).
causes: Chola conquest of the Kaveri delta (NCERT).
outcomes: Chola empire across the south and Sri Lanka.
Brihadeshvara temple (1010) (NCERT).
facts: Uttaramerur inscriptions describe the sabha (NCERT).
Chola bronzes made by the lost-wax technique (NCERT).
Land grants: brahmadeya (to brahmanas), devadana (to temples), shalabhoga, vellanvagai.
Village assemblies chose members by kudavolai (pot-ticket lots) and worked through variyams (committees).
Dravidian temples have a tall vimana over the shrine; Brihadeeswara (Thanjavur); Nataraja bronzes are a high point of Dravidian art.
Chola village terms: variyam = committee; kudumba = ward; kudavolai = lottery system; perumakkal = member of the village assembly (APPSC Group-1 key).
events.yearHook: 985: Rajaraja I takes the throne. The imperial Cholas run from Vijayalaya (850) to about 1279.
events.before: **Vijayalaya** (850) took Thanjavur; **Parantaka I** (907–955) took Madurai and recorded village self-rule at **Uttaramerur** (about 920).
events.after: Rajaraja I built the **Brihadishvara** temple (1010) and took the Maldives and north Sri Lanka. **Rajendra I** marched to the Ganga (Gangaikondachola) and sent a navy to **Srivijaya** (1025).
events.today: The Chola bronzes (Nataraja) and temples are world-famous; the Chola navy is studied by the Indian Navy.
events.mnemonic: Chola kings "V-P-R-R-K": Vijayalaya (founder, 850), Parantaka I (Madurai), Rajaraja I (985), Rajendra I (Ganga and Srivijaya), Kulottunga I (Vengi union, 1070).

examAngle.point: The imperial Cholas were founded by Vijayalaya, not Parantaka I; Parantaka I was "Maduraikondan" (conqueror of Madurai); Rajaraja I conquered the Maldives; Rajendra I built Gangaikonda Cholapuram.
examAngle.context: Match each king to one deed and one title. Rajaraja I = Mummadi Chola and Thanjavur; Rajendra I = Gangaikonda, Kadaram-konda (Srivijaya), Pandita Chola.

events.title: Tirumala–Tirupati temple tradition
events.summary: The Venkateswara temple at Tirumala grows into a great pilgrimage centre, patronised by the Pallavas, Cholas, Telugu Chodas and later Vijayanagara kings.
events.detail: Inscriptions from Pallava queen Samavai (966 CE) record gifts. Ramanuja is said to have organised the worship. Krishnadevaraya visited seven times and placed statues of himself and his queens there. Annamacharya wrote thousands of kirtanas on Venkateswara. TTD now administers it.
causes: Royal and popular patronage.
outcomes: One of the world's most visited shrines.
events.yearHook: About 1000: the shrine was already old; a Pallava queen gave its silver image in 966.
events.before: The **Alvars** had sung of Venkatam hill; **Ramanuja** is said to have set the worship rules.
events.after: **Annamacharya** (15th century) sang to the god; **Krishnadevaraya** gave gold and stands in copper statues with his queens. The **Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams** (TTD) took over management in 1932.
events.today: The Tirupati **laddu** got a GI tag (2009); Tirumala is one of the world's most visited shrines.
events.mnemonic: Tirumala patrons by age "P-C-V-T": Pallavas (Samavai, 966), Cholas, Vijayanagara (Krishnadevaraya visited about seven times), TTD (1932).

events.title: Mahmud of Ghazni raids Somnath
events.summary: Mahmud of Ghazni raids the subcontinent 17 times between 1000 and 1025 (NCERT); in 1025 he plunders the Somnath temple in Gujarat.
events.detail:
Mahmud ruled from Ghazni in Afghanistan. His targets were wealthy temples, including Somnath (NCERT). He used the wealth to build a splendid capital at Ghazni. He defeated the Hindushahi ruler Jayapala (1001) and Anandapala.

He was interested in learning about the people he conquered and asked Al-Biruni to write an account of the subcontinent (NCERT).
causes: Plunder of temple wealth (NCERT).
course: 1000: first raid.
1001: defeats Jayapala near Peshawar.
1018: Mathura and Kanauj.
1025: Somnath (NCERT).
losses: Temples plundered; Somnath destroyed.
outcomes: Punjab became a Ghaznavid province.
Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1025: the same year the Chola Rajendra I sends his navy to Srivijaya.
events.before: The **Arabs** had taken Sind (712). In Afghanistan the Turkish slave general **Alptigin** founded Ghazni; his successor **Sabuktigin** fought the Hindushahi king **Jayapala**.
events.after: Punjab stayed a Ghaznavid province with Lahore as its centre. About 150 years later **Muhammad Ghori** (Ghurid) came to conquer and rule (Tarain, 1191–92).
events.today: The Somnath temple was rebuilt after Independence (1951) with the help of Sardar Patel and K. M. Munshi.
events.mnemonic: "17 raids, 1000 to 1025": Mahmud came 17 times in 25 years to loot, never to stay.

examAngle.point: Al-Biruni came with Mahmud and wrote Kitab-ul-Hind (Tahqiq-i-Hind) in Arabic; Firdausi, the Persian poet of the Shahnama, was at Mahmud's court.
examAngle.context: Mahmud is remembered for loot, but his court had two great writers. Al-Biruni learnt Sanskrit and described Indian science and society; he complained that Indians were proud and did not share knowledge.

events.title: Nannaya begins the Telugu Mahabharatam
events.summary: At the request of the Eastern Chalukya king Rajaraja Narendra, Nannaya begins the Telugu Mahabharata at Rajahmundry (11th century), starting Telugu literature.
events.detail: Nannaya, called the "Adikavi", translated the Adi and Sabha parvas and part of the Aranya parva. He also wrote Andhra Shabda Chintamani, the first Telugu grammar (in Sanskrit). Rajaraja Narendra ruled from Rajamahendravaram.
causes: Royal patronage of Telugu.
outcomes: Tikkana and Errana completed the work (Kavitrayam).
events.yearHook: About 1050: 1,000 years ago. Kavitrayam "N-T-E": Nannaya (1050), Tikkana (1260), Errana (1350).
facts: Pavuluri Mallana wrote "Sarasangraha Ganitam", a mathematical work in Telugu (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

The Nandampudi grant of Rajaraja Narendra (1053) is the evidence that Narayana Bhatta assisted Nannaya in translating the Mahabharata; it was composed by Nannaya himself (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).
events.before: Telugu was used in inscriptions from **Kalamalla** (575); Rajaraja Narendra of Vengi wanted a Telugu Bharata for his court at **Rajahmundry**.
events.after: Nannaya finished the **Adi** and **Sabha** parvas and part of the **Aranya** parva. **Tikkana** wrote 15 parvas (Virata to the end) at Nellore; **Errana** finished the Aranya parva under the Reddis.
events.today: Adikavi Nannaya University (Rajamahendravaram, 2006) is named after him.
events.mnemonic: Kavitrayam titles "A-K-P": Nannaya Adi Kavi (and Vagnusasana), Tikkana Kavi Brahma, Errana Prabandha Parameswara.

examAngle.point: Nannaya wrote the Andhra Mahabharatam and the Andhra Shabda Chintamani (a Sanskrit grammar of Telugu); the Nandampudi grant of Rajaraja Narendra (1053), composed by Nannaya, shows Narayana Bhatta helped him.
examAngle.context: Two other early Telugu writers are also asked: **Pavuluri Mallana** (Ganitasara Sangraham, mathematics) and, much later, **Vinukonda Vallabharaya** (Kreedabhiramam, 15th century, a play on Warangal city life).

events.title: Simhachalam & Andhra temple architecture
events.summary: The Varaha-Lakshmi Narasimha temple at Simhachalam near Visakhapatnam is rebuilt in the Kalinga style; the Eastern Ganga king Narasimhadeva I adds to it (13th century).
events.detail: Inscriptions go back to the 11th century (Kulottunga I). The Eastern Gangas of Kalinga, who built Konark, rebuilt it; Krishnadevaraya visited after his Kalinga campaign (1516). The deity is covered in sandal paste except on Akshaya Tritiya (Chandanotsavam).
causes: Royal patronage.
outcomes: Major Vaishnava shrine of north coastal Andhra.
events.yearHook: Main rebuilding in the 13th century by Narasimhadeva I (1268 inscription), the same king who built Konark (about 1250).

participants.role: Earliest inscriptions date from his reign.

events.before: North coastal Andhra was ruled by the **Eastern Gangas** of Kalinga (Odisha), so its temples are in the Kalinga (Odisha) style.
events.after: **Krishnadevaraya** visited after defeating the Gajapatis (1516) and gave rich gifts.
events.today: Once a year at **Chandanotsavam** (Akshaya Tritiya) the sandal-paste cover is removed and the true image is shown.

events.title: Kakatiyas assert independence at Warangal
events.summary: The Kakatiya chief Rudradeva declares independence from the Chalukyas of Kalyani (c. 1163); the Anumakonda inscription records it, and he builds the Thousand Pillar temple.
events.detail: The Kakatiyas began as feudatories at Anumakonda (Hanamkonda). Prola II resisted the Chalukyas; his son Rudradeva (Prataparudra I) became independent and began the Warangal fort. The Kakatiyas brought the Telugu lands under one rule for the first time and built thousands of tanks for irrigation.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Decline of the Kalyani Chalukyas.
outcomes: Kakatiya kingdom until 1323.
events.yearHook: 1163: the Anumakonda inscription; 29 years before Tarain-2 (1192). Kakatiyas rule 160 years (1163–1323).
facts: The Thousand Pillar temple is also called the Rudreshwara temple (Hanumakonda), built 1163.
Kakatiyas ruled c. 1163–1323; Ganapatideva–Rudramadevi–Prataparudra.
Prolaraja bore the title Arikesari; Beta II was initiated into Saivism by Rameswara Pandita of Srisailam; the Nayankara system was NOT introduced by Prataparudra (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
events.before: The Kakatiyas were feudatories of the **Kalyani Chalukyas** at **Anumakonda**. When the Kalyani kings weakened (after 1150), **Prola II** fought the Chalukya side and his son **Rudradeva** declared independence.
events.after: Rudradeva began **Warangal** fort and the **Thousand Pillar temple** (1163). **Ganapati Deva** (1199) made the Kakatiyas masters of all Telugu lands.
events.today: Hanamkonda's Thousand Pillar temple is a protected monument; Telangana's Mission Kakatiya (2015) to restore village tanks is named after them.
events.mnemonic: Kakatiya line "B-P-B-P-R-M-G-R-P": Beta I, Prola I, Beta II, Prola II, Rudradeva, Mahadeva, Ganapati, Rudrama, Prataparudra II. Big four: "R-G-R-P" (Rudradeva, Ganapati, Rudrama, Prataparudra).

examAngle.point: Inscriptions and their kings: Sanigaram — Prolaraja; Anumakonda — Rudradeva; Bayyaram — Mailamba (Ganapati's sister); Motupalli — Ganapatideva.
examAngle.context: Order them by time: Sanigaram (early chief) → Anumakonda (1163, independence) → Bayyaram (family tree and tanks, Ganapati's time) → Motupalli (1244–45, sea trade).

examAngle.point: The Thousand Pillar temple is "trikuta" — three shrines to Rudreshwara (Shiva), Vasudeva (Vishnu) and Suryadeva; early Kakatiyas built Jain temples; Kalyani Chalukya influence is seen in Kakatiya temples.
examAngle.context: The Kakatiyas began as Jains, then became Shaivas (**Beta II** was initiated by **Rameswara Pandita** of Srisailam), but honoured Vishnu and Surya too.

examAngle.point: Prolaraja I built the Kesari Samudram tank and had the title Arikesari; the Pradvivaka was the king's adviser on justice.
examAngle.context: Tank-building began with the first chiefs and became the Kakatiya trademark: Pakhala, Ramappa, Laknavaram and Ghanpur lakes.

examAngle.point: Under the Kakatiyas the non-Brahmanisation of religion and politics peaked: Sudra rulers, Veerashaiva and Pasupata influence, and non-Brahmin warrior nayakas.
examAngle.context: The Kakatiyas called themselves **Sudras** proudly (in inscriptions), and power went to warrior families like the Reddis, Velamas and Kammas, who later ruled after 1323.

events.title: Second Battle of Tarain
events.summary: Prithviraj Chauhan defeats Muhammad Ghori in the First Battle of Tarain (1191) but loses the Second Battle of Tarain (1192) (NCERT), opening north India to Turkish rule.
events.detail: Tarain is near Thanesar in Haryana. In 1191 Prithviraj's army routed Ghori, who was wounded. Ghori returned in 1192 with mounted archers and a better plan; Prithviraj was defeated and killed. In 1194 Ghori defeated Jaichand of Kanauj at Chandawar. Ghori left Qutbuddin Aibak to rule his Indian conquests.
causes: Ghurid expansion into India.
course: 1191: First Battle — Ghori defeated (NCERT).
1192: Second Battle — Prithviraj defeated (NCERT).
1194: Battle of Chandawar — Jaichand defeated.
losses: Prithviraj killed (1192).
gains: Delhi and Ajmer for the Ghurids.
outcomes: Delhi Sultanate (1206).

alsoOn.text: First Battle of Tarain: Prithviraj Chauhan defeats Muhammad Ghori (NCERT).
Battle of Chandawar: Ghori defeats Jaichand of Kanauj.

events.yearHook: 1192: one year after the first battle (1191). The Delhi Sultanate begins 14 years later (1206).
events.before: Prithviraj had won the first battle (1191) but had not followed up.
events.after: Ghori's general **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** took Delhi and Ajmer; **Bakhtiyar Khalji** raided Bihar and Bengal (1193). When Ghori died (1206), Aibak founded the **Delhi Sultanate**.
events.today: The Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer was built by Aibak soon after.

events.title: Ganapati Deva — greatest Kakatiya
events.summary: Ganapati Deva (1199–1262), the greatest Kakatiya king, unites the Telugu lands, moves the capital to Warangal (Orugallu) and protects sea trade at Motupalli.
events.detail: His Motupalli abhaya-shasana (charter) promised safety and fair duties to foreign merchants. His general Recharla Rudra built the Ramappa temple (1213, UNESCO 2021) and the Ramappa lake. He extended the kingdom to Kanchi. Having no son, he named his daughter Rudramadevi heir.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Kakatiya expansion.
outcomes: Warangal became a great capital; Ramappa temple.
events.yearHook: 1199–1262: 63 years, one of the longest reigns in Indian history. Motupalli charter about 1244–45.
events.before: **Rudradeva** (1163) had made the Kakatiyas free; his brother **Mahadeva** died fighting the Yadavas (1199), and young Ganapati was captured, then released.
events.after: He ruled from the Godavari to Kanchi and from the sea to Bidar. With no son, he trained his daughter **Rudramadevi** and made her co-ruler (1262).
events.today: Warangal's Kakatiya Festival and Motupalli (Bapatla district) remember him.
events.mnemonic: Ganapati's "W-M-R-K": Warangal capital, Motupalli charter, Ramappa temple (1213, by Recharla Rudra), Kanchi reached.

examAngle.point: Motupalli was also called Desiyakkonda Pattanam; Pedaganjam and Chinaganjam were known for salt; trade routes included Motupalli–Tripurantakam–Ballari and Palnadu–Nalgonda–Nekarikallu–Orugallu.
examAngle.context: His **abhaya shasana** at Motupalli lowered duties and promised that ships wrecked on the coast would not be seized — the old "right of wreck" was given up to draw foreign merchants.

examAngle.point: Kakatiya caste associations were called Samayamu; the Chitrameli guild was formed by agriculturists; Jayana (Jayapa), author of Nritta Ratnavali, was a Gaja-Sahini (commander of elephants); the instrument Jalakaranda is in the Dharmasagar inscription.
examAngle.context: Kakatiya society was run by guilds (**samayams**) of traders and farmers who gave gifts to temples — the inscriptions recording those gifts are where these words come from.

events.title: Bhakti–Sufi movements spread
events.summary: Bhakti (devotion) and Sufi movements spread across India from about the 12th–13th centuries, building on the Alvars and Nayanars of Tamil Nadu (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Alvars (devotees of Vishnu) and Nayanars (devotees of Shiva) of the 6th–9th centuries sang in Tamil and came from all castes (NCERT). Ramanuja (11th–12th century) taught Vishishtadvaita and inspired Ramananda in the north (NCERT). Basavanna led the Virashaivas in Karnataka (NCERT).

Sufi silsilas such as the Chishtis (Muinuddin Chishti at Ajmer, Nizamuddin Auliya at Delhi) reached India in the 12th century (NCERT). Later saints include Kabir, Guru Nanak, Mirabai, Tulsidas and Chaitanya; in Andhra, Annamacharya, Potana and Ramadasu.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 6 "Bhakti-Sufi Traditions"
causes: Reaction to ritualism and caste (NCERT).
outcomes: Literature in regional languages; new communities such as the Sikhs (NCERT).
events.yearHook: The long arc: Alvars (600–900) → Ramanuja (1017) → Basava (1160) → Jnaneshwar (1290) → Kabir (1440) → Nanak (1469) → Chaitanya (1486) → Tulsidas (1574) → Tukaram (1600s).
facts: Nirguna bhakti (formless God: Kabir, Nanak) and Saguna bhakti (God with form: Tulsidas, Surdas, Mira).

Sufi terms: silsilah (order), pir (master), murid (disciple), khanqah (hospice), zikr (remembrance), sama (music), fanaa (passing away in God), maqamat (stages); wahdat-ul-wujud (unity of being) of Ibn Arabi.
Sheikh Ahmad Sirhindi (Naqshbandi) opposed it; Miyan Mir (Qadiri) laid the Golden Temple foundation, by tradition.
The southern teachers were called Acharyas; Lingayats wear the Ishtalinga.
Kabir wrote dohas; Sikh principles: Naam Japna, Kirat Karna (honest work), Vand Chhakna (sharing).
Varkari pilgrims of Maharashtra worship Vithoba (Vitthala) at Pandharpur.
events.before: Temple ritual, Sanskrit learning and caste kept many people out of worship.
events.after: Bhakti made regional languages literary (Tamil, Kannada, Marathi, Hindi, Telugu, Bengali), challenged caste, and with the Sufis created a shared culture (Kabir, Nanak). It led to Sikhism.
events.today: Gandhiji's favourite bhajan "Vaishnava jana to" is by **Narsinh Mehta** of Gujarat (15th century).
events.mnemonic: "South to North": bhakti started in Tamil land, went to Karnataka and Maharashtra, then via Ramananda to the Ganga valley, then east to Bengal and Assam.

events.title: Qutb-ud-din Aibak founds the Slave dynasty
events.summary: After Ghori's death Qutbuddin Aibak becomes the first Sultan of Delhi (1206–1210) (NCERT), founding the Mamluk ("Slave") dynasty.
events.detail:
Delhi first became an important city under the Tomara Rajputs, then the Chauhans; it became the capital of the Sultanate under the Turks (NCERT). Aibak had been a slave of Ghori. He began the Qutb Minar and the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque, and built the Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer. He died after falling from his horse while playing polo (1210).

The Sultanate had five dynasties: Mamluk, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid and Lodi (NCERT, Table 1).
causes: Ghori's death (1206).
outcomes: Delhi Sultanate 1206–1526 (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1206: Ghori is murdered; 14 years after Tarain-2. The Sultanate lasts 320 years (1206–1526).
facts: Ziauddin Barani wrote Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi; the Chihalgani (Chahalgani) were the Forty; Ranthambore was taken by Iltutmish and later Alauddin; Bahlol (Bahlul) Lodi founded the Lodis.
events.before: **Muhammad Ghori** won the **Second Battle of Tarain** (1192) and left his slave general **Qutb-ud-din Aibak** in charge of his Indian lands.
events.after: Aibak (1206–1210) ruled from **Lahore**. He died in a polo accident; his son **Aram Shah** was soon replaced by **Iltutmish** (1211), who made **Delhi** the capital.
events.today: The Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque at the Qutb and the Adhai Din ka Jhonpra at Ajmer were built from the materials of older temples.
events.mnemonic: "S-K-T-S-L, 1206-1290-1320-1414-1451": Slave, Khalji, Tughlaq, Sayyid, Lodi.

examAngle.point: Aibak was called Lakh Bakhsh (giver of lakhs) for his generosity; his capital was Lahore, not Delhi; he died playing chaugan (polo) in 1210.
examAngle.context: Three Slave-dynasty "names" are often mixed up: the dynasty is also called **Mamluk** (owned slaves) or **Ilbari** (the Turkish tribe of Iltutmish and Balban). The three great kings were all once slaves: Aibak, Iltutmish, Balban.

events.title: Iltutmish consolidates the Sultanate
events.summary: Iltutmish (1211–1236) consolidates the Delhi Sultanate, gets recognition from the Abbasid Caliph (1229), issues the silver tanka and copper jital, and organises the iqta system.
events.detail: He was Aibak's slave and son-in-law. He crushed rivals Yalduz and Qubacha, kept the Mongols away by refusing refuge to Jalaluddin Mangbarni, completed the Qutb Minar and formed the group of forty nobles (Chahalgani). He named his daughter Raziyya as heir (NCERT).
causes: Weak rule of Aram Shah.
outcomes: Sultanate made stable; Raziyya succeeded (1236) (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1211: five years after the Sultanate begins. Caliph's recognition 1229; dies 1236.
events.before: **Aibak** had died (1210); his son **Aram Shah** was weak. Rivals **Yalduz** (Ghazni) and **Qubacha** (Multan) claimed Ghori's Indian lands.
events.after: The **iqta** system he set up lasted through the Sultanate. He named his daughter **Razia** heir over his sons (1236). The **Forty** nobles became too strong until **Balban** broke them.
events.today: The silver **tanka** (about 175 grains) is the ancestor of the "taka" of Bangladesh and the rupee of later times.
events.mnemonic: Iltutmish "4 Cs": Capital Delhi, Coins (tanka and jital), Caliph's robe (1229), Chahalgani (the Forty).

examAngle.point: Iqta: land revenue of an area given to a military officer (muqti or iqtadar) in place of salary; he kept troops and kept order. It was NOT hereditary at first (Firoz Shah made it so).
examAngle.context: Think of it as "salary paid by a district". It let the Sultan pay a big army without cash in the treasury. It is the forerunner of the Mughal **jagir**.

events.title: Razia Sultana — first woman ruler of Delhi
events.summary: Raziyya, daughter of Iltutmish, becomes Sultan in 1236 and is removed in 1240 (NCERT) — the only woman Sultan of Delhi.
events.detail: NCERT says she was more able and qualified than her brothers, but the nobles were not happy with her attempts to rule independently. The chronicler Minhaj-i Siraj thought a queen went against the social order. NCERT contrasts her with Rudramadevi, who ruled successfully in Warangal.
causes: Iltutmish's choice of his daughter as heir (NCERT).
outcomes: Nobles (the Forty) dominated until Balban.
events.yearHook: 1236–1240: four years. The only woman to sit on the throne of Delhi.

participants.role: One of the Forty; later Sultan.

events.before: Iltutmish thought his sons unfit and named **Razia** heir. The nobles first put her brother **Ruknuddin Firuz** on the throne; the people of Delhi raised her instead.
events.after: She dressed like a man, rode an elephant in public and raised the Abyssinian **Yaqut** to a high post, which angered the Turkish nobles. **Altunia**, governor of Bhatinda, rebelled; she married him, but both were killed (1240). The **Forty** then ruled through weak kings until **Balban**.
events.today: Minhaj-us-Siraj's **Tabaqat-i-Nasiri** praises her; she is remembered as a symbol of women's rule in medieval India.

examAngle.point: Razia (1236–40): first and only woman ruler of the Delhi Sultanate; she gave up the purdah and favoured Jamaluddin Yaqut; defeated by the rebel Altunia, whom she later married.
examAngle.context: Minhaj-us-Siraj said she had every quality of a king, but she was not born a man, so in the eyes of the nobles all those virtues were worth nothing.

events.title: Rani Rudrama Devi rules the Kakatiyas
events.summary: Rudramadevi rules the Kakatiya kingdom of Warangal (1262–1289) (NCERT), defeating the Yadavas and putting down rebel nobles.
events.detail: NCERT notes that she changed her name on inscriptions and pretended to be a man, taking a male royal title. She completed the Warangal fort and promoted the Nayankara system of military chiefs. Marco Polo praised her rule. She was succeeded by her grandson Prataparudra II.
events.source: NCERT Class 7 Our Pasts II; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Ganapati Deva had no son.
outcomes: Kakatiya power held; Prataparudra II succeeded (1289).
events.yearHook: 1262–1289: 27 years. Razia ruled Delhi 1236–40, about 25 years earlier.
events.before: Her father **Ganapati Deva** made her co-ruler and gave her the male name **Rudradeva Maharaja**; nobles and the Yadavas opposed a woman king.
events.after: She defeated the Yadava **Mahadeva** of Devagiri, crushed the rebel **Ambadeva** and was probably killed in that fight (about 1289). Her grandson (daughter Mummadamma's son) **Prataparudra II** succeeded.
events.today: The 2015 Telugu film "Rudhramadevi" tells her story; she is a symbol of women's leadership in Telugu lands.
events.mnemonic: Two women rulers of the 13th century "R-R": Razia (Delhi, 4 years, fell) and Rudrama (Warangal, 27 years, held).

examAngle.point: Rudramadevi took the title "Rayagaja Kesari" for her victory over the Yadavas of Devagiri.
examAngle.context: "Rayagaja Kesari" = "lion to the elephant-kings". Her general **Gona Ganna Reddy** (and **Recharla Prasaditya**) fought for her.

events.title: Amir Khusrau — "Parrot of India"
events.summary: Amir Khusrau, poet and disciple of Nizamuddin Auliya, writes in Persian and Hindavi at the courts of the Khalji Sultans (from about 1290).
events.detail: He served seven Sultans from Balban to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq. NCERT quotes him (1318) noting that every region had its own language. He is credited with developing qawwali and instruments such as the sitar (by tradition), and wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh on Alauddin's conquests.
causes: Court patronage.
outcomes: Hindavi literature; Indo-Persian music.
events.yearHook: Khusrau lived 1253–1325 and served seven Sultans, from Balban's son to Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq; he died months after his teacher Nizamuddin Auliya (1325).
events.before: Persian was the court language of the Sultans; Sufi orders like the **Chishtis** spread in India.
events.after: He wrote **Khazain-ul-Futuh** (Alauddin's wars), **Nuh Sipihr** (praise of India), **Qiran-us-Sadain**, **Tughlaq Nama** and verses in **Hindavi**, the early form of Hindi-Urdu. His music mixed Persian and Indian styles.
events.today: His grave is beside Nizamuddin Auliya's dargah in Delhi; qawwalis there still sing his songs, like "Chhap Tilak".
events.mnemonic: Khusrau's "Q-T-S": Qawwali, Tabla (by tradition) and Sitar (by tradition); Tuti-i-Hind (Parrot of India).

examAngle.point: Amir Khusrau was a disciple of the Chishti saint Nizamuddin Auliya; he wrote Khazain-ul-Futuh about Alauddin Khalji's campaigns; he was called Tuti-i-Hind.
examAngle.context: Link him to three people: teacher Nizamuddin Auliya, patron Alauddin Khalji (his campaigns), and the last patron Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq (Tughlaq Nama).

events.title: Alauddin Khilji; market & revenue reforms
events.summary: Alauddin Khalji becomes Sultan (1296–1316) after murdering his uncle Jalaluddin; he repels the Mongols, controls market prices and raids the south through Malik Kafur (NCERT).
events.detail:
NCERT describes his measures: he raised a large standing army paid in cash, and to feed it fixed the prices of goods in Delhi, with strict officers. He built a garrison town called Siri. He collected tax on land at half the produce.

His generals took Gujarat (1299), Ranthambhor (1301), Chittor (1303) and Devagiri, and Malik Kafur raided Warangal (1309), Dwarasamudra and Madurai.
causes: Mongol threat; need for a big army (NCERT).
outcomes: Sultanate reached the far south.
Market control ended after his death.
events.yearHook: 1296–1316: 20 years. He kills his uncle Jalaluddin at Kara in 1296 after the Devagiri raid.
events.before: **Jalaluddin Khalji** (1290) had started the dynasty; Alauddin, his nephew, raided **Devagiri** (1296) and used its gold to buy support.
events.after: He beat the **Mongols** (Kili 1299 and later), took **Gujarat** (1299), **Ranthambore** (1301), **Chittor** (1303), **Malwa** (1305), and sent **Malik Kafur** south: Devagiri (1307), **Warangal** (1309), Dwarasamudra and Madurai (1310–11). After his death (1316) the price controls ended.
events.today: **Siri Fort** and **Hauz Khas** (his tank) are Delhi place names; the Alai Darwaza at the Qutb is his gate.
events.mnemonic: Alauddin's army reforms "D-H": Dagh (branding horses) and Huliya (descriptive roll of soldiers). Market officers: "Shahna-i-Mandi watches, Diwan-i-Riyasat rules".

examAngle.point: Alauddin was the first Sultan to keep a large permanent (standing) army paid in cash, with branding of horses (dagh) and a roll of soldiers (huliya or chehra).
examAngle.context: The Mongol threat made a big army necessary; cash pay made it costly; so he had to make food cheap — the market control follows from the army.

examAngle.point: Market control: separate markets for grain, cloth and horses-slaves-cattle; officers Diwan-i-Riyasat and Shahna-i-Mandi; prices fixed; spies reported cheating shopkeepers.
examAngle.context: Prices stayed low only in **Delhi**, not the whole empire, and only while he lived. Barani is the main source.

examAngle.point: Land revenue: half the produce (kharaj), measured land (masahat); new taxes ghari (house tax) and chari (grazing tax); Diwan-i-Mustakhraj collected arrears.
examAngle.context: He was the first Sultan to measure land for revenue; this idea leads to Sher Shah and Todar Mal.

examAngle.point: Titles: Sikandar-i-Sani (second Alexander). He took Ranthambore from Hammira Deva (1301) and Chittor from Rana Ratan Singh (1303), renaming Chittor Khizrabad.
examAngle.context: The Chittor siege is linked with the Padmini legend of Malik Muhammad Jayasi's **Padmavat** (1540), written more than 200 years later; historians treat it as a poem, not a record.

events.title: Fall of the Kakatiyas; Prataparudra captured
events.summary: Ulugh Khan (later Muhammad bin Tughlaq) captures Warangal (1323), ending the Kakatiya dynasty; Prataparudra II dies on the way to Delhi.
events.detail: A first Tughlaq attack in 1321 failed. In 1323 Warangal fell after a siege and was renamed Sultanpur. The 77 Nayakas who served the Kakatiyas soon led revolts; the Musunuri Nayakas freed Telangana (c. 1336), and the Reddis rose in coastal Andhra.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Prataparudra stopped paying tribute.
losses: Kakatiya kingdom annexed.
outcomes: Warangal renamed Sultanpur; Musunuri Nayakas and Reddis rose.
events.yearHook: Kakatiyas 1163 → 1323: 160 years.
events.before: Prataparudra II stopped paying tribute; the 1321 Tughlaq siege failed when Ulugh Khan's army broke up on a false rumour of Ghiyasuddin's death.
events.after: Telangana was ruled from Delhi as **Sultanpur** for about 13 years. Many nayakas went to their home areas and rebelled: **Musunuris** (1336), **Reddis** (1325), **Velamas**, and Vijayanagara's founders (1336), who by one tradition served the Kakatiyas.
events.today: The Kirti Toranas stand among the Warangal fort ruins; the Khush Mahal hall nearby was built later by Muslim governors.
events.mnemonic: "Telugu unity 160 years": 1163 to 1323.

events.title: Muhammad-bin-Tughlaq's experiments
events.summary: Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325–1351) tries bold plans — moving the capital to Daulatabad, token currency and the Khurasan army — which fail (NCERT).
events.detail:
NCERT explains: to face the Mongols he raised a huge standing army and, instead of building a new garrison town, emptied the oldest city, Delhi, sending people to Daulatabad in the south (1327). He paid the army with token currency of cheap metal, which people forged easily. The army raised for the Khurasan campaign was disbanded. Famine and rebellions followed.

Ibn Battuta served as qazi of Delhi under him (NCERT). In the south Vijayanagara (1336) and the Bahmanis (1347) rose during his reign.
causes: Mongol threat; plans to rule the south (NCERT).
outcomes: Rebellions; Vijayanagara and Bahmani kingdoms rose.
events.yearHook: 1325–1351: 26 years. Daulatabad 1327; token coins about 1329–30.
events.before: His father **Ghiyasuddin** (1320) had taken Warangal (1323). The empire now reached Madurai and was hard to rule from Delhi.
events.after: The plans failed; famine and revolts followed. **Madurai** (1335), **Vijayanagara** (1336), **Bengal** and the **Bahmani** kingdom (1347) broke away. He died chasing rebels in Sind (1351).
events.today: Historians call him a man of ideas who did not plan for people; "Tughlaqi farmaan" in Hindi means a foolish order.
events.mnemonic: MBT's five experiments "D-T-T-K-Q": Doab tax rise, Transfer of capital, Token currency, Khurasan plan, Qarachil expedition.

examAngle.point: Token currency: bronze (or copper) coins given the value of silver; people forged them at home and the state had to buy them back in gold and silver.
examAngle.context: The idea was not mad: China already used paper money. It failed because the coins were easy to copy. Silver was short in the world at the time.

examAngle.point: He set up a separate agriculture department, Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi, to bring more land under the plough; he gave loans (sondhar or taqavi) to farmers.
examAngle.context: This came after the Doab famine caused by his tax rise. It is the first farm department of the Sultanate.

examAngle.point: Ibn Battuta, the Moroccan traveller, was his qazi of Delhi and wrote the Rihla; Barani wrote about his reign in Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi.
examAngle.context: Two sources, two views: Barani (an insider who disliked his rational ideas) and Ibn Battuta (a foreigner who saw both his generosity and cruelty).

events.title: Reddi kingdoms rise in coastal Andhra
events.summary: After the Kakatiya fall, Prolaya Vema Reddi founds the Reddi kingdom in coastal Andhra (c. 1325) with capital Addanki, later Kondavidu and Rajahmundry.
events.detail: The Reddis repaired temples and tanks and patronised Telugu literature. Errana (Errapragada) completed the Telugu Mahabharata at Prolaya Vema's court; Srinatha was "Vidyadhikari" to Pedakomati Vema Reddi. The Reddis fought Vijayanagara, the Bahmanis, the Velamas of Rachakonda and the Gajapatis; Kondavidu fell to the Gajapatis (1448).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Kakatiya fall (1323).
outcomes: Reddi rule until c. 1448.
events.yearHook: About 1325: two years after Warangal falls. The Reddis rule about 120 years (to 1448).

participants.role: Court poet of the later Reddis.

facts: Reddi rule c. 1325–1448 CE. Kings: Prolaya Vema, Anavota, Anavema, Kumaragiri, Kataya Vema, Peda Komati Vema (Peda Komati Vema Reddy), Racha Vema.
Kondaveedu Fort was the Reddi stronghold; Anitalli was a Reddi queen (Kalayana grant); Ahobilam temple was patronised.
Srinatha was "Kavisarvabhauma".
events.before: The fall of Warangal (1323) left coastal Andhra open; **Prolaya Vema Reddi** joined the Musunuri revolt and made a kingdom at **Addanki**.
events.after: Capital moved to **Kondavidu**; a second branch ruled from **Rajahmundry** (about 1395). Telugu poetry flowered: **Errana** (Prolaya Vema), **Srinatha** (Pedakomati Vema). The **Gajapatis** ended both branches (1448–54).
events.today: Kondaveedu fort (near Guntur) is being developed as a heritage site.
events.mnemonic: Kondavidu Reddi kings "P-A-A-K-P-R" (Please Always Add Kondavidu's Proud Reddis): Prolaya Vema, Anavota, Anavema, Kumaragiri, Pedakomati Vema, Racha Vema.

examAngle.point: Reddi kings in order after the founder Prolaya Vema: Anavota, Anavema, Kumaragiri, Pedakomati Vema; the last, Racha Vema, was notorious for heavy taxes (including Puriti Pannu, a tax on childbirth) and was killed by a servant.
examAngle.context: Rise (Prolaya Vema, Anavota, Anavema), culture peak (Kumaragiri, Pedakomati Vema), fall (Racha Vema, about 1424). Two kings in a row named "Ana-" helps the order.

examAngle.point: Surambika, queen of Pedakomati Vema, dug the Santana Sagaram tank; Vasantotsavam was the Reddis' favourite festival; Pedakomati Vema wrote Sangita Chintamani on music.
examAngle.context: The Reddis were scholar-kings: Kumaragiri (Vasantarajiyam, dance), Pedakomati Vema (Sangita Chintamani, music; also a commentary on Amaru's poems).

events.title: Musunuri Nayaks recapture Warangal
events.summary: The Musunuri Nayakas, Prolaya and Kapaya, lead Telugu chiefs in a revolt that frees coastal Andhra and Telangana from Tughlaq rule; Kapaya Nayaka captures Warangal (c. 1336).
events.detail: Prolaya Nayaka's Vilasa grant describes the suffering under Tughlaq rule and the liberation. Kapaya Nayaka ruled from Warangal and helped Hasan Gangu found the Bahmani kingdom (1347), but later lost Warangal to the Bahmanis and the Recherla Velamas (1368).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Tughlaq oppression after 1323.
outcomes: Telugu rule restored; Reddis, Velamas and Vijayanagara rose.
events.yearHook: About 1336: the same year Vijayanagara is founded; 13 years after Warangal falls.

participants.role: Founded the Bahmani kingdom with Kapaya's help.

facts: Recherla Velamas ruled c. 1328–1482 in Telangana.
events.before: Tughlaq rule (1323–) was harsh; the **Vilasa grant** of Prolaya Nayaka lists temples destroyed and Brahmins harassed.
events.after: **Kapaya Nayaka** took the title **Andhra Suratrana** (Sultan of Andhra) and helped **Hasan Gangu** found the Bahmani kingdom (1347). The Bahmanis later turned on him and took **Golconda** from him; the Recherla **Velamas** killed him (about 1368).
events.today: Rekapalle, in the forest country on the Godavari, was Prolaya's base.
events.mnemonic: Musunuri cousins "P-K": Prolaya (began, Vilasa grant), Kapaya (took Warangal, "Andhra Suratrana").

events.title: Vijayanagara Empire founded
events.summary: Two brothers, Harihara and Bukka, found the Vijayanagara empire on the Tungabhadra in 1336 (NCERT); the Sangama dynasty rules till 1485 (NCERT).
events.detail:
They had served the Kakatiyas or Kampili, by tradition; the sage Vidyaranya is said to have inspired them. The capital Vijayanagara (Hampi) grew into a great walled city (NCERT). Dynasties: Sangama (till 1485), Saluva (till 1503), Tuluva and Aravidu (from 1542) (NCERT).

Rulers were called rayas; military chiefs called nayakas held land (amara) and supplied troops — the amara-nayaka system (NCERT). Ruins of Hampi were brought to light in 1800 by Colin Mackenzie (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"
causes: Weak Tughlaq control in the south.
outcomes: Vijayanagara–Bahmani wars for the Raichur doab (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Saluva Narasimha replaces the Sangama dynasty (NCERT).
The Tuluvas replace the Saluvas (NCERT).
Colin Mackenzie surveys the ruins of Hampi (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1336: 13 years after the Kakatiyas fall (1323); the same year the Musunuri Nayaks retake Warangal. The city lasts 229 years (to 1565).
facts: Village officials: the ayagar system (12 village functionaries).
Vijayanagara rulers worshipped Virupaksha and Pampadevi at Hampi; later Vittala.
Fernao Nunes (Nuniz) was a Portuguese horse-trader who described the city.
events.before: **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**'s plans (1325–1351) caused revolts across the south. Harihara and Bukka, by tradition once in Kakatiya or Kampili service, had been taken to Delhi and sent back to rule for the Sultan; they broke away.
events.after: Vijayanagara fought the **Bahmani** kingdom (1347) for the rich **Raichur doab** between the Krishna and Tungabhadra for 200 years. **Bukka I** made Hindus and Jains live in peace (his order of 1368). Four dynasties ruled until Talikota (1565).
events.today: The ruins at **Hampi** (Karnataka) are a UNESCO site (1986). The Sringeri math is linked to Vidyaranya (Madhava), author of works on Advaita.
events.mnemonic: "H-B-V 1336": Harihara and Bukka, guided by Vidyaranya, on the Tungabhadra.

examAngle.point: Amara-nayaka system: military chiefs (nayakas) got land (amaram) to collect revenue and kept soldiers and horses for the king; villages had 12 hereditary servants called ayagars.
examAngle.context: It is the Vijayanagara cousin of the Sultanate **iqta**, but the nayakas became hereditary local rulers. After 1565 they became independent: the **Nayaks** of Madurai, Thanjavur and the Palegars (Poligars) of Rayalaseema.

events.title: Bahmani Sultanate founded in the Deccan
events.summary: Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah founds the Bahmani sultanate at Gulbarga (1347), the rival of Vijayanagara for the Raichur doab (NCERT).
events.detail:
The capital later moved to Bidar. Mahmud Gawan, the great minister, reformed the administration and built a madrasa at Bidar; his execution (1481) hastened the break-up.

By the early 16th century the kingdom split into five sultanates: Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Golconda (Qutb Shahi) and Bidar (Barid Shahi) (NCERT names the Deccan Sultanates).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes in Indian History II, Ch. 7 "An Imperial Capital: Vijayanagara"; Standard ancient and medieval Indian history (R.S. Sharma / Satish Chandra / Upinder Singh)
causes: Revolt of Deccan nobles against Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
outcomes: Five Deccan sultanates.

alsoOn.text: Mahmud Gawan executed; the Bahmani kingdom begins to break up.
Bijapur, Ahmadnagar and Berar become independent.

events.yearHook: 1347: 11 years after Vijayanagara (1336). Lasts 180 years (to 1527).
facts: The Bahmani kingdom was divided into 4, later 8 tarafs (provinces) under tarafdars.
Nobles were split into Afaqis (foreigners) and Deccanis (locals).
Five sultanates: Bijapur–Adil Shahi, Ahmednagar–Nizam Shahi, Berar–Imad Shahi, Golconda–Qutb Shahi, Bidar–Barid Shahi.
Sufi saint Gesu Daraz (Gulbarga); Dakhini Urdu developed; Ibrahim Rauza (Bijapur).
events.before: The Deccan nobles (amiran-i-sada, "commanders of a hundred") rebelled against **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**; **Hasan Gangu** (Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah) was crowned at Daulatabad and chose **Gulbarga**.
events.after: Constant war with Vijayanagara over the **Raichur doab**. **Firoz Shah Bahmani** (1397–1422) built an observatory and took Brahmins into service. **Mahmud Gawan** (killed 1481) was its great minister. Then it split into five Deccan Sultanates (1490–1527).
events.today: The Chishti saint **Gesu Daraz** (Bande Nawaz) of Gulbarga is still revered; **Dakhini Urdu** grew in these courts.
events.mnemonic: Bahmani capitals "G-B": Gulbarga first, Bidar later (moved about 1425 by Ahmad Shah Wali).

events.title: Firoz Shah Tughlaq — canals & welfare
events.summary: Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388) rules Delhi; he builds canals and towns, imposes jizya on brahmanas, sets up a department of slaves and moves two Ashokan pillars to Delhi.
events.detail: He gave iqtas as hereditary grants and abolished harsh taxes, keeping only four sanctioned by the Sharia. He founded Firozabad, Jaunpur and Hisar and the Diwan-i-Khairat (charity) and Diwan-i-Bandagan (slaves). He wrote his memoirs, Futuhat-i-Firozshahi.
causes: Weakness after Muhammad bin Tughlaq.
outcomes: Sultanate weakened by hereditary iqtas.
events.yearHook: 1351–1388: 37 years, the longest Tughlaq reign.

participants.role: His pillars were moved to Delhi.

events.before: **Muhammad bin Tughlaq**'s plans had caused revolt and loss. The nobles and ulema chose his cousin Firoz.
events.after: He kept peace but made **iqtas** and army posts **hereditary**; the state grew weak. After him came quarrelling kings, and **Timur** sacked Delhi (1398).
events.today: The two **Ashokan pillars** he brought from **Topra** (Ambala) and **Meerut** stand in Delhi (Feroz Shah Kotla and the Ridge). The **Western Yamuna Canal** began as his canal.
events.mnemonic: Firoz's "Diwans": Khairat (charity), Bandagan (slaves), Istihqaq (pensions); hospital Dar-ul-Shifa; employment bureau.

examAngle.point: Firoz collected only the four taxes allowed by Sharia: kharaj (land tax), khams (one-fifth of war booty), jizya and zakat; he made Brahmins pay jizya, which they had not paid before.
examAngle.context: He wanted to rule as an orthodox Muslim king, so he dropped many taxes (24 according to his memoir) but brought jizya to Brahmins.

examAngle.point: Two books named Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi: by Ziauddin Barani and by Shams-i-Siraj Afif. Firoz wrote his own Futuhat-i-Firozshahi.
examAngle.context: Barani's book covers Balban to early Firoz; Afif's covers Firoz's reign only.

events.title: Timur sacks Delhi
events.summary: Timur invades India and sacks Delhi in December 1398; the Tughlaq dynasty collapses and the Sayyids (1414) follow.
events.detail: Timur came from Samarkand, defeated Nasiruddin Mahmud Tughlaq and massacred many in Delhi. He left Khizr Khan as governor of Multan; Khizr Khan took Delhi in 1414 and founded the Sayyid dynasty (NCERT: 1414–1421). Babur was descended from Timur (NCERT).
losses: Delhi plundered; thousands killed.
outcomes: Sayyid dynasty from 1414 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Khizr Khan founds the Sayyid dynasty (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1398: ten years after Firoz dies (1388). Exactly 128 years later Timur's descendant Babur wins Panipat (1526).
events.before: The later Tughlaqs were weak; Sultan **Nasiruddin Mahmud** ruled only Delhi.
events.after: Timur sacked Delhi for days and took craftsmen to build **Samarkand**. He left **Khizr Khan** as governor of Multan, who founded the **Sayyid** dynasty (1414). Provinces became free: Jaunpur (Sharqi), Malwa, Gujarat.
events.today: The Bibi Khanym mosque in Samarkand was built partly by Indian workers carried off in 1398.

events.title: Lodi dynasty; Sikandar founds Agra
events.summary: Bahlul Lodi founds the Lodi dynasty (1451), the first Afghan rulers of Delhi; Sikandar Lodi founds Agra (1504), and Ibrahim Lodi loses to Babur at Panipat (1526).
events.detail: Bahlul conquered the Sharqi kingdom of Jaunpur. Sikandar Lodi moved the capital to Agra and introduced a measuring rod (gaz-i-Sikandari). Ibrahim's quarrels with nobles made Daulat Khan Lodi and Alam Khan invite Babur.
causes: Decline of the Sayyids.
outcomes: First Battle of Panipat (1526).
events.yearHook: 1451–1526: 75 years. Bahlol 1451, Sikandar 1489, Ibrahim 1517.
