outcomes: The Godavari delta became one of India's richest rice-growing areas ("rice bowl").
Cotton is still honoured in the delta as a benefactor.
facts: V. Veeranna was the Andhra officer who helped Sir Arthur Cotton build the Dowleswaram anicut (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

The Buckingham Canal (salt-water navigation canal from Kakinada to Madras/Villupuram, built 1806 onward, extended 1877-78 as famine work) is the biggest canal of Andhra and gained commercial importance (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: Salar Jung reforms in Hyderabad State
events.summary: Salar Jung I modernises the Nizam's administration.
events.detail:
Legacy includes the Salar Jung Museum collection.

**Exam hooks:** Salar Jung — Diwan of Hyderabad; famous museum.

participants.role: Became Diwan in 1853 and carried out the reforms.

events.yearHook: Same year as the first railway: 1853.
causes: Hyderabad's finances were in disorder and the Nizam owed the Company money.
The Berar districts had been handed to the British (1853) to pay for the Hyderabad Contingent.
outcomes: Modern revenue, judicial and police systems in Hyderabad.
Hyderabad stayed loyal to the British in 1857.
events.before: Hyderabad was in debt; **Berar** had been handed to the British (1853) to pay for the Hyderabad Contingent.
events.after: **Salar Jung I** (Diwan 1853–83) set up districts (zillas), a modern revenue and police system, courts and schools, and kept Hyderabad loyal in 1857.
events.today: The **Salar Jung Museum** (Hyderabad, 1951) holds the collection of his grandson Salar Jung III.

events.title: First railway line: Bombay–Thane
events.summary: On 16 April 1853 the first passenger train ran from Bombay to Thane under Dalhousie.
events.detail:
Dalhousie pushed railways, the telegraph and a modern postal system. The first railway line, about 34 km long, ran from Bombay to Thane. The first telegraph line (Calcutta to Agra) and the Post Office Act followed in 1854.

Railways moved troops and raw materials quickly and opened Indian markets to British goods.
events.source: Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
causes: British need to move troops and raw cotton quickly.
British investors were guaranteed a return on railway capital.
outcomes: Railways helped the British move troops in 1857.
Opened India's interior to British manufactured goods.

participants.role: Governor-General who planned the railway network.

facts: First railway: Bombay to Thane, 16 April 1853.
First telegraph line (Calcutta–Agra) and the Post Office Act: 1854.

alsoOn.text: First telegraph line (Calcutta–Agra) and the Post Office Act under Dalhousie.

events.yearHook: Railway 1853, telegraph 1854 — "53 trains, 54 wires".
events.before: Britain wanted cotton from the interior and a market for its goods; troops had to move fast.
events.after: The **Bombay–Thane** line opened on 16 April 1853 (34 km); the east (Howrah–Hooghly, 1854) and south (Royapuram–Arcot, 1856) followed. Railways spread by the guarantee system, at India's cost.
events.today: Indian Railways is the world's fourth-largest network; the Vande Bharat trains mark its new phase.
events.mnemonic: Dalhousie's modern three "R-T-P": Railway (1853), Telegraph (1853–54), Postal (Post Office Act, 1854, half-anna stamp).

events.title: The Revolt of 1857
events.summary: On 10 May 1857 the sepoys at Meerut mutinied, marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader; the revolt spread across north India (NCERT).
events.detail:
Sepoys, peasants, zamindars and deposed rulers all had grievances against the Company. The spark was the new Enfield rifle cartridge, suspected of being coated with the fat of cows and pigs (NCERT).

From Meerut the rising spread to Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Bihar and central India. The British were outnumbered and lost many battles at first. They recaptured Delhi in September 1857, but it took them two years to crush the popular uprising (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 5 "When People Revolt"; NCERT Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 11 "Rebels and the Raj"
events.place: Meerut, Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, Bareilly, Arrah and central India

sides.name: Rebels
sides.ruler: Bahadur Shah Zafar (proclaimed leader by the sepoys)

causes: Annexations: the Doctrine of Lapse and the takeover of Awadh (1856) (NCERT).
Rulers lost honour and power: Lakshmibai's adopted son was not recognised; Nana Saheb's pension was refused (NCERT).
The Mughal name was removed from coins; Canning decided (1856) that Bahadur Shah Zafar would be the last Mughal king (NCERT).
Peasants and zamindars resented high taxes and rigid revenue collection; many lost their lands to moneylenders (NCERT).
Sepoys were unhappy about pay, allowances and service conditions; the 1856 Act made them serve overseas (NCERT).
Fear that the British wanted to convert Indians to Christianity; laws against sati and for widow remarriage were seen as interference (NCERT).
The new Enfield rifle cartridges, suspected to be greased with cow and pig fat (NCERT).
course: 29 March 1857: Mangal Pandey attacks his officers at Barrackpore; he is hanged on 8 April (NCERT).
9 May 1857: 85 sepoys at Meerut who refused the new cartridges are jailed for ten years (NCERT).
10 May 1857: the Meerut sepoys free them, kill British officers and ride all night to Delhi (NCERT).
11 May 1857: Delhi regiments join; the sepoys proclaim Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader (NCERT).
June 1857: Nana Saheb expels the British from Kanpur and proclaims himself Peshwa; at Lucknow, Birjis Qadr is made Nawab and Begum Hazrat Mahal leads (NCERT).
September 1857: the British recapture Delhi (NCERT).
March 1858: Lucknow is retaken (NCERT).
June 1858: Rani Lakshmibai is defeated and killed (NCERT).
April 1859: Tantia Tope is captured, tried and killed (NCERT).
losses: Huge loss of life on both sides; villages burned and rebels hanged in thousands.
Delhi and Lucknow were badly damaged.
gains: The British kept India, but the Company lost its rule.
outcomes: The British Parliament passed a new Act in 1858 and transferred power from the Company to the British Crown (NCERT).
Bahadur Shah Zafar was sentenced to life imprisonment and sent to Rangoon in October 1858; he died there in November 1862 (NCERT).
The army was reorganised: more European soldiers, fewer sepoys from Awadh and Bihar.
Annexation stopped; ruling chiefs could pass their kingdoms to adopted heirs (NCERT).

participants.role: Attacked his officers at Barrackpore; hanged on 8 April 1857 (NCERT).
Reluctantly accepted the sepoys' call to lead; exiled to Rangoon (NCERT).
Came from Bareilly with a large force and became the rebels' key military leader in Delhi (NCERT).
Drove the British out of Kanpur and proclaimed himself Peshwa under Bahadur Shah (NCERT).
Nana Saheb's general; fought with Lakshmibai; kept up guerrilla war till 1859 (NCERT).
Organised the rising at Lucknow; her son Birjis Qadr was proclaimed Nawab (NCERT).
Joined the rebel sepoys at Jhansi; killed in battle in June 1858 (NCERT).
Old zamindar of Bihar who fought the British for many months (NCERT).
Maulvi of Faizabad; raised a huge force and fought at Lucknow (NCERT).
Rani of Ramgarh; led 4,000 men against the British (NCERT).
Led the peasants of 84 villages near Barout; killed in July 1857 (NCERT Class 12).
Governor-General during the revolt; became the first Viceroy (1858).
Took Jhansi and defeated Lakshmibai near Gwalior.
Led the assault on Delhi; mortally wounded.
Deposed Nawab of Awadh whose son was proclaimed Nawab at Lucknow (NCERT).
Late Peshwa; the refusal of his pension to his adopted son Nana Saheb was a grievance (NCERT).
His annexations, including Awadh (1856), were a major cause (NCERT).

facts: 10 May 1857: mutiny at Meerut; 11 May: sepoys reach Delhi (NCERT).
Mangal Pandey was hanged on 8 April 1857 (NCERT).
Delhi was recaptured in September 1857; Lucknow in March 1858 (NCERT).
Rani Lakshmibai was killed in June 1858; Tantia Tope was killed in April 1859 (NCERT).
Bahadur Shah Zafar died in the Rangoon jail in November 1862 (NCERT).

Centres and leaders: Delhi–Bahadur Shah Zafar and Bakht Khan; Kanpur–Nana Saheb; Lucknow–Begum Hazrat Mahal; Jhansi–Rani Lakshmibai; Bihar–Kunwar Singh; Bareilly–Khan Bahadur Khan; Faizabad–Maulvi Ahmadullah.
It led to the GoI Act 1858 (Government of India Act).
15 November (Birsa Munda's birthday) is Janjatiya Gaurav Divas; the Mappila (Moplah) revolts of Malabar ran from 1836 and peaked in 1921.

alsoOn.text: Lucknow retaken (March); Rani Lakshmibai killed (June); Bahadur Shah Zafar sent to Rangoon (October) (NCERT).
Tantia Tope is captured, tried and killed (April 1859) (NCERT).
Bahadur Shah Zafar dies in the Rangoon jail (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 100 years after Plassey (1757) — the Company's rule began and ended in a "57".

images.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author Cambridge University Press; Stanford's Geogl. Estabt.. / Wikimedia Commons

events.before: A century of annexation (Plassey 1757 to Awadh 1856), new land taxes, the **Doctrine of Lapse**, and sepoy grievances (GSEA 1856, the **Enfield** cartridge).
events.after: The Company was abolished (**1858**); the army was reorganised (more British, "martial races"); princes were kept as allies. The educated middle class did not join, and the south and Punjab stayed calm.
events.today: V. D. Savarkar called it "The Indian War of Independence" (1909); the British called it a "Sepoy Mutiny"; 2007 marked 150 years.
events.mnemonic: 1857 centres and leaders "D-K-L-J-B": Delhi (Bahadur Shah, Bakht Khan), Kanpur (Nana Saheb, Tantia Tope), Lucknow (Begum Hazrat Mahal), Jhansi (Lakshmibai), Bihar (Kunwar Singh).

events.title: Government of India Act 1858 and the Queen's Proclamation
events.summary: The British Parliament transferred the powers of the East India Company to the British Crown (NCERT).
events.detail:
After the revolt the British Parliament passed a new Act in 1858 and transferred the Company's powers to the British Crown, to ensure a more responsible management of Indian affairs (NCERT). A member of the British Cabinet became Secretary of State for India, with a council to advise him. The Governor-General was given the title of Viceroy — a personal representative of the Crown (NCERT).

Lord Canning read Queen Victoria's Proclamation at Allahabad on 1 November 1858.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 5; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
causes: The revolt of 1857 showed that the Company could not govern India safely (NCERT).
course: August 1858: the Government of India Act is passed.
The Board of Control and Court of Directors are abolished.
A Secretary of State for India and a 15-member Council of India are created in London.
1 November 1858: the Queen's Proclamation is read at Allahabad.

treaties.name: Queen Victoria's Proclamation
between: the people and princes of India
terms: Ruling chiefs could pass their kingdoms to adopted heirs; no more annexation (NCERT).
Indian religions and customs would not be interfered with (NCERT).
Indians would be admitted to offices "freely and impartially".
Pardon for rebels, except those who had killed British subjects.

gains: Princes: security of their thrones.
losses: The East India Company lost its rule.
outcomes: The Governor-General became the Viceroy; Lord Canning was the first (NCERT).
The army was reorganised: more Europeans, recruitment from "loyal" groups (NCERT).
facts: Act of 1858: the Company's powers went to the British Crown (NCERT).
The Governor-General became the Viceroy (NCERT).
Queen's Proclamation: Allahabad, 1 November 1858.

pairs.left: First Secretary of State for India

events.yearHook: 2 August 1858: the Act; 1 November 1858: the Queen's Proclamation read at Allahabad by Canning.

participants.role: Became the first Viceroy and read the Proclamation at Allahabad.
In whose name India was now ruled.
First Secretary of State for India.

events.before: The revolt of **1857** showed the Company could no longer rule.
events.after: A **Secretary of State for India** with a council of 15 replaced the Board of Control and Directors; the Governor-General became **Viceroy** (Canning). The Proclamation promised no more annexations and respect for religion.
events.today: The India Office continued until 1947.

events.title: Dayananda founds the Arya Samaj
events.summary: Swami Dayananda Saraswati founds the Arya Samaj at Bombay to reform Hinduism (NCERT).
events.detail: Dayananda founded the Arya Samaj in 1875, an organisation that attempted to reform Hinduism (NCERT). He rejected idol worship, caste by birth and child marriage, and supported widow remarriage (NCERT). His call was "Back to the Vedas". After his death his followers started the Dayanand Anglo-Vedic (DAV) schools.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 7; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)
causes: Belief that Hinduism must return to the pure teachings of the Vedas.
Opposition to idol worship, caste and child marriage.
outcomes: Spread widely in the Punjab and north India.
DAV school founded at Lahore (1886); the Shuddhi movement.
facts: Dayanand founded the Arya Samaj in 1875 (NCERT).
Satyarth Prakash was his main book.

Reform bodies: Seva Sadan (Bombay, 1908) — Behramji M. Malabari with Dayaram Gidumal; Deva Samaj (Lahore, 1887) — Shiv Narayan Agnihotri (Radhakant Deb led the orthodox Dharma Sabha, 1830); Seva Samiti (Allahabad, 1914) — Hriday Nath Kunzru; Social Service League (Bombay, 1911) — N. M. Joshi (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).

alsoOn.text: The Prarthana Samaj is established at Bombay (NCERT).
The Veda Samaj is established at Madras (NCERT).
Keshab Chandra Sen founds the Brahmo Samaj of India after a split.

events.yearHook: 1875: Arya Samaj, Aligarh college and the Theosophical Society (New York) — one busy year.
events.before: **Dayananda Saraswati** (born in Gujarat, 1824) rejected idol worship, caste by birth and the Puranas.
events.after: The **DAV** (Dayanand Anglo-Vedic) schools began (Lahore, 1886); the Samaj split into the DAV group (Lala Hansraj) and the **Gurukul** group (Swami Shraddhanand, Kangri 1902). It was strong in Punjab.
events.today: DAV schools are one of India's largest private school networks.
events.mnemonic: Dayananda "B-V-S": Bombay (Arya Samaj, 1875), "Back to the Vedas", Satyarth Prakash, Shuddhi.

events.title: Kandukuri Veeresalingam — Telugu social reform
events.summary: Kandukuri Veeresalingam performs the first widow remarriage in Andhra at Rajahmundry (11 December 1881).
events.detail: By the second half of the 19th century the movement for widow remarriage spread to other parts of India. In the Telugu-speaking areas of the Madras Presidency, Veerasalingam Pantulu formed an association for widow remarriage (NCERT). He also founded schools for girls, wrote the first Telugu novel and ran the reform journal Vivekavardhini.
causes: The plight of child widows.
The 1856 Act made remarriage legal, but society resisted.
outcomes: Began the Telugu Renaissance; he is called the "Father of the Telugu Renaissance".
facts: Veerasalingam Pantulu formed an association for widow remarriage in the Telugu-speaking areas (NCERT).
First widow remarriage in Andhra: Rajahmundry, 1881.
M.G. Ranade praised Veeresalingam as "the South Indian Ishwarachandra Vidyasagar" (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
Veeresalingam's Rajasekhara Charitam (1878) is the first Telugu novel; he opened the first girls' schools at Rajahmundry (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
The earliest Prarthana Samaj in Andhra was established in 1878 (Rajahmundry) by Kandukuri Veeresalingam (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).
events.yearHook: Widow Remarriage Act 1856 → Veeresalingam's first remarriage 1881.

participants.role: Organised the marriage and led the movement (NCERT).

events.before: Child marriage and the cruel treatment of widows were common in the Telugu country; the 1856 Act had changed little.
events.after: He founded the **Hitakarini Samaj** (1906) and gave his property to it; Gurajada's **Kanyasulkam** (1892) carried his cause onto the stage.
events.today: His statue stands on the Tank Bund, Hyderabad; 16 April, his birthday, is remembered in Rajahmundry.
events.mnemonic: Veeresalingam's "V-R-W-G": Vivekavardhini (1874), Rajasekhara Charitam (1878, first Telugu novel), Widow remarriage (1881), Girls' school (1874).

events.title: Resolution on Local Self-Government
events.summary: Ripon's Resolution of 18 May 1882 sets up elected local boards in districts and towns.
events.detail: Ripon wanted Indians to learn self-government. His Resolution created district and taluk boards and municipal committees with a majority of non-official, mostly elected, members, and an elected chairman where possible. He is called the "Father of Local Self-Government in India".
causes: Ripon's liberal belief in political education.
Need to share local costs and tasks with Indians.
outcomes: Local boards and municipalities spread across India.
The basis of later Panchayati Raj institutions.
facts: Resolution on Local Self-Government: 18 May 1882.
Ripon is called the Father of Local Self-Government in India.
events.yearHook: 1882: Ripon's busiest year — local self-government, Hunter Commission, press freed.
events.before: **Mayo** (1870) had begun financial decentralisation.
events.after: Ripon is called the "**father of local self-government**". He also repealed the Vernacular Press Act, set up the **Hunter Commission** (education, 1882) and tried the Ilbert Bill (1883).
events.today: The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave panchayats and municipalities constitutional status.

events.title: Indian National Congress founded
events.summary: 72 delegates from all over India meet at Bombay in December 1885 and found the Indian National Congress (NCERT).
events.detail:
The need for an all-India organisation of educated Indians had been felt since 1880, and the Ilbert Bill controversy deepened it (NCERT). The first session met at Gokuldas Tejpal Sanskrit College, Bombay, under W.C. Bonnerjee.

The early leadership — Dadabhai Naoroji, Pherozeshah Mehta, Badruddin Tyabji, W.C. Bonnerji, Surendranath Banerji, Romesh Chandra Dutt, S. Subramania Iyer and others — was largely from Bombay and Calcutta (NCERT). A retired British official, A.O. Hume, helped bring Indians together (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement"
causes: Political associations had grown in the 1870s and 1880s (NCERT).
Anger at the Arms Act, the Vernacular Press Act and the Ilbert Bill episode (NCERT).
The need for one all-India body (NCERT).
course: 28–31 December 1885: first session at Bombay, 72 delegates (NCERT).
W.C. Bonnerjee presides; A.O. Hume is the first General Secretary.
1886: the second session at Calcutta under Dadabhai Naoroji; the Indian Association merges in.
outcomes: The main platform of the national movement until 1947.
In its first twenty years it was "moderate" in aims and methods (NCERT).
facts: The INC was established when 72 delegates met at Bombay in December 1885 (NCERT).
First president: W.C. Bonnerjee; first General Secretary: A.O. Hume.
events.yearHook: 28 December 1885: 72 delegates at Gokuldas Tejpal College, Bombay.

participants.role: Retired British official who helped bring Indians together (NCERT).
Guided the younger nationalists from London; president in 1886 (NCERT).
Early leader; his Indian Association merged into the Congress.
Viceroy at the time; later called the Congress a "microscopic minority".

events.before: The **Ilbert Bill** row (1883) and the Indian Association's work had prepared the ground; **A. O. Hume**, a retired civil servant, brought leaders together.
events.after: The early Congress met once a year and passed petitions (the Moderate phase, 1885–1905). Later sessions: first woman president **Annie Besant** (Calcutta, 1917), first Indian woman **Sarojini Naidu** (Kanpur, 1925).
events.today: The "safety valve" theory (Hume made it to release Indian anger) is rejected by most historians (Bipan Chandra: a "lightning conductor").
events.mnemonic: First three presidents "B-D-B": W. C. Bonnerjee (Bombay 1885), Dadabhai Naoroji (Calcutta 1886), Badruddin Tyabji (Madras 1887, first Muslim president).

events.title: The Moderate phase of the Congress
events.summary: For its first twenty years the Congress was "moderate": it petitioned for reforms through peaceful, constitutional means (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Moderates demanded a greater voice for Indians in government: more representative and powerful Legislative Councils, Indians in high posts, civil service exams in India as well as London, separation of judiciary and executive, repeal of the Arms Act and freedom of speech (NCERT). They also showed how British rule drained India's wealth: Dadabhai Naoroji's Drain Theory and R.C. Dutt's economic histories.

Their methods — petitions, speeches, articles — came to be criticised by the Radicals as "politics of prayers" (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement"
causes: Faith in British justice and in gradual reform.
course: Demand for expanded councils and Indianisation of services (NCERT).
Economic critique: the Drain of Wealth.
Petitions, resolutions and memorials to the government.
outcomes: Built national awareness and exposed the economic exploitation of India.
By the 1890s many Indians questioned their methods (NCERT); the Radicals rose after 1905.
facts: In its first twenty years the Congress was "moderate" in its objectives and methods (NCERT).
Radicals called the Moderates' methods "politics of prayers" (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Moderate phase: 1885–1905 — twenty years, ending with the partition of Bengal.

participants.role: Leading Moderate; founded the Servants of India Society (1905).
Moderate leader and reformer of Bombay.

events.before: Educated Indians believed in British justice and wanted reform within the empire.
events.after: They won the **1892 Act**, simultaneous ICS exam resolution (1893) and exposed the **drain of wealth** (Naoroji's *Poverty and Un-British Rule in India*, 1901). Their methods ("prayer, petition, protest") lost ground after 1905.
events.today: Naoroji was the first Asian member of the British Parliament (1892, Finsbury Central).
events.mnemonic: Moderate leaders "D-G-P-S-R": Dadabhai Naoroji (drain theory), Gokhale, Pherozeshah Mehta, Surendranath Banerjea, Ranade.

events.title: Gurajada Apparao writes Kanyasulkam
events.summary: Landmark Telugu social play attacking bride-price; modern Telugu literature.
events.detail: Kanyasulkam (1892) is a Telugu social play that mocks the custom of bride price — old men paying to marry young girls — and the hypocrisy of the village elite. It was written in spoken Telugu, not the formal literary language, and is counted among the great Indian plays.
causes: The social evil of kanyasulkam (bride price) and child marriage in coastal Andhra.
outcomes: Began modern Telugu drama and the use of spoken Telugu in literature.
events.yearHook: 1892: first staged at Vizianagaram; 11 years after Veeresalingam's first widow remarriage (1881).

participants.role: Earlier reformer whose campaign against such customs Gurajada carried into literature.

events.before: **Veeresalingam** had attacked child marriage and the bride price; Gurajada worked at the Vizianagaram court.
events.after: Kanyasulkam used **spoken** Telugu and characters like **Girisam** and **Madhuravani**; it supported the spoken-language movement of **Gidugu**. His song "Desamante matti kadoi" (Mutyala Saralu) is a national poem.
events.today: Gurajada's house at Vizianagaram is a memorial; Kanyasulkam is still staged.

events.title: GI Act 1999: Andhra handlooms protected
events.summary: The Geographical Indications of Goods Act, 1999 (in force 2003) lets traditional products be protected; Andhra handlooms such as Uppada Jamdani, Mangalagiri, Venkatagiri and Dharmavaram sarees later get GI tags.
events.detail:
The Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999 lets traditional products be registered. Andhra handlooms such as Uppada Jamdani, Mangalagiri, Venkatagiri and Dharmavaram sarees have GI tags.

**Exam hooks:** AP GI textiles — Uppada Jamdani, Mangalagiri, Venkatagiri, Dharmavaram.
causes: India's obligations under the WTO TRIPS agreement (1995).
outcomes: First Indian GI: Darjeeling tea (2004).
Andhra GIs include Kondapalli toys, Tirupati laddu, Srikalahasti Kalamkari and Etikoppaka toys.
events.yearHook: WTO 1995 → GI Act 1999.
events.before: TRIPS (WTO, 1994) required countries to protect geographical indications; India passed the GI Act (1999).
events.after: Darjeeling tea got India's first GI (2004–05). AP got many handloom and food GIs.
events.today: Araku Valley coffee (GI 2019) is grown by tribal farmers in the Eastern Ghats.
events.mnemonic: AP handloom GIs "U-M-V-D": Uppada Jamdani, Mangalagiri, Venkatagiri, Dharmavaram. Food GIs "T-B-B-A": Tirupati laddu, Bandar laddu, Banganapalle mango, Araku coffee.

events.title: Partition of Bengal
events.summary: In 1905 Viceroy Curzon partitioned Bengal; it infuriated people all over India (NCERT).
events.detail:
Bengal was the biggest province of British India and included Bihar and parts of Orissa. The British argued for dividing it for "administrative convenience". But instead of removing the non-Bengali areas, the government separated East Bengal and merged it with Assam. The main British motives were probably to curtail the influence of Bengali politicians and to split the Bengali people (NCERT).

All sections of the Congress — Moderates and Radicals — opposed it. Large public meetings and demonstrations were organised, and novel methods of mass protest developed (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement"; Standard modern Indian history (Spectrum / Bipan Chandra)

sides.name: Indian nationalists
sides.ruler: Moderates and Radicals of the Congress

causes: "Administrative convenience" — the official reason (NCERT).
To curtail the influence of Bengali politicians and split the Bengali people (NCERT).
East Bengal (Muslim majority) was separated and merged with Assam (NCERT).
course: July 1905: the partition is announced.
7 August 1905: a meeting at Calcutta Town Hall adopts the boycott of British goods.
16 October 1905: the partition comes into force; it is observed as a day of mourning. Rabindranath Tagore leads Raksha Bandhan as a sign of unity.
The Swadeshi movement spreads: boycott of foreign goods, national schools, swadeshi industries.
outcomes: The Swadeshi movement and the rise of the Radicals (NCERT).
The partition was annulled in 1911 and the capital moved to Delhi.
facts: In 1905 Viceroy Curzon partitioned Bengal (NCERT).
East Bengal was separated and merged with Assam (NCERT).
The partition took effect on 16 October 1905.

alsoOn.text: The partition of Bengal is annulled at the Delhi Durbar; the capital moves from Calcutta to Delhi.

events.yearHook: Announced 19 July 1905; in force 16 October 1905 (observed as a day of mourning, raksha bandhan). Annulled 1911.

participants.role: Led Raksha Bandhan and wrote songs of protest.
Condemned the partition as Congress president at Benares (1905).
Led the anti-partition campaign in Bengal.
Radical leader who spread the boycott beyond Bengal.
Took over as Viceroy in November 1905.

events.before: **Curzon** said Bengal was too large to rule; nationalists saw "divide and rule" — a Muslim-majority east and Hindu-majority west.
events.after: Swadeshi and boycott spread across India (Andhra: **Bipin Chandra Pal**'s tour, 1907). **Tagore** wrote "Amar Sonar Bangla". The Congress declared **swaraj** the goal (1906). The partition was annulled in **1911**.
events.today: "Amar Sonar Bangla" is Bangladesh's national anthem.
events.mnemonic: Swadeshi tools "B-S-N-S": Boycott, Swadeshi goods, National education, Samitis (volunteer bodies).

events.title: Curzon's reforms
events.summary: Curzon (1899–1905) reorganises the universities, police, frontier and archaeology — and treats Indian opinion with contempt.
events.detail: Curzon believed in efficient, centralised rule. He cut the elected members of the Calcutta Corporation (1899), created the North-West Frontier Province (1901), appointed Police (1902) and Universities (1902) Commissions, passed the Indian Universities Act (1904) and the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904), and sent the Younghusband mission to Tibet (1903–04). He resigned in 1905 after a quarrel with the commander-in-chief, Kitchener.
causes: Curzon's belief that Indians were not fit to govern themselves.
Fear of Russia in Tibet and the north-west.
course: 1899: Calcutta Corporation Act cuts elected members.
1901: North-West Frontier Province created.
1902: Police and Universities Commissions.
1903: Delhi Durbar for Edward VII.
1904: Universities Act; Ancient Monuments Preservation Act; Treaty of Lhasa.
1905: partition of Bengal; Curzon resigns.
outcomes: Educated Indians saw his measures as attacks on self-government and education.
His partition of Bengal united Indians against him.

alsoOn.text: Curzon creates the North-West Frontier Province.
Indian Universities Act and Ancient Monuments Preservation Act passed.
Curzon holds the Delhi Durbar for King Edward VII.

events.yearHook: Curzon: arrives 1899, partition 1905 — six years.

participants.role: Viceroy who carried out the reforms.

events.before: Curzon (1899–1905) was a confident imperialist who believed the Congress was "tottering to its fall".
events.after: The **Partition of Bengal** (1905) turned moderates into agitators and began the **Swadeshi** movement. Curzon resigned (1905) after a quarrel with Kitchener over the army.
events.today: The Archaeological Survey and the 1904 Monuments Act shaped how India protects its heritage; the Victoria Memorial was his idea.
events.mnemonic: Curzon's "U-P-A-N-B": Universities Act (1904), Police Commission (Fraser), Ancient Monuments Act (1904), NWFP (1901), Bengal partition (1905).

events.title: Surat split of the Congress
events.summary: At Surat in December 1907 the Congress split into Moderates and Radicals (NCERT).
events.detail: The Moderates were opposed to the use of boycott; they felt it involved the use of force. After the split the Congress was dominated by the Moderates, with Tilak's followers functioning from outside. The two groups reunited in December 1915 (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"

sides.name: Moderates
sides.ruler: Pherozeshah Mehta, Gokhale, Rash Behari Ghosh

sides.name: Radicals
sides.ruler: Tilak, Lajpat Rai, Bipin Chandra Pal, Aurobindo

causes: The Moderates opposed boycott (NCERT).
Dispute over who would preside and whether to continue Swadeshi and boycott.
course: December 1907: the session breaks up in chaos.
The Moderates hold their own session and keep the Congress.
outcomes: The Congress was dominated by the Moderates (NCERT).
Reunited in December 1915; Lucknow Pact next year (NCERT).
facts: The Congress split in 1907 (NCERT).
Rash Behari Ghosh was the president-designate at Surat.

pairs.right: Lajpat Rai, Tilak, Bipin Chandra Pal

events.yearHook: Split 1907, reunited 1915 (NCERT).
events.before: Extremists (Tilak) wanted Lajpat Rai as president and the Calcutta resolutions kept; Moderates chose **Rash Behari Ghosh**.
events.after: The Congress split; the government jailed Tilak (1908) and used repression and the 1909 reforms to win the Moderates. They reunited at **Lucknow** (1916).
events.today: A standard example of ideological split in a national movement.

events.title: First Andhra Mahasabha at Bapatla
events.summary: The first Andhra Mahasabha meets at Bapatla (May 1913) and demands a separate Andhra province.
events.detail: Telugu speakers felt neglected in the Madras Presidency, where Tamils dominated jobs and education. The first Andhra Conference (Mahasabha) met at Bapatla under Bayya Narasimha Sarma. Later sessions pressed for a separate province; in 1918 the Congress created a separate Andhra Provincial Congress Committee.
events.source: Andhra history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Telugu speakers were a minority in jobs and colleges of the Madras Presidency.
Linguistic pride after the Vandemataram movement.
outcomes: A separate Andhra PCC (1918) — the Congress accepted linguistic provinces in principle (Nagpur, 1920).
Led to Andhra State (1953).
facts: First Andhra Mahasabha: Bapatla, 1913; president Bayya Narasimha Sarma.
Andhra Provincial Congress Committee formed in 1918.

Andhra Mahasabha presidents: 1st (Bapatla, 1913) — Baiya Narasimheswara Sarma; 2nd — Nyapati Subba Rao; 3rd — Raja Rama Rayaningar (Raja of Panagal); 4th — Mocharla Ramachandra Rao (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

alsoOn.text: The Congress creates a separate Andhra Provincial Congress Committee.

events.yearHook: Andhra Mahasabha 1913 → Andhra State 1953 — forty years.

participants.role: A key organiser; first president of the Andhra PCC.

events.before: Telugu speakers were about 40% of the Madras Presidency but had few jobs and colleges. The **Bengal** partition debate had made language a political issue.
events.after: The Congress made a separate **Andhra PCC** (1918) and accepted language-based provinces at **Nagpur** (1920). The demand led to **Andhra University** (1926), the **Sri Bagh Pact** (1937) and **Andhra State** (1953).
events.today: Bapatla (now a district HQ) has a memorial to the first Andhra Mahasabha.
events.mnemonic: Andhra movement milestones "13-18-26-37-52-53-56": Bapatla, Andhra PCC, Andhra University, Sri Bagh, Potti Sriramulu, Andhra State, AP.

events.title: World War I
events.summary: Global war; India contributed troops and money, fuelling nationalist demands.
events.detail:
Post-war disillusion (Rowlatt, Jallianwala) intensified the freedom struggle.

**Exam hooks:** WWI (1914–18); Treaty of Versailles (1919); League of Nations.
causes: Rivalry among European powers.
outcomes: Defence spending, taxes and prices rose sharply in India; business groups profited (NCERT).
Soldiers returning from abroad wanted to oppose colonial rule (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1914–18: the war years; Gandhi came back in 1915.

events.title: Lucknow Pact and the Home Rule Leagues
events.summary: In 1916 the Congress and the Muslim League sign the Lucknow Pact; Tilak and Annie Besant start Home Rule Leagues (NCERT).
events.detail: After the Moderates and Radicals reunited (December 1915), the Congress and the League signed the historic Lucknow Pact and decided to work together for representative government (NCERT). The Congress accepted separate electorates. In 1916 Tilak (April, Poona) and Annie Besant (September, Madras) started Home Rule Leagues.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
causes: Both wanted self-government after the war.
Muslim anger at Britain's war against Turkey.

treaties.name: Lucknow Pact
terms: Joint demand for self-government.
The Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims.
Muslims to get more seats than their share in minority provinces.

outcomes: Hindu–Muslim cooperation until the Khilafat–Non-Cooperation movement.
Acceptance of separate electorates had lasting effects.
facts: Lucknow Pact: 1916, between the Congress and the League (NCERT).
Annie Besant founded the newspapers Commonweal and New India (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
events.yearHook: Congress reunites 1915, joins the League 1916.

participants.role: Played an important role in making the pact (NCERT).
Backed the pact; started a Home Rule League.
Started the Home Rule League at Madras.

events.before: The Moderates and Extremists reunited; the League under **Jinnah** came closer to the Congress during World War I.
events.after: The Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims; both demanded self-government. The **August Declaration** (1917) promised "responsible government".
events.today: The only time the Congress and League made a joint scheme; critics say it legitimised separate electorates.
events.mnemonic: 1916 "two leagues, one pact": Tilak's Home Rule League (April, Belgaum), Besant's (September, Madras); Lucknow Pact (December).

events.title: Champaran Satyagraha — Gandhi's first in India
events.summary: Indigo cultivators' struggle in Bihar; first Indian satyagraha.
events.detail: Indigo planters in Champaran (Bihar) forced peasants to grow indigo on part of their land (the tinkathia system). Raj Kumar Shukla invited Gandhi. Gandhi defied an order to leave and was joined by Rajendra Prasad and others (NCERT). The government appointed an inquiry; the tinkathia system was abolished.
causes: The tinkathia system: indigo on 3/20 of every peasant's land.
Low prices and illegal dues demanded by planters.
outcomes: The tinkathia system was abolished; peasants got part of their money back.
Gandhi's first satyagraha in India.
facts: Champaran (1917) was Gandhi's first satyagraha in India.
He was invited by Raj Kumar Shukla.
events.yearHook: April 1917: two years after Gandhi's return.
events.before: Indigo planters forced Bihar peasants to grow indigo on 3/20 of their land (**tinkathia**); **Rajkumar Shukla** invited Gandhi.
events.after: Gandhi defied an order to leave; an inquiry ended tinkathia. **Rajendra Prasad**, **J. B. Kripalani** and **Mazharul Haq** joined him.
events.today: Its centenary (2017) was marked as "Champaran Satyagraha Shatabdi".

events.title: Russian Revolution
events.summary: Bolshevik Revolution establishes the world's first socialist state.
events.detail:
Influenced socialist thought in the Indian national movement.

**Exam hooks:** 1917 October Revolution; Lenin; inspired "Socialist" in the Preamble (42nd).
causes: War, hunger and the autocracy of the Tsar.
outcomes: News of workers' and peasants' struggles and socialist ideas inspired Indian nationalists (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1917 Russia → 1925 Communist Party of India (Kanpur).

events.title: Rowlatt Satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh
events.summary: Gandhi calls a satyagraha against the Rowlatt Act; on 13 April 1919 General Dyer fires on a crowd at Jallianwala Bagh, Amritsar (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Rowlatt Act curbed fundamental rights such as freedom of expression and strengthened police powers. Gandhi, Jinnah and others called it "devilish" and tyrannical (NCERT). Gandhi asked people to observe 6 April 1919 as a day of "humiliation and prayer" and hartal. It became the first all-India struggle, though mostly in cities (NCERT).

The government used brutal measures. The Jallianwala Bagh atrocities, inflicted by General Dyer in Amritsar on Baisakhi day (13 April), were part of this repression. Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
causes: The Rowlatt Act (March 1919) allowed arrest and trial without normal legal safeguards (NCERT).
Arrest of local leaders Dr Satyapal and Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew in Amritsar.
course: 6 April 1919: all-India hartal (NCERT).
13 April 1919: Dyer's troops fire on a crowd in the walled compound with one narrow exit (NCERT).
Martial law in Punjab; the Hunter Committee inquires.
losses: Official figure: 379 killed; Indian estimates over 1,000.
outcomes: Tagore gave up his knighthood (NCERT).
Gandhi turned against British rule completely; led to Non-Cooperation (1920).
facts: Rowlatt Satyagraha was the first all-India struggle against the British (NCERT).
Jallianwala Bagh: 13 April 1919, Baisakhi day (NCERT).

C. Sankaran Nair resigned from the Viceroy's Executive Council in protest against the Jallianwala Bagh massacre; Rabindranath Tagore renounced his knighthood; Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr Satyapal were the Amritsar leaders whose arrest led to the 13 April 1919 meeting (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).
events.yearHook: 13 April 1919 (Baisakhi): 379 killed by official count, more than 1,000 by Indian accounts.
events.before: The **Rowlatt Act** (March 1919) allowed arrest without trial; Gandhi called a hartal (6 April). **Dr Satyapal** and **Dr Saifuddin Kitchlew** were arrested in Amritsar.
events.after: **Tagore** returned his knighthood; the **Hunter Committee** went easy on **General Dyer**. **Udham Singh** shot **Michael O'Dwyer** in London (1940). Gandhi launched Non-Cooperation (1920).
events.today: The memorial in Amritsar was renovated in 2021; the bullet marks on the walls are kept.

events.title: Khilafat and Non-Cooperation Movement
events.summary: Gandhi joins the Khilafat leaders to launch Non-Cooperation (1920–22) against the "Punjab wrongs", the Khilafat wrong, and for Swaraj (NCERT).
events.detail:
In 1920 the British imposed a harsh treaty on the Turkish Sultan or Khalifa. The Khilafat leaders, Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali, wished to start a full Non-Cooperation Movement. Gandhi supported them and urged the Congress to campaign against the "Punjab wrongs", the Khilafat wrong and to demand swaraj (NCERT).

Thousands of students left government schools; lawyers such as Motilal Nehru, C.R. Das, C. Rajagopalachari and Asaf Ali gave up their practice; titles were surrendered, legislatures boycotted and foreign cloth burnt. Imports of foreign cloth fell drastically between 1920 and 1922 (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
causes: Jallianwala Bagh and martial law in Punjab (NCERT).
The harsh treaty on the Khalifa (1920) (NCERT).
Disappointment with the 1919 reforms.
course: August 1920: Khilafat committee and Gandhi start Non-Cooperation.
September 1920: special Calcutta Congress approves it; December 1920: Nagpur Congress confirms.
1921–22: boycott of schools, courts, councils and foreign cloth (NCERT).
February 1922: called off after Chauri Chaura (NCERT).
outcomes: Turned the Congress into a mass organisation.
Hindu–Muslim unity reached its height.
facts: Non-Cooperation gained momentum through 1921–22 (NCERT).
Imports of foreign cloth fell drastically between 1920 and 1922 (NCERT).

National institutions of Non-Cooperation: Jamia Millia Islamia (Aligarh, 1920; later Delhi), Kashi Vidyapith, Gujarat Vidyapith and Bihar Vidyapith. Not from NCM: Aligarh Muslim University (1920, from the 1875 MAO College) and Besant Theosophical College, Madanapalle (1915) (APPSC Group-1 key).

The All India Trade Union Congress (AITUC) was founded at Bombay on 31 October 1920; its first session was presided over by Lala Lajpat Rai, with N. M. Joshi among the founders (APPSC Group-II 2023 key).
events.yearHook: Approved at Calcutta (special session, September 1920) and Nagpur (December 1920); called off February 1922.

participants.role: Presided over the special Calcutta session.

events.before: Jallianwala Bagh (1919), the Hunter report, and the harsh **Treaty of Sevres** on the Turkish Caliph (Khilafat; **Ali brothers**).
events.after: Lawyers like **C. R. Das** and **Motilal Nehru** gave up practice; national schools (**Jamia Millia**, **Kashi Vidyapith**) were founded; in Andhra came Chirala-Perala and Palnadu. It ended after **Chauri Chaura** (1922).
events.today: Its Hindu-Muslim unity is seen as the high point of joint struggle.
events.mnemonic: Non-Cooperation "B-B-B-B": Boycott of councils, courts, colleges and British cloth; plus swadeshi, khadi and the Tilak Swaraj Fund.

events.title: Pingali Venkayya designs the national flag
events.summary: Machilipatnam-born freedom fighter designs the tricolour.
events.detail: At the Congress meeting at Bezawada (Vijayawada) in 1921, Pingali Venkayya presented a flag design to Gandhi — red and green for the two main communities, to which a white stripe and the charkha were added. In 1931 the Congress adopted the saffron-white-green tricolour with the charkha; in 1947 the Ashoka Chakra replaced the charkha.
causes: The Congress needed a common flag for the national movement.
outcomes: Basis of the national flag adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 22 July 1947.
events.yearHook: Bezawada 1921 → tricolour adopted 1931 → Ashoka Chakra 1947.

participants.role: Asked for the white stripe and charkha.
The Ashoka Chakra is on the flag.

events.before: Pingali, born at Bhatlapenumarru near Machilipatnam (1876), had served in the Boer War and in 1916 published a book of 30 flag designs.
events.after: The Congress Flag Committee (1931) chose saffron, white and green with the charkha; the Constituent Assembly adopted the flag with the Ashoka Chakra on **22 July 1947**.
events.today: A postage stamp was issued in his honour (2009).

events.title: Harappa discovered (ASI, 1921)
events.summary: Daya Ram Sahni excavates Harappa; Mohenjo-daro (Banerji) follows in 1922.
events.detail:
Brought the Indus Civilisation to modern knowledge.

**Exam hooks:** Harappa 1921 (Sahni); Mohenjo-daro 1922 (R.D. Banerji); John Marshall announced it.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Themes I, Ch. 1 "Bricks, Beads and Bones"
causes: Seals found at Harappa were in layers much older than early historic levels (NCERT).
outcomes: John Marshall announced a new civilisation in 1924 (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1921 Harappa (Daya Ram Sahni), 1922 Mohenjodaro (R. D. Banerji), 1924 announced by John Marshall.
events.before: In 1875 Alexander Cunningham had found a Harappan seal but did not know how old it was. For long, Indian history was thought to begin with the Vedas.
events.after: The discovery pushed Indian civilisation back by about 2,000 years, to the time of Egypt and Mesopotamia.
events.today: After 1947 most big sites were in Pakistan, so India searched afresh and found Kalibangan, Lothal, Dholavira and Rakhigarhi.

events.title: Rampa (Manyam) rebellion led by Alluri Sitarama Raju
events.summary: Tribal armed revolt in the Andhra Agency led by Alluri Sitarama Raju ("Manyam Veerudu").
events.detail:
The Madras Forest Act stopped the hill people of the Godavari and Visakhapatnam Agency from shifting cultivation (podu) and from using forest produce, and forced them to work on roads for contractors. Alluri Sitarama Raju organised them in guerrilla war. In August 1922 they raided the police stations at Chintapalle, Krishnadevipeta and Rajavommangi and took arms.

The British sent the Malabar Special Police and Assam Rifles. Alluri was captured and shot at Koyyuru on 7 May 1924.
events.place: Godavari and Visakhapatnam Agency (Rampa / Manyam hills)
causes: Forest laws banned podu cultivation and use of forest produce.
Forced labour on roads for contractors.
Exploitation by contractors and officials.
course: August 1922: raids on Chintapalle, Krishnadevipeta and Rajavommangi police stations.
1922–24: guerrilla war in the hills.
7 May 1924: Alluri captured and shot at Koyyuru.
outcomes: Crushed after two years; Alluri became a legend of Andhra.
facts: Alluri Sitarama Raju was shot at Koyyuru on 7 May 1924.
Gam Gantam Dora and Gam Mallu Dora were Alluri's chief lieutenants.
The first police station Alluri attacked was Chintapalli (August 1922) (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

pairs.right: Gam Gantam Dora, Gam Mallu Dora

alsoOn.text: Alluri Sitarama Raju is captured and shot at Koyyuru (7 May).

events.yearHook: August 1922: six months after Chauri Chaura (Feb 1922). Alluri is killed on 7 May 1924, aged 26.
events.before: The **1879 Rampa rebellion** had been crushed; new **forest laws** and **forced road labour** under contractors (and the officer Bastian) angered the Koyas and Konda Doras again.
events.after: The British spent lakhs and sent the **Malabar Special Police** and Assam Rifles; Alluri was caught and shot at **Koyyuru** (1924). His lieutenants **Gam Gantam Dora** and **Gam Mallu Dora** were later killed or jailed.
events.today: A new district (2022) is named Alluri Sitharama Raju; a 30-foot statue of him was unveiled at Bhimavaram (2022) for his 125th birth year.
events.mnemonic: Alluri's raids "C-K-R": Chintapalle, Krishnadevipeta, Rajavommangi (August 1922).

events.title: Tanguturi Prakasam "Andhra Kesari"
events.summary: Bared his chest to police guns in Madras; later first CM of Andhra State.
events.detail:
Symbol of Andhra nationalism; Prakasam district named after him.

**Exam hooks:** Tanguturi Prakasam = "Andhra Kesari"; first CM of Andhra State (1953).
causes: The Simon boycott in Madras (1928).
outcomes: Became a hero of Andhra; later first Chief Minister of Andhra State (1953).
events.yearHook: February 1928: the Simon Commission lands in Madras. First CM of Andhra State on 1 October 1953.

participants.role: Faced police guns at Madras; called "Andhra Kesari".

events.before: A successful lawyer, he gave up his practice for Non-Cooperation (1921) and started the paper **Swarajya**.
events.after: He was revenue minister in Madras (1937), briefly Premier of Madras (1946–47) and first CM of **Andhra State** (1953–54).
events.today: Prakasam district (1970) and the **Prakasam Barrage** at Vijayawada carry his name.
events.mnemonic: Prakasam "S-S-A": Simon (bared chest, 1928), Swarajya (his paper, 1921), Andhra State (first CM, 1953).

events.title: Bardoli Satyagraha
events.summary: Patel leads a no-tax peasant movement; earns the title "Sardar".
events.detail: The Bombay government raised land revenue in Bardoli taluka by about 22%. Vallabhbhai Patel organised a no-revenue campaign; the women of Bardoli gave him the title "Sardar". The government appointed the Maxwell–Broomfield inquiry, which cut the increase.
causes: A 22% increase in land revenue despite falling prices.
outcomes: The increase was reduced to about 6%; confiscated lands were returned.
events.yearHook: February–August 1928: the same year the Simon Commission came.

participants.role: Led the satyagraha; given the title "Sardar".

events.before: The Bombay government raised land revenue at **Bardoli** (Gujarat) by about 22%.
events.after: Peasants refused to pay; the **Maxwell-Broomfield** inquiry cut the increase to about 6%. Women of Bardoli gave Patel the title "**Sardar**".
events.today: Bardoli is the classic Gandhian peasant victory.

events.title: Simon Commission boycotted
events.summary: The all-white Simon Commission arrives in 1928 and is met everywhere with "Simon Go Back" (NCERT).
events.detail: In 1927 the British government decided to send a commission headed by Lord Simon to decide India's political future. It had no Indian representative, which created an outrage; all political groups decided to boycott it (NCERT). At Lahore, Lala Lajpat Rai was badly injured in a police lathi-charge and died. At Madras, Tanguturi Prakasam bared his chest to the police.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
causes: The commission had no Indian member (NCERT).
course: November 1927: commission announced (NCERT).
February 1928: it arrives; black flags and "Simon Go Back" (NCERT).
October 1928: lathi-charge at Lahore; Lajpat Rai dies in November.
outcomes: The Nehru Report (1928) answered the British challenge.
Bhagat Singh and his comrades avenged Lajpat Rai (NCERT).
facts: The Simon Commission had no Indian representative (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Arrives 3 February 1928; "Simon Go Back".

participants.role: Led the protest at Lahore; died after the lathi-charge (NCERT).
Bared his chest to police guns at Madras.
His League faction joined the boycott.
Avenged Lajpat Rai's death by killing Saunders (NCERT).

events.before: The 1919 Act had promised a review after ten years; the British sent seven MPs, all white (Attlee among them).
events.after: Protests everywhere: **Lala Lajpat Rai** was beaten at Lahore and died (November 1928); **Prakasam** bared his chest at Madras. The Congress answered with the **Nehru Report** (1928).
events.today: The commission's report (1930) fed into the 1935 Act.

events.title: Purna Swaraj declaration (Lahore Congress)
events.summary: Congress adopts complete independence; 26 Jan 1930 first Independence Day.
events.detail: The decade closed with the Congress resolving to fight for Purna Swaraj (complete independence) in 1929 under the presidentship of Jawaharlal Nehru. "Independence Day" was observed on 26 January 1930 all over the country (NCERT). Nehru hoisted the tricolour on the banks of the Ravi at Lahore.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
causes: The British did not accept the Nehru Report's Dominion Status by the end of 1929.
Younger leaders wanted complete independence.
outcomes: Independence Day observed on 26 January 1930 (NCERT) — later chosen as Republic Day (1950).
Civil Disobedience began in 1930.
facts: Purna Swaraj: Lahore Congress, 1929, president Jawaharlal Nehru (NCERT).
Independence Day: 26 January 1930 (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 31 December 1929: flag hoisted on the Ravi; 26 January 1930 observed as Independence Day.

participants.role: Moved the resolution and was asked to lead civil disobedience.

events.before: The British did not accept the Nehru Report's dominion status within the one-year deadline.
events.after: Under **Jawaharlal Nehru** the Congress declared complete independence and authorised civil disobedience. 26 January was chosen later as Republic Day (1950) in memory.
events.today: Republic Day (26 January) remembers the first Purna Swaraj Day.

events.title: Dandi March and Civil Disobedience
events.summary: Gandhi marches over 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi (12 March–6 April 1930) and breaks the salt law (NCERT).
events.detail:
Purna Swaraj had to be fought for. The state had a monopoly on making and selling salt; Gandhi reasoned it was sinful to tax so essential a food. The Salt March linked the desire for freedom to a grievance shared by everybody, and did not divide the rich and the poor (NCERT).

Gandhi and his followers marched over 240 miles from Sabarmati to Dandi, where they broke the law by gathering natural salt and boiling sea water (NCERT). Peasants and tribals joined; women took part — Sarojini Naidu had to persuade Gandhi to let them (NCERT). The government acted brutally and thousands were jailed (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
events.place: Sabarmati to Dandi (Gujarat), then all India
causes: The Purna Swaraj resolution (1929) (NCERT).
The salt tax hurt everyone (NCERT).
course: 12 March 1930: Gandhi leaves Sabarmati with 78 followers.
6 April 1930: he picks up salt at Dandi (NCERT).
Salt laws broken everywhere — Rajaji at Vedaranyam, Konda Venkatappayya and others along the Andhra coast.
May 1930: Gandhi arrested; Sarojini Naidu leads the raid on the Dharasana salt works.
Peshawar: Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan's Khudai Khidmatgars; Garhwal Rifles refuse to fire.
outcomes: Mass participation including women (NCERT).
Led to the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (1931).
facts: Dandi March: Sabarmati to Dandi, over 240 miles (NCERT).
Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930 (NCERT).
Sarojini Naidu is called Bharat Kokila, the "Nightingale of India"; she led the Dharasana salt raid after Gandhi's arrest (APPSC Group-II Mains 2018 P1 key).
events.yearHook: 12 March to 6 April 1930: 24 days, about 385 km, 78 marchers from Sabarmati.

participants.role: Persuaded Gandhi to include women; led the Dharasana raid (NCERT).
Led the movement in the North-West Frontier.

events.before: The Lahore Congress (1929) had authorised civil disobedience; Gandhi's **11 demands** to Irwin were ignored.
events.after: Salt laws were broken across India; **Dharasana** salt works raid (May 1930, Sarojini Naidu); about 90,000 arrested. It ended with the **Gandhi-Irwin Pact** (1931) and restarted in 1932.
events.today: The Dandi memorial (2019) stands at the beach in Navsari, Gujarat.
events.mnemonic: Salt marches by region "D-V-K-P": Dandi (Gandhi), Vedaranyam (Rajagopalachari, Tamil Nadu), Kakinada and Masulipatnam (Andhra), Peshawar (Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, Khudai Khidmatgars).

events.title: Gandhi–Irwin Pact
events.summary: Civil Disobedience suspended; Gandhi attends the Second Round Table Conference.
events.detail: After talks at Delhi, Gandhi and Irwin signed a pact. Gandhi called off Civil Disobedience and agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference; the government released prisoners not guilty of violence and allowed salt-making for personal use on the coast.
causes: Civil Disobedience and the failure of the First RTC.

treaties.name: Gandhi–Irwin Pact (Delhi Pact)
terms: Civil Disobedience suspended.
Congress to attend the Second RTC.
Release of non-violent prisoners.
Salt-making allowed for personal use near the coast.
Return of confiscated property not yet sold.

outcomes: Gandhi went to London; the pact did not save Bhagat Singh, which angered many young Indians.
events.yearHook: 5 March 1931 (Delhi Pact).

participants.role: Executed weeks later; the pact did not save him.

events.before: The Civil Disobedience movement had filled the jails; both sides wanted a pause.
events.after: Prisoners (except those charged with violence) freed; salt for personal use allowed near the sea; Congress to attend the 2nd RTC. The pact did not save **Bhagat Singh** (hanged 23 March 1931), angering the young.
events.today: The only time a Viceroy negotiated as an equal with Gandhi; Churchill sneered at the "half-naked fakir".

events.title: Poona Pact (Gandhi–Ambedkar)
events.summary: Replaces separate electorates for Depressed Classes with reserved seats.
events.detail: The Communal Award (August 1932) of Ramsay MacDonald gave separate electorates to the depressed classes. Gandhi, in Yerawada jail, fasted against it, fearing it would divide Hindu society. Ambedkar agreed to give up separate electorates in return for many more reserved seats in joint electorates.
causes: The Communal Award gave separate electorates to the depressed classes.
Gandhi's fast unto death in Yerawada jail (from 20 September 1932).

treaties.name: Poona Pact
terms: No separate electorates for the depressed classes.
148 seats reserved for them in provincial legislatures, instead of 71 under the Award.
Reserved seats in the central legislature too.

outcomes: Joint electorates with reserved seats — the basis of reserved constituencies today.
Gandhi began the Harijan campaign (Harijan Sevak Sangh, 1932).
events.yearHook: 24 September 1932: Gandhi's fast in Yerawada jail from 20 September.

participants.role: Fasted against the Award and signed the pact.

facts: Ramsay MacDonald announces the Communal Award (August); Third RTC in London.
events.before: The **Communal Award** (1932) gave separate electorates to the Depressed Classes; Gandhi fasted against it.
events.after: Ambedkar agreed to joint electorates with **148 reserved seats** (in place of 71 in the Award). Gandhi founded the **Harijan Sevak Sangh** (1932) and the paper **Harijan** (1933).
events.today: Reserved seats for SCs in the Constitution (Article 330, 332) grew out of it.

events.title: Visakhapatnam Port — a major eastern gateway
events.summary: One of India's major ports; deep natural harbour on the east coast.
events.detail:
Anchors AP's industrial & shipbuilding base.

**Exam hooks:** Vizag = major port + Eastern Naval Command HQ.
causes: Need for a deep-water port on the east coast between Madras and Calcutta.
outcomes: Grew into a major port and, later, a steel and shipbuilding centre.
events.yearHook: Vizag port 1933 → Hindustan Shipyard 1941.
facts: Visakhapatnam district's manganese industry once stood first in the world (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

events.title: Government of India Act, 1935
events.summary: Provincial autonomy & an all-India federation scheme — a template for the Constitution.
events.detail: The longest Act passed by the British Parliament for India. It prescribed provincial autonomy (NCERT): dyarchy ended in the provinces, and elected ministries ran all provincial subjects. An All-India Federation of provinces and princely states was planned but never came into being because the princes did not join. Dyarchy was introduced at the centre (on paper), a Federal Court (1937) was set up, Burma was separated from India, and separate electorates were extended.
causes: The Simon Report, the Round Table Conferences and the White Paper (1933).
The combined struggles of the Indian people (NCERT).
course: Provincial autonomy; dyarchy ended in provinces (NCERT).
Three lists of subjects: federal, provincial, concurrent.
Bicameral legislatures in six provinces.
Federal Court (1937); Reserve Bank of India (1935).
Franchise widened to about 10% of the population.
outcomes: Elections in 1937; Congress ministries in 7 of 11 provinces (NCERT).
Much of the Act was later used in the Constitution of India.

participants.role: Viceroy when the Act was passed.
Viceroy when it came into force (1937).

events.before: The Simon report, three Round Tables and a **White Paper** (1933).
events.after: Dyarchy moved from the provinces to the centre (never applied); provinces got autonomy and elections (1937). About 250 articles of the Constitution draw on it.
events.today: Called the "blueprint" of the Indian Constitution; Burma separated in 1937 under it.
events.mnemonic: 1935 Act "P-F-R-F": Provincial autonomy, Federation (never formed), RBI (1935), Federal Court (1937). The longest Act passed by the British Parliament for India.

events.title: Reserve Bank of India established
events.summary: India's central bank set up on the Hilton-Young Commission recommendation.
events.detail:
Nationalised in 1949.

**Exam hooks:** RBI (1935); functions — monetary authority, banker's bank, currency issue.
causes: The Hilton Young Commission (1926) recommended a central bank.
outcomes: Nationalised in 1949.
events.yearHook: RBI 1 April 1935 — the same year as the 1935 Act.

events.title: Sri Bagh Pact
events.summary: Coastal-Andhra & Rayalaseema leaders agree to share benefits within a future Andhra state.
events.detail: Rayalaseema leaders feared that coastal Andhra would dominate a future Andhra province. On 16 November 1937, leaders of both regions met at "Sri Bagh", the Madras house of Kasinathuni Nageswara Rao, and agreed on safeguards for Rayalaseema.

sides.name: Coastal Andhra leaders
sides.ruler: Pattabhi Sitaramayya, Konda Venkatappayya and others

causes: Rayalaseema's fear of domination by the more developed coastal districts.
Andhra University had been set up at Waltair, far from Rayalaseema.

treaties.name: Sri Bagh Pact
terms: A university centre in Rayalaseema (Anantapur).
Priority to Rayalaseema in Krishna, Tungabhadra and Pennar irrigation for ten years.
The capital and the High Court to be in different regions — one in Rayalaseema if wished.
Equal seats for both regions in the legislature.

outcomes: Basis of Kurnool becoming the capital of Andhra State (1953) and Guntur getting the High Court.
Sri Venkateswara University (Tirupati, 1954).
events.yearHook: 16 November 1937 — the year Congress ministries took office.

participants.role: The pact was signed at his house.

events.before: **Andhra University** went to Waltair (1926); Rayalaseema leaders formed their own Mahasabha and feared coastal domination.
events.after: When Andhra State was formed (1953) **Kurnool** became the capital and the High Court went to **Guntur** — the Sri Bagh idea in practice. The capital moved to Hyderabad in 1956.
events.today: After 2014 the pact was cited again in debates over the capital (Amaravati) and the High Court (the 2019 plan to make Kurnool a judicial capital).
events.mnemonic: Sri Bagh's four promises "U-W-S-C": University centres for Rayalaseema, Water (Krishna-Tungabhadra) first for Rayalaseema, Seats shared equally, Capital or High Court — Rayalaseema chooses.

events.title: World War II
events.summary: In September 1939 the Second World War breaks out; the Viceroy drags India into it, and the Congress ministries resign (NCERT).
events.detail:
Ended with the atomic bombings; reshaped the post-colonial order.

**Exam hooks:** WWII (1939–45); Cripps Mission & Quit India context.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
causes: German invasion of Poland (1 September 1939).
outcomes: Congress leaders were ready to support the war if India got independence after it; the British refused, and the Congress ministries resigned (NCERT).
The League celebrated "Deliverance Day" (22 December 1939).
events.yearHook: 1939: war, ministries resign, Bose's Forward Bloc.

participants.role: Declared India at war without consulting Indians.
Called the resignation of the ministries "Deliverance Day".

events.title: Quit India Movement
events.summary: "Do or Die"; the final mass movement demanding British withdrawal.
events.detail:
Gandhi decided to begin a new phase in the middle of the Second World War: the British must quit India immediately, and the people must "do or die" — but non-violently (NCERT). The resolution was passed at Gowalia Tank, Bombay, on 8 August 1942. Gandhi and other leaders were jailed at once, but the movement spread, attracting peasants and the youth (NCERT).

Communications and symbols of state authority were attacked; in many areas people set up their own governments (Ballia, Tamluk, Satara). By the end of 1943 over 90,000 people had been arrested and around 1,000 killed in police firing (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
causes: Failure of the Cripps Mission.
Japanese advance and British unwillingness to grant freedom.
course: 8 August 1942: Quit India resolution at Bombay; "Do or Die" (NCERT).
9 August: leaders arrested; Aruna Asaf Ali hoists the flag at Gowalia Tank.
Underground leadership: Jayaprakash Narayan, Ram Manohar Lohia; Usha Mehta's secret Congress Radio.
Parallel governments at Ballia, Tamluk and Satara.
Machine-gunning of crowds from aircraft in some areas (NCERT).
losses: Over 90,000 arrested and around 1,000 killed by the end of 1943 (NCERT).
outcomes: The rebellion ultimately brought the Raj to its knees (NCERT).
facts: Quit India: 8 August 1942; "Do or Die" (NCERT).
By the end of 1943 over 90,000 were arrested and around 1,000 killed (NCERT).
In Andhra the "Kurnool Circular" (1942) was drafted by Kala Venkata Rao (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
events.yearHook: 8 August 1942: resolution at Gowalia Tank, Bombay; 9 August: leaders arrested ("August Kranti").

participants.role: Hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank.

events.before: Cripps failed (April 1942); Japan was at India's door.
events.after: Without leaders, people attacked railways and police stations; parallel governments arose in **Ballia**, **Tamluk** (Jatiya Sarkar) and **Satara** (Prati Sarkar). In Andhra, **Tenali** and **Bhimavaram** rose. About 100,000 were arrested.
events.today: 9 August is Quit India Day (August Kranti Din).
events.mnemonic: Quit India "D-O-D": "Do or Die" (Karo ya Maro); Underground leaders "J-A-U-R": JP, Aruna Asaf Ali, Usha Mehta (Congress Radio), Ram Manohar Lohia.

events.title: Subhas Bose leads the INA
events.summary: In Singapore Subhas Bose takes charge of the Indian National Army and proclaims the Provisional Government of Free India (21 October 1943).
events.detail: A radical nationalist with socialist leanings, Bose did not share Gandhi's ideal of ahimsa, though he respected him as the "Father of the Nation" (NCERT). In January 1941 he secretly left his Calcutta home, went to Singapore via Germany, and raised the Azad Hind Fauj or INA (NCERT). In 1944 the INA tried to enter India through Imphal and Kohima, but the campaign failed (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
causes: Bose believed India should use the war to win freedom by force.
course: January 1941: Bose escapes from Calcutta (NCERT).
1942: the INA is formed from Indian prisoners of war (Mohan Singh, Rash Behari Bose).
July 1943: Bose takes command in Singapore; "Delhi Chalo".
21 October 1943: Provisional Government of Free India.
1944: the INA tries to enter India through Imphal and Kohima and fails (NCERT).
outcomes: INA soldiers were tried after the war; the trials united India (NCERT).
Bose was reported killed in an air crash at Taipei (August 1945).
facts: In 1944 the INA tried to enter India through Imphal and Kohima (NCERT).
Bose called Gandhi the "Father of the Nation" (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: Subhas Bose secretly leaves his Calcutta home and reaches Germany (NCERT).
The INA tries to enter India through Imphal and Kohima; the campaign fails (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 21 October 1943: Azad Hind government at Singapore; INA crosses into India (Manipur) in March–April 1944.

participants.role: Commanded the Rani of Jhansi Regiment.

events.before: **Mohan Singh** formed the first INA (1942) from Indian prisoners of Japan; **Rash Behari Bose** led the **Indian Independence League**.
events.after: Bose gave the slogan "**Dilli Chalo**" and "Give me blood, I will give you freedom"; the INA hoisted the flag at **Moirang** (Manipur, April 1944) and fought at **Imphal-Kohima**, then retreated. Bose died in a plane crash at Taipei (18 August 1945), by most accounts.
events.today: Port Blair's islands were renamed (Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose Island, 2018); his statue stands at India Gate (2022).
events.mnemonic: INA brigades "G-N-A + J": Gandhi, Nehru, Azad brigades, and the Rani of Jhansi regiment (Lakshmi Swaminathan).

events.title: Bretton Woods — IMF & World Bank
events.summary: Post-war monetary order; creates the IMF and the World Bank.
events.detail:
Foundation of the global financial architecture.

**Exam hooks:** IMF (stability) & World Bank (development); India a founder member.
causes: Planning for the post-war world economy.
outcomes: India was a founder member of the IMF and World Bank.
events.yearHook: Bretton Woods 1944 — IMF and World Bank.

events.title: United Nations founded
events.summary: UN established after WWII; India a founding member.
events.detail:
Security Council, ICJ, specialised agencies (UNESCO, WHO).

**Exam hooks:** UN (1945) HQ New York; India seeks a permanent UNSC seat.
causes: The failure of the League of Nations and the devastation of the Second World War.
outcomes: India, though not yet independent, signed the UN Charter as a founding member.
events.yearHook: UN Day: 24 October 1945.

events.title: Constituent Assembly convened
events.summary: First sitting under the Cabinet Mission Plan; Rajendra Prasad elected president.
events.detail:
Drafting Committee chaired by B.R. Ambedkar; Objectives Resolution by Nehru (1946).

**Exam hooks:** CA took 2 yrs 11 mo 18 days; B.N. Rau constitutional adviser.
causes: The Cabinet Mission plan provided for it.
outcomes: Framed the Constitution, adopted on 26 November 1949.
events.yearHook: First sitting 9 December 1946; Sachchidananda Sinha temporary chairman; Rajendra Prasad elected president on 11 December.

participants.role: Elected President of the Assembly (11 December 1946).

events.before: Members were elected by the provincial assemblies (July 1946) under the Cabinet Mission plan.
events.after: Nehru moved the **Objectives Resolution** (13 December 1946); the League boycotted. The Assembly took about 2 years 11 months to finish the Constitution (26 November 1949).
events.today: 26 November is Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas, since 2015).

events.title: Cabinet Mission Plan
events.summary: A three-member British cabinet mission (March 1946) proposes a united India as a loose confederation (NCERT).
events.detail: The mission (Pethick-Lawrence, Stafford Cripps and A.V. Alexander) suggested that India should remain united and constitute itself as a loose confederation with some autonomy for Muslim-majority areas. It could not get the Congress and the League to agree to details (NCERT). Its 16 May plan grouped provinces into three groups and provided for a constituent assembly and an interim government.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"
causes: The 1946 elections: the League swept the Muslim seats and pressed for Pakistan (NCERT).
course: March 1946: mission arrives in Delhi (NCERT).
16 May 1946: plan of groups A, B and C.
June–July 1946: both accept, then disagree over grouping.
outcomes: Partition now became more or less inevitable (NCERT).
The League called Direct Action Day (16 August 1946) (NCERT).
facts: In March 1946 the British cabinet sent a three-member mission to Delhi (NCERT).
events.yearHook: March 1946 → Direct Action August 1946.

participants.role: His remarks on grouping alarmed the League.

events.before: Attlee's Labour government (1945) wanted a quick, peaceful handover.
events.after: The plan (16 May 1946) rejected Pakistan but grouped provinces; it set up the **Constituent Assembly** (elected July 1946) and an **interim government**. The League withdrew and called **Direct Action** (16 August 1946).
events.today: The last attempt to keep India united.
events.mnemonic: Cabinet Mission members "P-C-A": Pethick-Lawrence, Cripps, A. V. Alexander. Groups "A-B-C": Hindu-majority (A), north-west Muslim (B), east Muslim (C).

events.title: Royal Indian Navy Mutiny
events.summary: Naval ratings revolt in Bombay — a final push before transfer of power.
events.detail: Ratings of HMIS Talwar in Bombay struck against bad food and racial insults; the strike spread to 78 ships and shore stations from Karachi to Calcutta. Patel persuaded them to surrender.
causes: Racial discrimination and poor conditions.
Inspiration from the INA trials.
outcomes: Showed that the British could no longer rely on Indian forces.
events.yearHook: 18 February 1946: HMIS Talwar, Bombay; spread to 78 ships and 20 shore units.
events.before: INA trials, racism and poor food angered Indian sailors.
events.after: Patel and Jinnah persuaded them to surrender; the British saw the armed forces could no longer be trusted. The **Cabinet Mission** arrived a month later.
events.today: Its memorial stands at Colaba, Mumbai.

events.title: Cold War & bipolar world order
events.summary: US–USSR rivalry; India's response was non-alignment.
events.detail:
Shaped India's foreign policy for decades.

**Exam hooks:** Cold War (1947–91); NAM as India's middle path.
causes: Rivalry between the USA and the USSR after the Second World War.
outcomes: India chose non-alignment; the Non-Aligned Movement was founded at Belgrade (1961).
events.yearHook: Cold War 1947–91 — it began the year India became free.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.summary: India becomes independent; Partition creates India and Pakistan.
events.detail: India became free at midnight on 14–15 August 1947, and Pakistan a day earlier. Partition, drawn by the Radcliffe Line, was followed by terrible violence: many hundred thousand people were killed and millions became refugees (NCERT). Gandhi spent the day in Calcutta working for peace. Nehru became Prime Minister and Mountbatten the first Governor-General of free India.
events.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"; NCERT Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 14 "Understanding Partitions"
causes: The Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947).
The Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947).
course: 14 August 1947: Pakistan becomes independent.
Midnight 14–15 August: Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech.
17 August: the Radcliffe Line is announced.
Months of riots and migration in Punjab and Bengal.
losses: Many hundred thousand killed; millions displaced (NCERT).
outcomes: Two dominions: India and Pakistan.
The integration of the princely states began.
events.yearHook: Midnight, 14–15 August 1947: Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny".

participants.role: Spent the day in Calcutta for peace.

events.before: The Indian Independence Act (18 July 1947) created two dominions.
events.after: About 10–15 million people moved across the new borders; perhaps a million died. **Mountbatten** stayed as Governor-General of India; Jinnah became Pakistan's Governor-General. Patel began integrating the princely states.
events.today: 14 August is now observed as Partition Horrors Remembrance Day (since 2021).

events.title: Integration of Princely States (Sardar Patel)
events.summary: Patel & V.P. Menon integrate 560+ princely states via the Instrument of Accession.
events.detail:
Junagadh, Hyderabad and Kashmir were the difficult cases.

**Exam hooks:** Patel = "Iron Man / Bismarck of India"; Statue of Unity.
causes: British paramountcy lapsed on 15 August 1947; over 560 princely states had to choose.
outcomes: Almost all states joined India by 15 August 1947; Junagadh (plebiscite, 1948), Hyderabad (police action, 1948) and Kashmir (accession, October 1947) were special cases.
events.yearHook: Most states signed by 15 August 1947; Hyderabad (1948), Manipur (1949) and others later.

participants.role: As Home Minister, led the integration.
Persuaded princes to sign the Instrument of Accession.
Secretary of the States Department who worked with Patel.

facts: Praja Mandal / states people's leaders: Vijay Singh Pathik (Rajasthan, Bijolia), Sewa Singh Thikriwala (Punjab, Patiala), Sarangadhar Das (Orissa), Balwant Rai Mehta (Kathiawar/Gujarat — not Madhya Pradesh) (APPSC Group-1 key).
The All India States People's Conference was formed in 1927.
events.before: The Indian Independence Act let the 560-plus princely states choose India or Pakistan, or stay free. The **All India States People's Conference** (1927) had fought for democracy in the states.
events.after: Patel and **V. P. Menon** used the **Instrument of Accession** (defence, foreign affairs, communications) and then mergers and unions (Rajasthan, PEPSU, Saurashtra). **Privy purses** were given to princes and abolished by the 26th Amendment (1971).
events.today: Patel's Statue of Unity (2018) honours this work.
events.mnemonic: Three hard cases "J-H-K": Junagadh (plebiscite, February 1948), Hyderabad (Operation Polo, September 1948), Kashmir (accession, October 1947).

events.title: Objectives Resolution → Preamble
events.summary: Nehru's Objectives Resolution (1946) becomes the basis of the Preamble.
events.detail:
Sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic; justice, liberty, equality, fraternity.

**Exam hooks:** Preamble = "identity card of the Constitution" (N.A. Palkhivala).
causes: The Assembly needed guiding principles.
outcomes: Its ideas became the Preamble of the Constitution.
events.yearHook: Moved by Nehru on 13 December 1946; adopted on 22 January 1947.

participants.role: Drafting Committee chairman who shaped the Preamble.
Called the Preamble the "identity card of the Constitution".

events.before: The Assembly met first on 9 December 1946; the League stayed away.
events.after: It became the **Preamble**: sovereign, democratic republic; justice, liberty, equality, fraternity. "**Socialist**", "**secular**" and "**integrity**" were added by the **42nd Amendment** (1976).
events.today: The Supreme Court held the Preamble part of the Constitution (Kesavananda, 1973), reversing Berubari (1960).

events.title: Operation Polo — Hyderabad joins India
events.summary: The Indian army moves into Hyderabad on 13 September 1948; the Nizam surrenders on 17 September and Hyderabad joins India (NCERT).
events.detail:
Hyderabad, the largest princely state, was surrounded entirely by Indian territory. Its ruler, the Nizam, wanted independence and signed a Standstill Agreement with India in November 1947 for a year (NCERT).
