Meanwhile a people's movement against the Nizam gathered force, especially among the Telangana peasantry; the Communists and the Hyderabad Congress were in the forefront (NCERT). The Nizam let loose the razakars, a para-military force whose atrocities "knew no bounds" (NCERT).

In September 1948 the army moved in. After a few days of intermittent fighting the Nizam surrendered, and Hyderabad acceded to India (NCERT). J.N. Chaudhuri became Military Governor; the Nizam was later made Rajpramukh.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"

sides.name: India
sides.strength: One armoured division and supporting brigades

causes: The Nizam wanted independent status (NCERT).
Razakar atrocities against the people (NCERT).
The Telangana people's revolt against the Nizam (NCERT).
Hyderabad was surrounded by India (NCERT).
course: November 1947: Standstill Agreement for one year (NCERT).
13 September 1948: the army moves in from Sholapur and Bezawada.
17 September: the Nizam announces surrender; El Edroos surrenders to J.N. Chaudhuri on 18 September.
losses: Several hundred soldiers and razakars killed in five days; communal killings followed in some districts.
outcomes: Hyderabad joined India (NCERT).
Military government under J.N. Chaudhuri (1948–49), then M.K. Vellodi; elected government under Burgula Ramakrishna Rao (1952).
The state was split in 1956: Telangana went to Andhra Pradesh, other parts to Bombay (Maharashtra) and Mysore (Karnataka) (NCERT).

treaties.name: Standstill Agreement
terms: Status quo for one year while talks went on (NCERT).

facts: Officially called a "police action".
17 September is marked in Telangana as the day Hyderabad joined India.
The Nizam was one of the world's richest men (NCERT).
562 princely states joined India; Puducherry (French) came in 1954, Goa in 1961.
JVP Committee (Nehru, Patel, Pattabhi): set up in 1948, report April 1949.
Mir Osman Ali Khan was the last Asaf Jahi Nizam (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

alsoOn.text: The Nizam signs the Standstill Agreement with India (November 1947) (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 13–17 September 1948: five days; two days after Jinnah's death (11 September).

participants.role: Home Minister who ordered the action.
Led the operation; became Military Governor.
Led the Communist-led peasant struggle in Telangana.
Became the first elected CM of Hyderabad State (1952).

events.before: The Nizam **Mir Osman Ali Khan** wanted independence and signed a Standstill Agreement; the **Razakars** terrorised people; the Telangana struggle was at its height.
events.after: Major General **J. N. Chaudhuri** became military governor; **M. K. Vellodi** headed the civil government (1950); **Burgula Ramakrishna Rao** became the first elected CM (1952). Hyderabad State merged into AP in 1956.
events.today: 17 September is marked in Telangana; the Nizam became Rajpramukh (1950–56).
events.mnemonic: Hyderabad 1947–48 "S-R-P": Standstill Agreement (November 1947), Razakars of Qasim Razvi, Polo (September 1948).

events.title: Constitution adopted
events.summary: The Constituent Assembly adopts the Constitution on 26 November 1949; it is signed on 24 January 1950 and comes into force on 26 January 1950 (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Constituent Assembly first met on 9 December 1946. Its Drafting Committee, chaired by B.R. Ambedkar, was set up on 29 August 1947; B.N. Rau, the Constitutional Adviser, prepared the first draft. Rajendra Prasad was President of the Assembly.

The Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days. On 25 November 1949 Ambedkar warned that India was entering "a life of contradictions" — political equality but social and economic inequality. The Constitution was adopted the next day (NCERT). 26 November is now Constitution Day.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 2 "Era of One-party Dominance"; Constitution of India / M. Laxmikanth (standard)
causes: Independence required a constitution made by Indians themselves.
course: 9 December 1946: first meeting.
29 August 1947: Drafting Committee formed.
26 November 1949: Constitution adopted (NCERT).
24 January 1950: members sign it (NCERT).
outcomes: Some provisions (citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament) took effect at once on 26 November 1949.
The rest came into force on 26 January 1950 (NCERT).
facts: It took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days.
26 November is Constitution Day (since 2015).

Key dates: first sitting 9 Dec 1946 (Sachchidananda Sinha, provisional president); Objectives Resolution 13 Dec 1946; Drafting Committee 29 Aug 1947; adopted 26 Nov 1949; time taken 2y 11m 18d; 389 members originally (299 after partition).
events.yearHook: Adopted 26 November 1949; in force exactly two months later.

participants.role: Chaired the Drafting Committee; gave the closing speech (NCERT).

events.before: The Drafting Committee's draft (February 1948) was debated in three readings; thousands of amendments were proposed.
events.after: Some parts (citizenship, elections, provisional Parliament) came into force at once (26 November 1949); the rest on **26 January 1950**. Ambedkar warned of "a life of contradictions" — political equality with social inequality.
events.today: 26 November is Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas, since 2015).
events.mnemonic: Constitution numbers "3-11-18; 395-22-8": 2 years 11 months 18 days; 395 articles, 22 parts, 8 schedules in the original.

events.title: Comptroller & Auditor-General (CAG) office
events.summary: The Comptroller and Auditor-General (Article 148) audits the accounts of the Union and the states; V. Narahari Rao is the first CAG.
events.detail:
"Guardian of the public purse" — Ambedkar.

**Exam hooks:** CAG Art. 148–151; reports tabled before PAC.
causes: The Auditor-General office dates from 1858.
outcomes: His reports go to the Public Accounts Committee of Parliament.
events.yearHook: Auditor-General 1858 → CAG 1950.

participants.role: Called the CAG the most important officer under the Constitution.

events.title: Directive Principles (Part IV)
events.summary: Part IV (Articles 36–51) lists Directive Principles — goals for the state that courts cannot enforce, borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
events.detail:
Gandhian, socialist & liberal-intellectual principles.

**Exam hooks:** DPSP from Ireland; "instrument of instructions".
causes: Social and economic justice was a goal of the freedom movement.
outcomes: Laws on land reform, panchayats (Art. 40) and free education drew on them.
Minerva Mills (1980) said Part III and Part IV must be balanced.
events.yearHook: In force with the Constitution on 26 January 1950.

events.title: Election Commission of India established
events.summary: The Election Commission is set up on 25 January 1950 under Article 324, with Sukumar Sen as the first Chief Election Commissioner (NCERT).
events.detail:
Sukumar Sen the first CEC; multi-member since 1993.

**Exam hooks:** Art. 324; 25 Jan = National Voters' Day.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 2 "Era of One-party Dominance"
causes: The Constitution promised elections under universal adult franchise.
outcomes: Ran the first general election (1951–52) (NCERT).
25 January is National Voters' Day.
events.yearHook: 25 January 1950 — one day before the Republic.

events.title: Fundamental Rights (Part III) enacted
events.summary: Part III (Articles 12–35) guarantees Fundamental Rights from 26 January 1950; Article 32 lets anyone go straight to the Supreme Court.
events.detail:
Right to Property removed (44th, 1978).

**Exam hooks:** FR = equality, freedom, against exploitation, religion, cultural-educational, constitutional remedies (Art.32 — "heart & soul").
causes: Karachi resolution of 1931 and the Nehru Report (1928).
Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, chaired by Patel.
outcomes: Seven rights originally; the right to property was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978).
Ambedkar called Article 32 "the heart and soul" of the Constitution.
events.yearHook: Karachi 1931 → Part III 1950.

participants.role: Called Article 32 the heart and soul.
Chaired the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights.

events.title: Planning Commission established
events.summary: The Planning Commission is set up in March 1950 by a simple government resolution, with Nehru as chairman (NCERT); it is replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015 (NCERT).
events.detail: It was neither a constitutional nor a statutory body (NCERT). Even before independence, a group of big industrialists had drafted the Bombay Plan (1944) for a planned economy (NCERT). The Prime Minister chaired the Commission, which drew up the Five Year Plans. The National Development Council (1952) brought the Chief Ministers in.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 3 "Politics of Planned Development"
causes: The leaders agreed that development meant growth with social and economic justice (NCERT).
Example of the Soviet Union's planning.
outcomes: Made the First Five Year Plan (1951) (NCERT).
Replaced by NITI Aayog on 1 January 2015 (NCERT).
facts: Set up by a simple resolution of the Government of India (NCERT).
Bombay Plan (1944) was drafted by industrialists (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: National Development Council set up (August 1952).

events.yearHook: 1950 Planning Commission → 2015 NITI Aayog: 65 years.

events.title: Constitution comes into force — Republic Day
events.summary: The Constitution comes into force on 26 January 1950; India becomes a republic and Rajendra Prasad becomes its first President (NCERT).
events.detail:
26 January was chosen because the Congress had observed it as Purna Swaraj Day from 1930. The office of Governor-General ended; Rajendra Prasad was sworn in as President, and the Federal Court became the Supreme Court (28 January 1950).

Three stamps were issued in 1950 to mark the first Republic Day (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 2 "Era of One-party Dominance"
causes: Purna Swaraj resolution (Lahore, 1929) and Independence Day celebrations from 26 January 1930.
outcomes: India became a sovereign democratic republic.
The Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950.
Rajendra Prasad became the first President.
events.yearHook: Purna Swaraj Day 26 January 1930 → Republic Day 26 January 1950: exactly 20 years.

participants.role: Sworn in as the first President.

events.before: 26 January was chosen because it was **Purna Swaraj Day** (1930).
events.after: India's first general elections were held in 1951–52; the **Election Commission**, **Supreme Court** (28 January 1950) and Planning Commission (March 1950) began work.
events.today: Republic Day parade on Kartavya Path; Beating Retreat on 29 January.
events.mnemonic: First holders "R-N-S-V": Rajendra Prasad (President), Nehru (PM), Sukumar Sen (Chief Election Commissioner, 1950), Harilal Kania (Chief Justice).

events.title: Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)
events.summary: The Federal Public Service Commission becomes the Union Public Service Commission on 26 January 1950 (Articles 315–323).
events.detail:
Conducts the Civil Services Examination.

**Exam hooks:** UPSC Art. 315; State PSCs (like APPSC) parallel it.
causes: The Public Service Commission first set up in 1926 (Lee Commission) became the Federal PSC under the 1935 Act.
outcomes: Recruits for the all-India and central services.
events.yearHook: 1926 PSC → 1937 Federal PSC → 1950 UPSC.

events.title: First Constitutional Amendment
events.summary: The First Amendment (June 1951) adds the Ninth Schedule to protect land-reform laws and adds "reasonable restrictions" on free speech.
events.detail: Courts had struck down zamindari abolition laws (e.g. Kameshwar Singh in Patna) and press bans (Romesh Thapar, Brij Bhushan). The provisional Parliament, led by Nehru, passed the amendment. It added Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule, allowed special provisions for backward classes (Article 15(4)) after the Champakam Dorairajan case, and widened the grounds for restricting speech (public order, friendly relations with foreign states).
causes: Courts struck down land-reform laws.
Champakam Dorairajan case (1951) struck down caste-based reservation in Madras.
Romesh Thapar case on press freedom.
outcomes: Ninth Schedule created; land reforms protected.
Article 15(4) allowed reservations for backward classes.
events.yearHook: First Amendment in 1951, before the first election.

participants.role: Moved the amendment in the provisional Parliament.

events.title: First Finance Commission
events.summary: The First Finance Commission (Article 280) is set up in 1951 under K.C. Neogy to share taxes between the Union and the states.
events.detail:
K.C. Neogy chaired the first (1951).

**Exam hooks:** Finance Commission Art. 280; vertical & horizontal devolution.
causes: Article 280 requires a Finance Commission every five years.
outcomes: Recommended the share of income tax and excise for states (1952).
events.yearHook: Every five years since 1951.

events.title: First Five-Year Plan launched
events.summary: The First Five Year Plan (1951–56), released in December 1951, focuses on agriculture, dams and irrigation (NCERT).
events.detail: The economist K.N. Raj argued that India should "hasten slowly" (NCERT). The plan aimed to get the economy out of the cycle of poverty; it put the largest money into agriculture, including dams and irrigation such as Bhakra-Nangal (NCERT). It was based on the Harrod–Domar model and achieved its targets. Land reform was seen as the key to agricultural growth (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 3 "Politics of Planned Development"
causes: Partition had hit agriculture badly (NCERT).
Food shortages.
outcomes: Growth of about 3.6% a year, above the 2.1% target.
Led to the bolder Second Plan (1956) (NCERT).
facts: The draft and the plan document (December 1951) generated a lot of excitement (NCERT).
K.N. Raj: "hasten slowly" (NCERT).
events.yearHook: First Plan 1951 → Second Plan 1956 (Mahalanobis).

events.title: Potti Sriramulu's fast & martyrdom
events.summary: Potti Sriramulu fasts unto death for a separate Andhra state from 19 October 1952 and dies on 15 December 1952 after 56 days; Nehru announces Andhra State in December 1952 (NCERT).
events.detail:
The Vishalandhra movement demanded that the Telugu-speaking areas be separated from Madras province; nearly all political forces in the Andhra region supported it (NCERT). The movement grew because the Centre kept hesitating (NCERT).

Potti Sriramulu, a Congress leader and veteran Gandhian, began an indefinite fast on 19 October 1952 at Bulusu Sambamurthy's house in Mylapore, Madras. He died on 15 December after 56 days (NCERT). This caused great unrest and violent outbursts in Andhra; many died in police firing, and several legislators in Madras resigned (NCERT). On 19 December 1952 Nehru announced in Parliament that a separate Andhra state would be formed (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: The Dar Commission and JVP Committee had postponed linguistic states (NCERT).
The Centre's vacillation (NCERT).
Dispute over Madras city.
course: 19 October 1952: fast begins.
15 December 1952: Sriramulu dies on the 56th day (NCERT).
16–18 December: riots and police firing in Andhra (NCERT).
19 December 1952: Nehru announces Andhra State (NCERT).
outcomes: Andhra State formed on 1 October 1953.
Forced the Centre to appoint the States Reorganisation Commission (1953) (NCERT).
facts: Earlier fasted in 1946 for temple entry for Dalits in Madras province (NCERT).
Honoured as "Amarajeevi" (immortal being).
Riots broke out on 16 Dec 1952, the day after his death; the Visalandhra movement wanted all Telugu areas in one state.
Swami Sitaram gave up his fast-unto-death for Andhra (1951) on Vinoba Bhave's appeal (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).
events.yearHook: 19 October → 15 December 1952: 56 days. Nehru announces Andhra State on 19 December 1952, four days after his death.

participants.role: Hosted the fast at his Madras house.
Chief Minister of Madras, who opposed giving Madras city to Andhra.

events.before: Swami Sitaram's fast (1951) had failed; the Centre would not move unless the Telugus gave up Madras city.
events.after: Riots broke out across Andhra; Nehru gave way. Andhra State came on **1 October 1953** without Madras city. The Centre then set up the **States Reorganisation Commission** (December 1953).
events.today: Nellore district was renamed **Sri Potti Sriramulu Nellore** (2008); the Telugu University in Hyderabad was named after him (now in Telangana).
events.mnemonic: "56 days in '52 → state in '53": a 56-day fast in 1952 brings Andhra State in 1953.

events.title: Andhra State formed (capital Kurnool)
events.summary: Andhra State — India's first state formed on the basis of language — is created on 1 October 1953 with Kurnool as capital and T. Prakasam as Chief Minister.
events.detail:
The Andhra State Act, 1953 separated eleven Telugu districts of Madras State — seven coastal and four Rayalaseema districts (Kurnool, Anantapur, Cuddapah, Chittoor). Madras city stayed with Madras State. The Wanchoo Committee examined the financial and administrative questions. Kurnool became the capital, as promised by the Sri Bagh Pact of 1937, and Guntur got the High Court (1954).

Nehru inaugurated the state at Kurnool. Prakasam became Chief Minister and C.M. Trivedi the Governor. Prakasam's ministry fell in November 1954; after the 1955 mid-term election Bezawada Gopala Reddy became CM.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Potti Sriramulu's death and the unrest that followed (NCERT).
The Vishalandhra demand (NCERT).
outcomes: First linguistic state; it encouraged demands elsewhere and led to the SRC (1953) (NCERT).
Merged with Telangana to form Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956.
facts: Eleven districts: seven coastal and four Rayalaseema.
High Court at Guntur (1954).
Kurnool was chosen under the Sri Bagh Pact (1937).
First CM: Tanguturu (Tanguturi) Prakasam Pantulu.
The Madras government's Partition Committee for the new state was chaired by Kumaraswamy Raja (Madras CM) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
In 1953 the Krishikar Lok Party wanted Tirupati as the capital of Andhra (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

alsoOn.text: Prakasam's ministry falls (November 1954); President's Rule in Andhra State.
Andhra mid-term election: the Congress defeats the Communists; Bezawada Gopala Reddy becomes CM.

events.yearHook: 1 October 1953: the first linguistic state; 40 years after Bapatla (1913).

participants.role: Whose sacrifice led to the state.

events.before: **Potti Sriramulu** died (December 1952); the Centre passed the **Andhra State Act** (1953) on the advice of the **Wanchoo Committee**.
events.after: Prakasam's ministry fell (1954) and a mid-term election (1955) brought the Congress back under **Bezawada Gopala Reddy**. The new state pressed for **Vishalandhra** — union with the Telugu areas of Hyderabad State.
events.today: Kurnool, with its Konda Reddy fort, remembers its three years (1953–56) as capital.
events.mnemonic: Andhra State "K-G-P": Kurnool capital, Guntur High Court, Prakasam CM.

events.title: Andhra Pradesh formed (Vishalandhra)
events.summary: Andhra State and the Telangana region of Hyderabad State merge to form Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956, with Hyderabad as capital and Neelam Sanjiva Reddy as Chief Minister.
events.detail:
The SRC had advised keeping Telangana as a separate state until 1961 and then letting its legislature decide. Andhra leaders wanted Vishalandhra at once, and the Hyderabad Assembly supported a merger with safeguards. The Gentlemen's Agreement (20 February 1956) set out those safeguards.

Andhra Pradesh came into being on 1 November 1956 under the States Reorganisation Act. Nehru inaugurated it, likening it to a marriage with the right to divorce. C.M. Trivedi was Governor; Neelam Sanjiva Reddy became Chief Minister and K.V. Ranga Reddy later Deputy CM.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: The Vishalandhra ideal of all Telugu people in one state.
Hyderabad city as a ready capital.
outcomes: Telugu speakers of Andhra and Telangana in one state.
Breach of safeguards later fuelled the Telangana (1969) and Jai Andhra (1972) movements.
facts: 1 November is Andhra Pradesh Formation Day (residual AP observes it).
Chief Ministers in order: Damodaram Sanjivaiah (1960) → Kasu Brahmananda Reddy (1964) → P.V. Narasimha Rao (1971) → Tanguturi Anjaiah (1980) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).
events.yearHook: 1 November 1956: three years after Andhra State; it lasts 57 and a half years (to 2 June 2014).

participants.role: Last CM of Hyderabad State; backed the merger.

events.before: The **Gentlemen's Agreement** (20 February 1956) promised Telangana safeguards on jobs (Mulki rules), education, revenue and a Regional Council.
events.after: The safeguards were weakly kept. Telangana rose in **1969**, Andhra in **1972 (Jai Andhra)**. The **Six-Point Formula** (1973) and Article **371-D** held the state together until 2014.
events.today: AP Formation Day: 1 November (kept by residual AP); Telangana Formation Day: 2 June.
events.mnemonic: AP's early CMs "N-D-K-P": Neelam Sanjiva Reddy (1956), Damodaram Sanjivaiah (1960, first Dalit CM in India), Kasu Brahmananda Reddy (1964), P. V. Narasimha Rao (1971).

events.title: States Reorganisation Act, 1956
events.summary: On the SRC's report the States Reorganisation Act (1956) creates 14 states and 6 Union Territories from 1 November 1956 (NCERT).
events.detail:
The struggles for linguistic states forced the Centre to appoint the States Reorganisation Commission in 1953 (NCERT). Its chairman was Fazl Ali; K.M. Panikkar and H.N. Kunzru were members. Its report (30 September 1955) accepted that state boundaries should reflect language, but rejected "one language, one state" (NCERT).

The Act passed in 1956 together with the 7th Amendment, which abolished the Part A, B, C and D categories of states. The SRC had suggested keeping Hyderabad (Telangana) separate until 1961; the government instead merged it with Andhra.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"
causes: Andhra State (1953) and other language movements (NCERT).
course: December 1953: SRC appointed (NCERT).
30 September 1955: report submitted; it recommended 16 states and 3 UTs.
1956: Act passed (NCERT); 7th Amendment.
1 November 1956: new states come into being.
outcomes: 14 states and 6 Union Territories (NCERT).
Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Mysore and an enlarged Bombay formed.
Bombay was split in 1960 and Punjab in 1966 (NCERT).
facts: Language became a basis of states, but unity was not harmed — it strengthened democracy (NCERT).
SRA 1956 = States Reorganisation Act; the Imperial Bank became the SBI in 1955.

alsoOn.text: States Reorganisation Commission appointed (December 1953) (NCERT).
SRC report submitted (30 September 1955).

events.yearHook: SRC 1953 → report 1955 → Act 1956.
events.before: **Andhra State** (1953) had shown that language movements could not be ignored.
events.after: The **7th Amendment** (1956) abolished Part A, B, C and D states; the country got 14 states and 6 UTs. Later reorganisations followed one by one.
events.today: India now has 28 states and 8 Union Territories (after J&K was reorganised in 2019).
events.mnemonic: After 1956: "Bombay 60, Punjab 66": Maharashtra-Gujarat (1960), Punjab-Haryana (1966); then NE states (1972), and 2000 (Chhattisgarh, Uttarakhand, Jharkhand), 2014 (Telangana).

events.title: Berubari Union case
events.summary: In the Berubari Union case (1960) the Supreme Court advises that India can give territory to another country only by amending the Constitution under Article 368; the 9th Amendment follows.
events.detail: The Nehru–Noon Agreement (1958) divided the Berubari Union in West Bengal with East Pakistan. On a Presidential reference (Article 143) the Court said a treaty ceding territory needed a constitutional amendment, not just a law under Article 3. It also said the Preamble is not a part of the Constitution — a view reversed in Kesavananda (1973).
causes: Nehru–Noon Agreement (1958) with Pakistan.
outcomes: 9th Amendment (1960).
Preamble held not a part of the Constitution (reversed in 1973).
events.yearHook: 1960 Berubari said "Preamble is not part"; 1973 Kesavananda said it is.

participants.role: Signed the agreement with Pakistan's PM Feroz Khan Noon.

events.title: Liberation of Goa (Operation Vijay)
events.summary: The Indian army liberates Goa, Daman and Diu from Portugal in "Operation Vijay" (18–19 December 1961) after barely two days (NCERT).
events.detail: Portugal refused to withdraw from Goa, Diu and Daman, held since the sixteenth century (NCERT). Satyagrahis marched in 1955 and many were shot. Nehru hoped for peaceful talks, but Portugal under Salazar refused. In December 1961 the army went in; Governor-General Vassalo e Silva surrendered on 19 December (NCERT). Goa became a Union Territory (12th Amendment, 1962). The opinion poll of January 1967 kept Goa separate from Maharashtra, and Goa became a state in 1987 (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 7 "Regional Aspirations"
causes: Portugal refused to leave (NCERT).
Firing on satyagrahis (1955).
course: 18 December 1961: troops enter.
19 December: Portuguese surrender (NCERT).
outcomes: Goa, Daman and Diu became a UT (1962).
Opinion poll 1967: Goa stayed separate (NCERT).
Goa became a state in 1987 (NCERT).

alsoOn.text: French settlements (Pondicherry etc.) transferred de facto to India (1 November 1954); de jure treaty 1962.
Goa opinion poll (January 1967) keeps Goa separate from Maharashtra (NCERT).
Goa becomes a state (NCERT).

events.yearHook: Goa freed 1961 → opinion poll 1967 → statehood 1987.

participants.role: Led the land forces; Military Governor.

events.before: Portugal refused to leave; satyagrahis (1955) were fired on; **Pondicherry** (French) had joined in 1954.
events.after: Goa, Daman and Diu became a UT (12th Amendment, 1962); Goa became a state in **1987**. **Dadra and Nagar Haveli** had been freed in 1954 (integrated 1961, 10th Amendment).
events.today: 19 December is Goa Liberation Day.

events.title: Non-Aligned Movement founded
events.summary: The first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement is held at Belgrade in September 1961; Nehru, Tito, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah are its founders (NCERT).
events.detail: Non-alignment meant staying away from both Cold War blocs while taking an independent stand on each issue — it was not isolation or neutrality (NCERT). Nehru was a co-founder with Tito (Yugoslavia), Nasser (Egypt), Sukarno (Indonesia) and Nkrumah (Ghana) (NCERT). The Bandung Conference of 1955 had paved the way (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
causes: Cold War between the US and USSR blocs (NCERT).
Newly free nations wanted independence in foreign policy (NCERT).
outcomes: India led the newly independent nations (NCERT).
India signed a treaty with the USSR in 1971 but called it consistent with non-alignment (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Bandung 1955 → Belgrade 1961.

events.title: Green Revolution
events.summary: From 1965–66 the government backs high-yielding seeds, fertiliser, irrigation and support prices in irrigated areas, starting the Green Revolution, mainly in wheat (NCERT).
events.detail:
Droughts in 1965–67 and the need for American food aid (PL-480) pushed the government to a new strategy (NCERT). It gave high-yielding seeds, fertilisers, pesticides and better irrigation at subsidised prices to areas already irrigated, and guaranteed purchase at a fixed price (NCERT).

Food output rose, but rich peasants and large landholders gained most, and the gap between regions grew; Punjab, Haryana and western UP became prosperous (NCERT). It also gave rise to a middle peasant class that became politically important (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 3 "Politics of Planned Development"
causes: Droughts and famine conditions (1965–67) (NCERT).
Dependence on US food aid (NCERT).
outcomes: Wheat output more than doubled; self-sufficiency in food grains (NCERT).
Gains went mainly to big farmers and irrigated regions (NCERT).
Food Corporation of India (1965) and the Agricultural Prices Commission (1965).

pairs.left: Father of the Green Revolution in India

alsoOn.text: Food Corporation of India and Agricultural Prices Commission set up (1965).

events.yearHook: 1965 war + 1966 drought → Green Revolution.

events.title: Nagarjunasagar Dam completed
events.summary: Nagarjunasagar dam on the Krishna, whose foundation Nehru laid on 10 December 1955, is inaugurated by Indira Gandhi in 1967; it was then the world's largest masonry dam.
events.detail: Designed by K.L. Rao, it lies between Nalgonda (Telangana) and Guntur/Palnadu (AP). Its Right Canal (Jawahar) and Left Canal (Lal Bahadur) irrigate lakhs of acres. The Buddhist remains of Nagarjunakonda were moved to an island museum before the reservoir filled.
causes: Need for irrigation in the Krishna basin (First and Second Plans).
outcomes: Irrigates over 20 lakh acres; hydro-power.
Nagarjunakonda relics moved to the island museum.

alsoOn.text: Nehru lays the foundation stone of Nagarjunasagar (10 December 1955).

events.yearHook: Foundation 1955 → water released 1967.

events.title: Golaknath case
events.summary: In Golaknath v. State of Punjab (27 February 1967) an 11-judge bench rules 6:5 that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights; Chief Justice Koka Subba Rao writes the majority.
events.detail: The Golaknath family challenged the Punjab land-ceiling law. The Court said an amendment is a "law" under Article 13, so it cannot take away Fundamental Rights. It used "prospective overruling" so that earlier land laws stayed valid. Parliament answered with the 24th Amendment (1971).
causes: Land-ceiling laws and earlier amendments that curbed property rights.
outcomes: 24th Amendment (1971) said Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution.
Overruled by Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
events.yearHook: Golaknath (1967) → 24th Amendment (1971) → Kesavananda (1973).

events.title: Bank nationalisation
events.summary: On 19 July 1969 the government nationalises 14 major private banks (deposits over ₹50 crore) by ordinance (NCERT).
events.detail: Indira Gandhi took Finance from Morarji Desai, who resigned. The aim was to take credit to agriculture, small industry and rural areas. Six more banks were nationalised on 15 April 1980. NCERT lists it among her "big and popular policy measures" of 1969.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 5 "Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System"
causes: Rivalry with the Syndicate (NCERT).
Banks lent mostly to big business.
outcomes: Branches spread to villages; priority-sector lending.
Six more banks nationalised in 1980.

alsoOn.text: Six more private banks nationalised (15 April 1980).

events.title: ISRO founded
events.summary: The Indian Space Research Organisation is formed on 15 August 1969, replacing INCOSPAR (1962); Vikram Sarabhai is its founder.
events.detail: INCOSPAR was set up in 1962 under the Department of Atomic Energy. India's first rocket was launched from Thumba near Thiruvananthapuram on 21 November 1963. The Department of Space and the Space Commission came in 1972.
causes: Sarabhai's vision of space for development.
outcomes: Aryabhata (1975), SLV-3 (1980) and the PSLV followed.
Sriharikota range (1971).

pairs.left: Father of the Indian space programme

alsoOn.text: First rocket launched from Thumba (21 November 1963).
Rakesh Sharma becomes the first Indian in space (April 1984).

events.yearHook: INCOSPAR 1962 → ISRO 1969 → Department of Space 1972.

participants.role: India's first satellite was named after him.

events.title: Satish Dhawan Space Centre (Sriharikota)
events.summary: The Sriharikota range (SHAR) in Nellore district becomes India's main launch centre; its first rocket flies on 9 October 1971. It was renamed Satish Dhawan Space Centre in 2002.
events.detail: Sriharikota, a barrier island between Pulicat Lake and the Bay of Bengal, was chosen for its eastward launch advantage near the equator and its safe sea corridor. SLV-3 (1980), PSLV, GSLV and Chandrayaan missions were launched from here.
causes: Need for a launch site on the east coast close to the equator.
outcomes: India's spaceport; renamed after Satish Dhawan (2002).

alsoOn.text: SHAR renamed Satish Dhawan Space Centre.

events.yearHook: First launch October 1971.

participants.role: The centre is named after him.

events.title: Visakhapatnam Steel Plant sanctioned
events.summary: After the 1966 "Visakha Ukku – Andhrula Hakku" (Visakha steel is the right of Andhras) agitation, Indira Gandhi lays the foundation of the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant on 20 January 1971; it is dedicated in 1992.
events.detail: In 1966 students and leaders such as Tenneti Viswanatham and T. Amrutha Rao (who fasted) demanded a steel plant; police firing killed about 32 people. Indira Gandhi announced the plant in Parliament in April 1970. Run by Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Ltd (RINL), it is India's first shore-based integrated steel plant; P.V. Narasimha Rao dedicated it to the nation on 1 August 1992.
causes: The 1966 agitation.
outcomes: RINL plant completed and dedicated (1992).

alsoOn.text: "Visakha Ukku – Andhrula Hakku" agitation; about 32 killed in police firing.
P.V. Narasimha Rao dedicates the Visakhapatnam Steel Plant (1 August 1992).

events.yearHook: Agitation 1966 → foundation 1971 → dedicated 1992.

events.title: Jai Andhra & Six-Point Formula
events.summary: When the Supreme Court upholds the Mulki rules (October 1972), the coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema regions launch the Jai Andhra movement demanding a separate Andhra state; it ends with the Six-Point Formula (1973).
events.detail:
The Mulki rules gave Telangana residents preference in local jobs. The AP High Court had struck them down, but the Supreme Court upheld them on 3 October 1972. Andhra and Rayalaseema leaders saw this as making them second-class citizens in their own capital and demanded separation ("Jai Andhra").

Kakani Venkataratnam resigned as minister to lead it and died during the agitation (December 1972). Parliament passed the Mulki Rules Act (December 1972), but the protests grew; ministers from the region resigned and P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned as CM. President's Rule followed on 18 January 1973.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Supreme Court verdict upholding the Mulki rules (1972).
course: 3 October 1972: Supreme Court verdict.
December 1972: Mulki Rules Act; Kakani Venkataratnam dies.
January 1973: PV resigns; President's Rule (18 January).
21 September 1973: Six-Point Formula.
outcomes: President's Rule (1973).
Six-Point Formula and Article 371-D.

pairs.left: Mulki rules upheld by the Supreme Court

alsoOn.text: President's Rule in Andhra Pradesh (18 January – 10 December 1973).

events.yearHook: 1969 Telangana wanted out; 1972 Andhra wanted out.
events.before: The **Supreme Court** upheld the Mulki rules on 3 October 1972, giving Telangana people priority in Hyderabad jobs.
events.after: Andhra and Rayalaseema leaders resigned; **Kakani Venkataratnam** died during the agitation. P. V. Narasimha Rao resigned and **President's Rule** came (January 1973). The **Six-Point Formula** (September 1973) ended both agitations.
events.today: Jai Andhra is the mirror image of 1969: the same Mulki question, seen from the other side.

events.title: Kesavananda Bharati — Basic Structure doctrine
events.summary: In Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (24 April 1973) a 13-judge bench rules 7:6 that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but not its "basic structure".
events.detail:
Swami Kesavananda Bharati of the Edneer Mutt challenged Kerala's land-reform laws; Nani Palkhivala argued the case. The bench, led by Chief Justice S.M. Sikri, overruled Golaknath but laid down the basic-structure doctrine. It also held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution.

Immediately afterwards the government set aside the seniority of three judges and made Justice A.N. Ray Chief Justice (NCERT) — the first supersession.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 6 "The Crisis of the Democratic Order"; Constitution of India / M. Laxmikanth (standard)
causes: The 24th, 25th and 29th Amendments after Golaknath.
outcomes: Basic-structure doctrine.
Supersession of three judges (1973) (NCERT).
Used later in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) and Minerva Mills (1980).
events.yearHook: 1967 Golaknath (11 judges) → 1973 Kesavananda (13 judges).

participants.role: PM whose government superseded the judges (NCERT).
The basic structure was applied in Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975).

facts: A.N. Ray appointed Chief Justice superseding three senior judges (NCERT).

events.title: Pokhran-I nuclear test (Smiling Buddha)
events.summary: India conducts its first nuclear explosion at Pokhran, Rajasthan, on 18 May 1974 ("Smiling Buddha"), calling it a peaceful nuclear explosion (NCERT).
events.detail: India had refused to sign the NPT (1968), calling it discriminatory (NCERT). The test was led by Raja Ramanna of BARC under AEC chairman Homi Sethna. Western countries imposed curbs, and the Nuclear Suppliers Group was formed. India said it was committed to using nuclear energy only for peaceful purposes (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
causes: China's nuclear test (1964) (NCERT).
The discriminatory NPT (NCERT).
outcomes: India became the sixth country to test.
Nuclear Suppliers Group formed; sanctions.
events.yearHook: Pokhran-I 1974 → Pokhran-II 1998: 24 years.

events.title: Aryabhata — India's first satellite
events.summary: Aryabhata, India's first satellite, is launched by a Soviet rocket from Kapustin Yar on 19 April 1975.
events.detail:
Named after the ancient astronomer-mathematician.

**Exam hooks:** Aryabhata (1975); first Indian-launched satellite = Rohini via SLV-3 (1980).
causes: ISRO's satellite programme.
outcomes: Bhaskara (1979) followed; first Indian launch with SLV-3 (1980).
events.yearHook: April 1975 — two months before the Emergency.

participants.role: The satellite was named after him.

events.title: National Emergency (1975–77)
events.summary: After the Allahabad High Court sets aside Indira Gandhi's election (12 June 1975), the government declares an internal Emergency under Article 352 on 25 June 1975; it lasts until March 1977 (NCERT).
events.detail:
On 12 June 1975 Justice Jagmohan Lal Sinha declared her 1971 election invalid on Raj Narain's petition (NCERT). The Supreme Court gave a partial stay on 24 June: she could stay an MP but not vote. On 25 June JP led a massive rally at Ramlila grounds and called on the army, police and government employees not to obey "illegal and immoral orders" (NCERT).

That night the PM recommended the Emergency to President Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed, citing a threat of internal disturbance (NCERT). Opposition leaders were arrested, the press was censored, the RSS and Jamaat-e-Islami were banned, and preventive detention was used widely (NCERT). In April 1976 the Supreme Court (ADM Jabalpur case) accepted that citizens could not challenge detention (NCERT). Sanjay Gandhi's forced sterilisation and slum demolitions made it hated in the north (NCERT). Elections were announced in January 1977 (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 6 "The Crisis of the Democratic Order"
causes: Allahabad High Court verdict (12 June 1975) (NCERT).
JP movement and opposition demand for her resignation (NCERT).
Gujarat and Bihar movements, railway strike (NCERT).
course: 12 June 1975: verdict (NCERT).
25 June: Ramlila rally; Emergency proclaimed that night (NCERT).
26 June: leaders arrested; press censored.
April 1976: ADM Jabalpur judgment (NCERT).
January 1977: elections announced (NCERT).
March 1977: Emergency lifted.
outcomes: 42nd Amendment (1976).
Congress defeat in 1977 (NCERT).
Shah Commission (1977) (NCERT).
44th Amendment (1978) made a repeat harder.
facts: The Nai Dunia editorial page of 27 June 1975 was left blank in protest (NCERT).
It was the third national Emergency (after 1962 and 1971) but the only one on grounds of "internal disturbance".

pairs.left: Judge who set aside Indira Gandhi's election

alsoOn.text: ADM Jabalpur case: Supreme Court accepts that the right to life can be suspended during Emergency (NCERT).
Emergency lifted (21 March 1977) after the Congress defeat.

events.yearHook: 25 June 1975 → 21 March 1977: about 21 months.

events.title: 42nd Amendment — the "Mini-Constitution"
events.summary: The 42nd Amendment (1976), passed during the Emergency, adds "socialist", "secular" and "integrity" to the Preamble and Fundamental Duties (Part IVA), and extends the Lok Sabha's term to six years (NCERT).
events.detail: It followed the Swaran Singh Committee's advice on duties and added Directive Principles such as equal justice and free legal aid (39A), workers' participation in management (43A) and environment protection (48A). It curbed judicial review and moved education, forests and some other subjects to the Concurrent List. Because it changed so much it was called a "mini-Constitution". NCERT notes the term extension meant the next election was due only in 1978.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 6 "The Crisis of the Democratic Order"; Constitution of India / M. Laxmikanth (standard)
causes: The Emergency government's wish to curb the courts.
outcomes: Many changes reversed by the 43rd (1977) and 44th (1978) Amendments.
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down parts of it.
events.yearHook: 1976 42nd → 1978 44th undid much of it.

events.title: 44th Amendment — restores balance
events.summary: The Janata government's 44th Amendment (1978) makes another Emergency harder — "armed rebellion" replaces "internal disturbance" — and turns the right to property into a legal right (Article 300A).
events.detail: Emergency now needs the cabinet's written advice; Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended; the Lok Sabha's term went back to five years. Law Minister Shanti Bhushan piloted it.
causes: Emergency excesses.
outcomes: Right to property removed from Part III; Article 300A.
Safeguards on Article 352.

pairs.left: Right to property made a legal right

events.yearHook: 42nd (1976) undone by 44th (1978).

events.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
events.summary: In Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978) a 7-judge bench rules that any law taking away life or liberty under Article 21 must be "just, fair and reasonable", widening Article 21.
events.detail: Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded without giving reasons. Justice P.N. Bhagwati held that Articles 14, 19 and 21 are linked, so the procedure must be fair — effectively reading "due process" into the Constitution. It overruled the narrow A.K. Gopalan view (1950).
causes: Impounding of a passport without a hearing.
outcomes: Article 21 became the source of many new rights (privacy, livelihood, clean environment).
events.yearHook: Gopalan 1950 narrow → Maneka 1978 wide.

events.title: Minerva Mills v. Union of India
events.summary: In Minerva Mills v. Union of India (1980) the Supreme Court strikes down the parts of the 42nd Amendment that gave Parliament unlimited amending power, holding that limited amending power and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are basic features.
events.detail:
Struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment.

**Exam hooks:** judicial review & limited amending power are basic features.
causes: The 42nd Amendment's clauses 4 and 5 of Article 368.
outcomes: Judicial review confirmed as a basic feature.

pairs.left: Balance of Part III and Part IV

events.yearHook: Kesavananda 1973 → Minerva 1980.

participants.role: Chief Justice who led the bench.

events.title: SLV-3 launches Rohini — first Indian launch
events.summary: On 18 July 1980 SLV-3 puts the Rohini satellite into orbit from Sriharikota, making India the sixth nation able to launch its own satellite; A.P.J. Abdul Kalam is project director.
events.detail:
Put Rohini RS-1 into orbit.

**Exam hooks:** SLV-3 (1980); Kalam = "Missile Man".
causes: ISRO's launch-vehicle programme.
outcomes: Led to the ASLV, PSLV and GSLV.
events.yearHook: Aryabhata on a Soviet rocket (1975) → own rocket (1980).

events.title: Srisailam Dam on the Krishna
events.summary: The Srisailam dam on the Krishna (foundation 1963) is completed in 1981; its reservoir is named Neelam Sanjiva Reddy Sagar.
events.detail: Built in a gorge of the Nallamala hills (Kurnool district), it began as a hydro-power project; later the Srisailam Right Branch Canal, the Telugu Ganga project (water to Chennai) and the Handri–Neeva scheme drew on it.
causes: Power and water needs of Rayalaseema.
outcomes: Major hydro-power station; Telugu Ganga water to Chennai.

alsoOn.text: Work begins on the Srisailam project.

events.yearHook: Begun 1963 → completed 1981.

participants.role: The reservoir is named after him.

facts: Telugu Ganga canal water goes to Tamil Nadu (Chennai) (APPSC Group-II 2025 key).

events.title: N.T. Rama Rao founds the Telugu Desam Party
events.summary: Film star N.T. Rama Rao founds the Telugu Desam Party on 29 March 1982 to restore "Telugu self-respect"; in January 1983 it wins 199 of 294 seats and NTR becomes the first non-Congress CM of Andhra Pradesh.
events.detail:
Frequent changes of Congress chief ministers chosen in Delhi — four between 1978 and 1982 — and the public insult of CM T. Anjaiah by Rajiv Gandhi at Begumpet airport fed the anger. NTR toured the state in his "Chaitanya Ratham".

In August 1984, while NTR was in the US for heart surgery, Governor Ram Lal dismissed him and swore in Nadendla Bhaskara Rao. A month-long "Save Democracy" movement, with opposition parties parading TDP MLAs before the President, forced his restoration (16 September 1984). TDP was the main opposition party in the 1984 Lok Sabha.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Delhi's control over Congress CMs; "Telugu self-respect".
Frequent changes of CMs (1978–82).
course: 29 March 1982: TDP founded.
January 1983: TDP wins; NTR CM on 9 January.
August 1984: dismissed; Nadendla installed.
16 September 1984: NTR restored.
March 1985: TDP wins again.
outcomes: First non-Congress government in AP.
Rise of regional parties nationally; NTR became National Front chairman (1988).
Debate on the Governor's role (Sarkaria Commission).

alsoOn.text: TDP wins the Assembly election; NTR becomes CM (9 January 1983).
NTR dismissed by Governor Ram Lal (August) and restored (September 1984).
TDP returns with 216 seats; NTR CM again (December 1994).

events.yearHook: Party founded March 1982 → in power January 1983: nine months.

participants.role: Installed as CM for a month (1984).
Congress general secretary whose treatment of Anjaiah became an issue.

facts: The TDP was founded during the Chief Ministership of Bhavanam Venkatarami Reddy (Congress); Kotla Vijaya Bhaskara Reddy was CM at the 1983 election (APPSC Group-II Screening 2018 key).

events.title: NABARD established
events.summary: NABARD, the apex bank for agriculture and rural development, is set up on 12 July 1982 on the advice of the Sivaraman committee (CRAFICARD).
events.detail:
Refinances rural credit; SHG-bank linkage.

**Exam hooks:** NABARD (1982); SIDBI (1990) for small industry.
causes: Need for one apex body for rural credit.
outcomes: Took over the RBI's agricultural credit functions.
events.yearHook: RBI 1935 → NABARD 1982.

events.title: 52nd Amendment — Anti-Defection Law
events.summary: The 52nd Amendment (1985) adds the Tenth Schedule — the anti-defection law — disqualifying legislators who leave their party or defy its whip; the Speaker decides.
events.detail: Defection had become common after 1967 (NCERT). Rajiv Gandhi's government passed it with his large majority. It allowed a "split" of one-third, which the 91st Amendment (2003) removed, keeping only mergers of two-thirds. Kihoto Hollohan (1992) upheld it but made the Speaker's decision subject to judicial review.
causes: "Aaya Ram, Gaya Ram" politics after 1967 (NCERT).
outcomes: 91st Amendment (2003) removed the split clause.
Kihoto Hollohan (1992) upheld it.
events.yearHook: Defections from 1967 → law in 1985.

events.title: Shah Bano case & aftermath
events.summary: In the Shah Bano case (1985) the Supreme Court upholds a divorced Muslim woman's right to maintenance under Section 125 CrPC; the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 nullifies the verdict (NCERT).
events.detail: Shah Bano, a 62-year-old divorced woman from Indore, won maintenance. On the demand of some Muslim leaders the Rajiv Gandhi government passed the 1986 Act (NCERT). The BJP called this appeasement, and the issue, with the opening of the Ayodhya site in 1986, became central to its politics (NCERT).
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
causes: A divorced woman's claim for maintenance.
outcomes: 1986 Act nullified the judgment (NCERT).
Became a major issue for the BJP (NCERT).
Danial Latifi case (2001) read the Act to give fair maintenance.

pairs.left: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act

alsoOn.text: Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act; Faizabad court orders the Ayodhya structure unlocked (NCERT).

events.yearHook: 1985 verdict → 1986 Act.

participants.role: Chief Justice who led the bench.
PM whose government passed the 1986 Act (NCERT).

events.title: Agni missile series (IGMDP)
events.summary: Agni, India's first intermediate-range ballistic missile, is first test-fired on 22 May 1989 under the Integrated Guided Missile Development Programme (1983) led by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.
events.detail:
Kalam led the IGMDP (Prithvi, Agni, Trishul, Akash, Nag).

**Exam hooks:** IGMDP (1983); Agni = surface-to-surface ballistic.
causes: IGMDP (1983): Prithvi, Agni, Trishul, Akash, Nag.
outcomes: Agni series up to Agni-V (2012).
events.yearHook: IGMDP 1983 → Agni 1989.

events.title: Fall of the Berlin Wall
events.summary: The Berlin Wall falls on 9 November 1989; Germany reunites in 1990 and the Soviet Union breaks up in December 1991, ending the Cold War.
events.detail:
Ushered in a unipolar moment & globalisation.

**Exam hooks:** 1989 wall falls; 1991 Soviet collapse.
causes: Reforms of Mikhail Gorbachev (glasnost, perestroika).
outcomes: German reunification (3 October 1990).
USSR dissolved (26 December 1991); India lost a key ally (NCERT).
events.yearHook: Wall 1989 → USSR gone 1991 — the year India liberalised.

events.title: LPG Economic Reforms of 1991
events.summary: Facing a balance-of-payments crisis, the P.V. Narasimha Rao government with Finance Minister Manmohan Singh launches liberalisation, privatisation and globalisation (LPG) in July 1991 (NCERT).
events.detail:
India had foreign exchange for only about two weeks of imports; gold was pledged to the Bank of England. The rupee was devalued (July 1991), the New Industrial Policy (24 July 1991) ended licensing for most industries, and the budget the same day cut tariffs and opened the door to foreign investment. An IMF loan came with conditions.

NCERT notes that Rajiv Gandhi had started these changes and that they became very visible in 1991, radically changing the direction the economy had pursued since independence.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
causes: Balance-of-payments crisis; Gulf War oil price rise.
Fiscal deficits; fall of the USSR.
outcomes: Licence raj ended; FDI allowed.
Higher growth; criticism over inequality (NCERT).
events.yearHook: 1956 Industrial Policy → 1991 New Industrial Policy.

participants.role: PM when gold was first pledged.

events.title: PARAM supercomputer developed (C-DAC)
events.summary: C-DAC, set up in 1988 after the US refused India a Cray supercomputer, builds PARAM 8000, India's first supercomputer, in 1991 under Vijay Bhatkar.
events.detail:
Developed by C-DAC under Vijay Bhatkar.

**Exam hooks:** PARAM (1991); National Supercomputing Mission today.
causes: US denial of a Cray supercomputer (1987).
outcomes: PARAM series of supercomputers.
events.yearHook: C-DAC 1988 → PARAM 1991.

events.title: 73rd & 74th Amendments — local self-government
events.summary: Parliament passes the 73rd (panchayats, Part IX) and 74th (municipalities, Part IXA) Amendments in December 1992; they come into force on 24 April and 1 June 1993.
events.detail:
Rajiv Gandhi's 64th Amendment Bill (1989) had failed in the Rajya Sabha. The P.V. Narasimha Rao government passed the new amendments. They made three-tier panchayats compulsory (except in states under 20 lakh people), with elections every five years by a State Election Commission, a State Finance Commission every five years, and reservation of at least one-third of seats and chairperson posts for women and for SCs/STs in proportion.

The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects for panchayats; the Twelfth lists 18 for municipalities. PESA (1996) extended them to Scheduled Areas.
causes: Weak, irregular local bodies after 1959.
Committees: Balwant Rai Mehta (1957), Ashok Mehta (1978), G.V.K. Rao (1985), L.M. Singhvi (1986).
outcomes: 24 April is National Panchayati Raj Day.
About 14 lakh women elected representatives.
PESA Act, 1996.

alsoOn.text: 73rd Amendment in force (24 April 1993); 74th in force (1 June 1993).
PESA Act extends panchayats to Scheduled Areas.
Rajiv Gandhi's 64th Amendment Bill on panchayats fails in the Rajya Sabha.

events.yearHook: Nagaur 1959 → constitutional status 1992–93.

participants.role: His 1957 committee first proposed three-tier panchayats.

events.title: Indra Sawhney (Mandal) case
events.summary: In Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (16 November 1992) a 9-judge bench upholds 27% OBC reservation but excludes the "creamy layer" and caps reservation at 50% (NCERT).
events.detail: The case challenged the 1990 Mandal decision and the Narasimha Rao government's extra 10% for poorer sections of upper castes (1991), which was struck down. The Court also said there should be no reservation in promotions; the 77th Amendment (1995) restored it for SCs/STs.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 8 "Recent Developments in Indian Politics"
causes: The 1990 Mandal decision (NCERT).
outcomes: Creamy-layer rule; 50% ceiling.
National Commission for Backward Classes (1993).
77th Amendment (1995).
events.yearHook: Mandal decision 1990 → upheld 1992 (NCERT).

participants.role: PM; his 10% scheme was struck down.

events.title: SEBI gets statutory status
events.summary: SEBI, set up in 1988, becomes a statutory regulator for the securities market by the SEBI Act, 1992 (ordinance of 30 January 1992).
events.detail:
Protects investors; regulates stock exchanges.

**Exam hooks:** SEBI Act 1992; Harshad Mehta scam context.
causes: Harshad Mehta securities scam (1992).
outcomes: Controller of Capital Issues abolished (1992); market reforms.
events.yearHook: 1988 non-statutory → 1992 statutory.

events.title: S.R. Bommai v. Union of India
events.summary: In S.R. Bommai v. Union of India (11 March 1994) a 9-judge bench rules that President's Rule under Article 356 is open to judicial review, that majority must be tested on the floor, and that secularism is a basic feature.
events.detail: S.R. Bommai's Karnataka government had been dismissed in 1989 without a floor test. The Court upheld the dismissal of the BJP governments after the Ayodhya demolition (1992) because secularism is part of the basic structure. It drew on the Sarkaria Commission.
causes: Misuse of Article 356 (Kerala 1959, NTR 1984, Karnataka 1989).
outcomes: Far fewer arbitrary dismissals of state governments.
events.yearHook: Kerala 1959 → AP 1984 → Bommai 1994.

participants.role: His 1984 dismissal was an example of misuse.

events.title: PSLV's first successful flight
events.summary: The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle makes its first successful flight on 15 October 1994 from Sriharikota, after a failed first flight in 1993; it becomes ISRO's workhorse.
events.detail:
Later launched Chandrayaan-1 & Mangalyaan; 104-satellite record (2017).

**Exam hooks:** PSLV workhorse; GSLV for heavier/geostationary payloads.
causes: Need to launch remote-sensing satellites in polar orbit.
outcomes: Launched Chandrayaan-1 (2008), Mangalyaan (2013) and a record 104 satellites (2017).

events.title: India joins the WTO
events.summary: India becomes a founder member of the World Trade Organization on 1 January 1995, after the Uruguay Round (Marrakesh Agreement, 1994) replaced GATT.
events.detail:
Rules on trade, TRIPS, agriculture and services.

**Exam hooks:** WTO (1995) HQ Geneva; India uses the peace-clause on MSP/food security.
causes: Uruguay Round of GATT (1986–94).
outcomes: Patent law changed (2005); tariffs cut; TRIPS obligations.
events.yearHook: GATT 1947 → WTO 1995.

events.title: Vishaka Guidelines on workplace harassment
events.summary: In Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997) the Supreme Court, under Chief Justice J.S. Verma, lays down binding guidelines against sexual harassment at the workplace until a law is made.
events.detail: The case arose from the gang-rape of Bhanwari Devi, a social worker in Rajasthan who tried to stop a child marriage (1992). The Court used CEDAW and Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21. The POSH Act (2013) replaced the guidelines.
causes: The Bhanwari Devi case (1992).
outcomes: POSH Act, 2013.
events.yearHook: Vishaka 1997 → POSH 2013.

participants.role: Chief Justice who led the bench.

events.title: Pokhran-II (Operation Shakti)
events.summary: India conducts five nuclear tests at Pokhran on 11 and 13 May 1998 (Operation Shakti) and declares itself a nuclear weapon state (NCERT).
events.detail: India had opposed the indefinite extension of the NPT (1995) and refused to sign the CTBT (NCERT). The tests, ordered by the Vajpayee government, were led by A.P.J. Abdul Kalam (DRDO) and R. Chidambaram (Atomic Energy Commission). Pakistan tested at Chagai on 28 May. The US and others imposed sanctions. India declared "no first use" and a moratorium on further tests.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 4 "India's External Relations"
causes: Discriminatory NPT and CTBT regime (NCERT).
Security threats from China and Pakistan.
outcomes: India a declared nuclear power (NCERT).
Sanctions; Pakistan's tests; later the Indo-US nuclear deal (2008).
11 May is National Technology Day.
events.yearHook: Pokhran-I 1974 (Indira) → Pokhran-II 1998 (Vajpayee).

events.title: BrahMos supersonic cruise missile
events.summary: BrahMos, the India–Russia supersonic cruise missile (named after the Brahmaputra and Moskva rivers), is first test-fired on 12 June 2001 from Chandipur.
events.detail:
Named after the Brahmaputra & Moskva rivers.

**Exam hooks:** BrahMos (DRDO + NPOM); now exported (Philippines).
causes: India–Russia joint venture (1998).
outcomes: Inducted by the army, navy and air force; exported to the Philippines.
events.yearHook: JV 1998 → first test 2001.

participants.role: Signed the joint venture as DRDO chief.

events.title: FRBM Act, 2003
events.summary: The Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management Act (August 2003) commits the Centre to cutting the fiscal deficit (target 3% of GDP) and ending the revenue deficit.
events.detail:
Targets for fiscal & revenue deficits.

**Exam hooks:** FRBM (2003); N.K. Singh Committee review.
causes: High deficits in the 1990s.
outcomes: In force July 2004; targets relaxed after 2008; reviewed by the N.K. Singh committee (2016).
events.yearHook: FRBM 2003 — same year as the 91st Amendment.
facts: 91st Amendment caps the size of ministries at 15% of the House and tightens the anti-defection law.

events.title: Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy becomes CM
events.summary: After his 2003 padayatra, Y.S. Rajasekhara Reddy leads the Congress–TRS alliance to victory and becomes CM on 14 May 2004; his welfare schemes include free power to farmers, Jalayagnam and Rajiv Arogyasri.
events.detail:
His Praja Prasthanam padayatra (April–June 2003) covered about 1,500 km in the summer heat. As CM he gave free electricity to farmers, began Jalayagnam (a large irrigation programme including Polavaram and Pranahita–Chevella), Rajiv Arogyasri health insurance (2007), Indiramma houses and fee reimbursement for students.

He was re-elected in 2009 but died in a helicopter crash in the Nallamala forest on 2 September 2009. K. Rosaiah succeeded him.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Drought and farm distress under the previous government.
outcomes: Arogyasri became a model for other states.
His death (2009) revived the Telangana movement.

alsoOn.text: YSR's Praja Prasthanam padayatra (about 1,500 km).
YSR re-elected; dies in a helicopter crash in Nallamala (2 September 2009); K. Rosaiah CM.
N. Kiran Kumar Reddy becomes CM (25 November 2010).

events.yearHook: Padayatra 2003 → CM 2004 → died 2009.
facts: YSR's Indira Prabha scheme aimed at developing uncultivable barren lands of the poor (APPSC Group-II 2018 key).

events.title: MGNREGA enacted
events.summary: The National Rural Employment Guarantee Act (September 2005) gives every rural household a legal right to 100 days of wage work a year; it is launched on 2 February 2006 at Bandlapalli in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh.
events.detail: PM Manmohan Singh launched it in 200 districts; it covered the whole country by 2008. Work must be given within 15 days of asking, within 5 km, with a third of jobs for women; otherwise an unemployment allowance is due. It was renamed after Mahatma Gandhi on 2 October 2009.
causes: Rural distress; UPA's Common Minimum Programme.
outcomes: World's largest public-works programme.
Social audits pioneered in Andhra Pradesh.

alsoOn.text: NREGA launched at Bandlapalli, Anantapur district, AP (2 February 2006).

events.yearHook: Act 2005 → launch 2006 → renamed 2009.

participants.role: UPA chairperson who pushed for it.
The scheme was renamed after him (2009).

events.title: Right to Information Act, 2005
events.summary: The Right to Information Act, 2005 comes into force on 12 October 2005, letting any citizen ask for information from public authorities, to be given within 30 days.
events.detail: The Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan of Aruna Roy began the demand in Rajasthan's villages in the 1990s. Tamil Nadu (1997) and other states passed laws first; the weak Freedom of Information Act (2002) was replaced. Information Commissions hear appeals.
causes: MKSS campaign (1990s).
outcomes: Central and State Information Commissions.
A powerful tool against corruption.

events.title: Chandrayaan-1 finds water on the Moon
events.summary: Chandrayaan-1, India's first Moon mission, is launched by PSLV-C11 from Sriharikota on 22 October 2008; its instruments help confirm water molecules on the Moon (2009).
events.detail: Its Moon Impact Probe hit the lunar surface on 14 November 2008 carrying the Indian flag. NASA's Moon Mineralogy Mapper on board detected water. Contact was lost in August 2009.
causes: ISRO's planetary programme.
outcomes: Chandrayaan-2 (2019) and Chandrayaan-3 (2023, south pole landing).
events.yearHook: Chandrayaan-1 2008 → Mangalyaan 2013.

events.title: 97th Amendment — Co-operative societies
events.summary: The 97th Amendment (2011) makes forming co-operative societies a fundamental right (Article 19(1)(c)), adds Article 43B and a new Part IXB on co-operatives.
events.detail:
Some provisions later struck down for states' domain.

**Exam hooks:** 97th (2011) → co-operative societies.
causes: Need for democratic, autonomous co-operatives.
outcomes: Part IXB was partly struck down for state co-operatives (Gujarat HC 2013, upheld by the Supreme Court 2021).
events.yearHook: 97th Amendment, 2011.

events.title: Mangalyaan (Mars Orbiter Mission)
events.summary: The Mars Orbiter Mission (Mangalyaan) is launched on 5 November 2013 and enters Mars orbit on 24 September 2014, making India the first country to succeed at its first attempt and the first in Asia to reach Mars.
events.detail:
Most cost-effective interplanetary mission at the time.

**Exam hooks:** MOM (2013); India = first Asian & first-attempt success at Mars.
causes: ISRO's planetary programme.
outcomes: Low cost (about ₹450 crore).

alsoOn.text: Mangalyaan enters Mars orbit (24 September 2014).

events.yearHook: Launched 2013, reached Mars 2014.

events.title: APCRDA & Amaravati capital region
events.summary: After choosing the Vijayawada–Guntur region (Amaravati) as capital in September 2014, Andhra Pradesh sets up the AP Capital Region Development Authority by an Act of December 2014; Modi lays the foundation stone on 22 October 2015.
events.detail: The Sivaramakrishnan committee (August 2014) had warned against concentrating the capital on fertile delta land. The state chose Amaravati on the Krishna, named after the ancient Satavahana-era Buddhist site, and acquired land through a land-pooling scheme (2015).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Section 6 of the AP Reorganisation Act.
outcomes: Land-pooling scheme (2015).
Foundation stone at Uddandarayunipalem (22 October 2015).

alsoOn.text: Narendra Modi lays the foundation stone of Amaravati (22 October 2015).

events.yearHook: Chosen September 2014 → APCRDA December 2014 → foundation October 2015.

events.title: AP–Telangana Krishna/Godavari water sharing
events.summary: The AP Reorganisation Act sets up the Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards under an Apex Council (Union Water Resources Minister and both CMs) to manage water between AP and Telangana.
events.detail: The boards regulate projects listed in the Act; new projects need the Apex Council's approval. Disputes later arose over Telangana's Kaleshwaram and Palamuru–Rangareddy projects and AP's Pothireddypadu and Rayalaseema lift schemes. The Krishna Water Disputes Tribunal (Brijesh Kumar) was asked to divide AP's share between the two states.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Sections 84–89 of the AP Reorganisation Act.
outcomes: KRMB at Hyderabad (later Visakhapatnam proposed), GRMB at Hyderabad.
events.yearHook: Boards from 2014.

events.title: AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 passed
events.summary: Parliament passes the Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Bill (Lok Sabha 18 February, Rajya Sabha 20 February 2014); with the President's assent on 1 March 2014 it becomes the Act that creates Telangana.
events.detail:
The AP Assembly had rejected the draft bill (January 2014), but under Article 3 its view is not binding. CM Kiran Kumar Reddy resigned on 19 February, and President's Rule was imposed on 1 March 2014.

Key provisions: Telangana with 10 districts and residual Andhra Pradesh with 13; Hyderabad the common capital for up to ten years (Section 5); an expert committee to advise on AP's new capital (Section 6; K.C. Sivaramakrishnan); special packages for Rayalaseema and north coastal Andhra (Section 46); Polavaram a national project (Section 90); Krishna and Godavari River Management Boards under an Apex Council (Sections 84–85); a common High Court and Governor at first; and the Thirteenth Schedule promises of new national institutions (IIT, IIM, NIT, AIIMS, central and tribal universities) and infrastructure (a steel plant at Kadapa, a port at Dugarajapatnam, a new railway zone).
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: The Telangana movement (1969, 2009–13).
Union cabinet decision (3 October 2013).
course: January 2014: AP Assembly rejects the bill.
18 February: Lok Sabha passes it.
19 February: Kiran Kumar Reddy resigns.
20 February: Rajya Sabha passes it; PM promises Special Category Status.
1 March 2014: President's assent; President's Rule in AP.
outcomes: Telangana formed on 2 June 2014.
Seven Polavaram-affected mandals of Khammam moved to AP (2014).
Lok Sabha seats: AP 25, Telangana 17; Assembly seats: AP 175, Telangana 119.
events.yearHook: 18 February (LS) → 20 February (RS) → 1 March (assent) → 2 June 2014.
events.before: The Union cabinet had approved Telangana (October 2013); the AP Assembly rejected the bill (January 2014), which was not binding under **Article 3**.
events.after: Telangana formed on **2 June 2014**. Hyderabad stayed the common capital for up to 10 years (ended 2 June 2024). **Polavaram** was made a national project; the special category promise led to years of politics.
events.today: Many issues in the Act's **Schedules IX and X** (division of institutions) are still being settled between the two states.
events.mnemonic: Act numbers "AP 13-25-175, Telangana 10-17-119": districts, Lok Sabha seats, Assembly seats.

events.title: AP Special Category Status demand
events.summary: On 20 February 2014 PM Manmohan Singh promises in the Rajya Sabha that residual Andhra Pradesh will get Special Category Status for five years; it is never granted.
events.detail: Special Category Status gave hill and border states a 90:10 share in central schemes and tax breaks. The Fourteenth Finance Commission (2015) did not distinguish special and general states, and the Centre announced a "special assistance" package instead (September 2016). The demand remained a major issue in AP politics.
events.source: Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: Loss of Hyderabad's revenue after bifurcation.
outcomes: Special assistance package (2016) instead.
TDP left the NDA over it (2018).

alsoOn.text: Centre announces a special assistance package for AP instead of SCS.

events.yearHook: Promised February 2014.
events.before: The PM's promise of 20 February 2014 was made in the Rajya Sabha, not written into the Act.
events.after: The **14th Finance Commission** ended the special-general distinction in its formula; a **special assistance** package came in 2016. The TDP left the NDA over this in 2018 and rejoined in 2024.
events.today: Special status remains a live demand in AP politics.

events.title: Appointed Day — Telangana & residual AP
events.summary: On the Appointed Day, 2 June 2014, Telangana becomes India's 29th state (NCERT) with K. Chandrasekhar Rao as its first CM; Chandrababu Naidu is sworn in as CM of residual Andhra Pradesh on 8 June 2014.
events.detail: President's Rule ended in both states. E.S.L. Narasimhan was the common Governor; the High Court at Hyderabad served both until 2019, when AP got its own High Court at Amaravati. AP lost Hyderabad, its main revenue and IT centre, and had to build a new capital.
events.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"; Andhra Pradesh history (AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi syllabus)
causes: AP Reorganisation Act, 2014.
outcomes: Telangana: 10 districts, capital Hyderabad.
Residual AP: 13 districts; new capital Amaravati announced (September 2014).
events.yearHook: 1 November 1956 together → 2 June 2014 apart: 57½ years.
events.before: The **AP Reorganisation Act** (March 2014) set 2 June as the Appointed Day.
events.after: Residual AP chose **Amaravati** as capital (2015), lost the three-capital years (2019–24) and returned to Amaravati. AP got its own High Court at Amaravati (1 January 2019).
events.today: Telangana is India's 29th state formed (now one of 28 states after J&K became a UT in 2019).

events.title: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana
events.summary: Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana, announced on 15 August 2014, is launched on 28 August 2014 to give every household a bank account with RuPay card and insurance.
events.detail:
Backbone of Direct Benefit Transfer (JAM trinity).

**Exam hooks:** PMJDY (2014); JAM = Jan Dhan-Aadhaar-Mobile.
causes: Financial exclusion of the poor.
outcomes: Guinness record for most accounts opened in a week; basis of the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan–Aadhaar–Mobile).
events.yearHook: Announced 15 August → launched 28 August 2014.

events.title: Swachh Bharat Mission launched
events.summary: Swachh Bharat Mission is launched on 2 October 2014, Gandhi's birthday, to make India open-defecation-free by 2 October 2019.
events.detail:
Rural & urban components; toilets & solid-waste management.

**Exam hooks:** SBM (2014); ODF declarations.
causes: Poor sanitation.
outcomes: Over ten crore toilets built; ODF declared in 2019.
events.yearHook: Gandhi Jayanti 2014 → 150th Jayanti 2019.

events.title: Amaravati chosen as AP's greenfield capital
events.summary: Amaravati on the Krishna designated the new capital; land-pooling model.
events.detail:
APCRDA & the land-pooling scheme aggregated farmland from farmers.

**Exam hooks:** Amaravati capital; land-pooling (not acquisition); strained state finances.
outcomes: Foundation stone laid by Narendra Modi at Uddandarayunipalem (22 October 2015).
events.yearHook: Chosen 2014 → foundation 22 October 2015.
events.before: The **Sivaramakrishnan Committee** (2014) studied capital options; the state chose a greenfield capital between Vijayawada and Guntur.
events.after: Farmers gave about 33,000 acres under **land pooling**. Work slowed after 2019 when the three-capital plan was announced; it restarted after 2024.
events.today: Amaravati takes its name from the ancient Satavahana-era Buddhist town (Dharanikota-Amaravati) nearby.

events.title: Amaravati as an ancient toponym revived
events.summary: The new capital revives the name of the ancient Buddhist Amaravati.
events.detail:
Links modern statehood to Satavahana-era heritage.

**Exam hooks:** Amaravati — ancient stupa town & modern capital both on the Krishna.
events.before: **Dharanikota-Amaravati** was the Satavahana-era Buddhist centre (Dhanyakataka), with the great **Amaravati Stupa**.
events.after: The Dalai Lama held the **Kalachakra** at Amaravati (2006). The new capital (2015) took the ancient name.
events.today: Amaravati sculptures are in the Chennai Government Museum and the British Museum, London.

events.title: Godavari & Krishna Pushkaram traditions
events.summary: Twelve-yearly river festivals draw millions to AP's riverbanks.
events.detail:
Rajahmundry (Godavari) & Vijayawada (Krishna) are focal points.

**Exam hooks:** Pushkaram = river festival every 12 years.
outcomes: Godavari Pushkaram 2015 (Rajahmundry); Krishna Pushkaram 2016.
events.yearHook: Pushkaram comes once in 12 years for each river.
events.before: Pushkaralu are held at each of 12 rivers in turn, when Jupiter enters a given zodiac sign — so each river's turn comes once in 12 years.
events.after: A stampede at Rajahmundry on the first day of the 2015 Godavari Pushkaralu killed 27 people; crowd management became a policy issue.
events.today: Godavari Pushkaralu next in 2027; Krishna Pushkaralu in 2028.

events.title: NITI Aayog replaces the Planning Commission
events.summary: A think-tank for cooperative & competitive federalism.
events.detail:
No longer allocates funds; advisory & monitoring role.

**Exam hooks:** NITI = National Institution for Transforming India; Governing Council of CMs.
outcomes: Prime Minister is chairperson; focus on cooperative federalism.
events.yearHook: Planning Commission 1950 → NITI Aayog 1 January 2015 (NCERT).

events.title: NJAC struck down; collegium retained
events.summary: SC voids the 99th Amendment/NJAC — judicial-appointments primacy retained.
events.detail:
Reaffirmed judicial independence as basic structure.

**Exam hooks:** collegium system continues; NJAC (2014) unconstitutional (2015).
outcomes: The collegium system of judges' appointment continues.
events.yearHook: 99th Amendment (2014) → struck down 16 October 2015.

events.title: Paris Climate Agreement
events.summary: Global pact to limit warming to well below 2°C; India ratified 2016.
events.detail:
Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs).

**Exam hooks:** India's Panchamrit & net-zero-2070 at COP26.

events.title: 101st Amendment — Goods & Services Tax
events.summary: Constitutional basis for GST; creates the GST Council (Article 279A).
events.detail:
One-nation-one-tax; concurrent taxing power for the Union & States.

**Exam hooks:** 101st Amendment (2016) → GST rollout 1 July 2017.
outcomes: GST Council under Article 279A; GST from 1 July 2017.
events.yearHook: Amendment 2016 → GST from 1 July 2017.

events.title: Visakhapatnam–Chennai Industrial Corridor
events.summary: First phase of the East Coast Economic Corridor (ADB lead partner).
events.detail:
India's first coastal economic corridor; aligned with the Golden Quadrilateral.

**Exam hooks:** VCIC = ECEC phase-1; ADB partner.

events.title: Demonetisation of ₹500 & ₹1000 notes
events.summary: High-value notes withdrawn to curb black money & counterfeiting; push to digital.
events.detail:
Upheld by the SC (Jan 2023) as within the government's power.

**Exam hooks:** demonetisation 8 Nov 2016; boosted UPI/digital payments.

events.title: Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 2016
events.summary: Unified, time-bound framework to resolve corporate insolvency.
events.detail:
NCLT adjudicates; improved ease-of-doing-business ranking.

**Exam hooks:** IBC (2016); resolution vs liquidation.

events.title: Inflation-targeting framework (MPC)
events.summary: RBI adopts a 4% (±2%) CPI target; Monetary Policy Committee created.
events.detail:
Statutory MPC under the RBI Act amendment.

**Exam hooks:** flexible inflation targeting; repo rate as the policy tool.

events.title: Startup India launched
events.summary: Ecosystem push for startups — funding, tax breaks, ease of compliance.
events.detail:
Complements Make in India & Digital India.

**Exam hooks:** Startup India (2016); India = 3rd-largest startup ecosystem.

events.title: UPI transforms digital payments
events.summary: NPCI's Unified Payments Interface enables instant mobile payments.
events.detail:
Now the world's largest real-time payments system.

**Exam hooks:** UPI (2016) by NPCI; boosted after demonetisation.

events.title: GST rolled out — "One Nation, One Tax"
events.summary: Goods & Services Tax subsumes most indirect taxes nationwide.
events.detail:
GST Council (Art. 279A) sets rates; multiple slabs (0/5/12/18/28).

**Exam hooks:** rollout 1 July 2017; CGST/SGST/IGST structure.
outcomes: Replaced many central and state indirect taxes.
events.yearHook: 1 July 2017 — midnight session of Parliament.

events.title: Puttaswamy — Right to Privacy
events.summary: 9-judge bench declares privacy a Fundamental Right under Article 21.
events.detail:
Overruled ADM Jabalpur; underpins the Aadhaar and data-protection debates.

**Exam hooks:** privacy = intrinsic to life & liberty (Art. 21).
outcomes: Privacy is part of Article 21 (nine-judge bench, 24 August 2017).
events.yearHook: 24 August 2017.

events.title: Triple Talaq struck down (Shayara Bano)
events.summary: SC voids instant triple talaq; law criminalising it follows in 2019.
events.detail:
Grounded in Articles 14 & 21.

**Exam hooks:** Shayara Bano (2017); Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act 2019.
